MIDSUMMER NIGHT. Mother of balms and soothings manifold. Quiet-breathed night, whose brooding hours are seven, To whom the voices of all rest are given. And those few stars whose scattered names are told, FAX off beyond the westward hills outrolted, Darker than thou, more still, more dreamy even,- The golden moon leans in the dusky heaven, And under her one star, a point of gold; MO all go slowly lingering toward the West, As we go down forgetfully to our rest, Weary of daytime, tired of noise and light. kb, it was time that thou shouldst come, for we Were sore athirst, and had great need of thee, Thou sweet physician, balmy bosomed night. --Bcribner's Magazine. A. LAMPIIIAN.
"GIVE A HAND TO YOUR BROTHER." Give a hand to your brother Wrestling with wind and wave, Eav,k,rly help another— You are saved that you may save!

Heavily seas are breaking O'er his drooping form, Hope is his heart forsaking, Help! warriors of the storm! Out of the depths of sorrow Calls he with bitter cry, Wait for no other morrow. But grasp him ere he die. Cometh no shining angel In swift, unwearied flight, With the voice of the glad evangel, Down from the courts of light. Hearts and hands that are human In pitying haste must move, Throw him out the rope of promise, Draw him with cords of love. Give a hand ta your brother Wrestling with wind and wave, Eagerly help another— You are saved that you may save! —Sunday 3fagazine. C. T. CARISEROOKE.

Vein Expectations—Prospectieg for gold. High Rent—A hole in the top of your hat. The Winter of our Discontent—Midsummer. In the game of life men most frequently play the knave and women the deuce. The man who rang the bell to give an alarm of fire when there was none tolled a lie. Soulful Youth (languidly): "Do you sing 'For Ever and for Ever?'" She (practically) : "No, I stop for meals." When rain falls, if she gets the bigger half of the \. Umbrella, they are lovers; if he take the bigger half, they are married. "What is the difference between a than who is shut up inside a country coach and one who is seated opposite two pretty girls? One misses the views, and the other views the misses. "Bridget, did you hear the door befl ?" ".Yis, mum." "Then, why 'didn't you go to the door ?" "Shure, mum, I don't be expectifn anybody to call on me. It must be somebody to see yersilf." "I was completely carried away with your sermon this morning," said a leading somnambulist to his pastor. "Ah, Yes," replied the minister, "so I observed, Into dreamland, too, wasn't it?" Wife 'with her head out of the second storey window, to husband at front door) : "Cant you find the keyhole. Henry ?" Henry (doubtedly): "No, m' dear. You mush've took 'tup itairsh wiz you." A young man who was to be married in church to a Miss Way, after a courtship of four years. privately re- quested the choir not to open the service by singing, "This is the way I long have sought." Mistress (to servant): "I want you to do your best to-day, Bridget, and have everything pat for to-night's dinner." Bridget: "Shim' an' oi wull, mum, fer it's Pat himself wat'll be here this blissed avenin'." "Jim," said an honest coal dealer to one of his drivers; Tim, make that ton of coal 200 pounds short. It is for a meor, delicate widow, ancl as she will have to carry all of it up two flights of stairs I don't want her to overtax her strength." "How much cider did you make this year ?" inquired one farmer of another who had offered a specimen for trial. "Fifteen barrels." was the answer. Another sip, "Well, if you had another apple you might have made another barrel." The ruin of most men dates from some vacant hour. Occupation is the armour of the soul. There is a satirical poem in which the devil is represeeted as fishing for men, and fitting his bait to the taste and business of his prey; "but the idler," he said, "gave him no trouble, as he bit the naked hook." /or want of self-restraint many men are engaged all their lives in fighting with difficulties of their own making, and rendering success impossible by their own cross-erained ungentleness ; whilst others, it may be much less gifted, make their Way easily and steadily, slid achieve success besimple patience, eananireity, and self-control. Young artist (to friend): "Charlie. do you see that lady and gentleman who are looking at my picture and talking in such low earnest tones?" Friend: "Yes." Young artist: "I wish you would saunter carelessly by and find out what they are saying. It looks like business." Friend (after sauntering carelessly by) : "She is blowing hien up, Gus. for taking off his flannels tee soon." EishopWilberforce rather plumed himself on remem- bering faces, and justly so. One day, however, he received a somewhat rude shock. A Hampshire lout appeared in a country church among the candidates. The bishop felt sure he had confirmed him before, so he leaned over and said very softly, "My boy, I think I have confirmed you before." The lad opened his great, wide eves and replied, " You be a liar." Wilberforce knew that this was only the ordinary way a clown knew how to deny what was not true. So lie was told to kneel down, and he was confirmed. There is n capital anecdote related of the late Emperor William. how his valet one morning, on presenting him his coat, ventured on the remark that it was about time his Majesty had a new one. Before replying to this, the Emperor examined his coat inside and out, and then asked how much it would be worth at an old clothes shop. The valet replied, "Three thalers, your Majesty !" Whereupon the Emperor, not wishing to keep his servant out of property which, according to Custom, was already his, at once handed him the three thalers out of his purse, saying, "Now. I suppose I have acquired the right of wearing it a little longer." A FIGHT WITH Al; ALLIGATOR.— One of my men rushed round from the back of the island andcried out, "stases, n'a dugout upset, an' de man calling for help." As lie spoke, a shrill halloo! and the cry of the boy was again heard from tilt direction. I followed the men round the island, apprehending nothing, and expecting to see the occupants of the canoe wading ashore, or again in- side of it. The man was standing in about four feet of water and mud, with paddle in hand, pushing and strik- ing at the water, while the canoe floated slowly down with the tide. The boy, still screaming, swam rapidly towards the far shore. "But why let the canoe drift away upside down when he can so easily regain it?" I said, speaking more to myself than the MeTIL Yet, as I spoke, there was a commotion in the waters, and the man, a powerful fellow, began bitting out with all his might at a huge dripping body, now slowly raising it- self a few paces before him. "fly heavens! an fillip. tor !" I cried, as the monster stood high out ot the water, the ugly head craned forward, and the two front legs battling with the doomed negro. "My gun and shot bag quick !" and suiting the action to the word, I tore round to the rock where I had left them, arid returned panting with the exertion, and earnestly excited, that I might be in time. Yes, there they were still, about 80 yards off, the man fighting for dear life, hitting out hard 'and strong, at the massive saurian but a few feet from him. The blows fell harmlessly upon the thick head and body of the brute while the man endeavoured to back farther away. There was not a foot between them now, aud it was impossible to fire, as with anxious heart I dropped on one knee, and tried in vain to take a true sight. It was impossible to do so, as the man's body was constantly covering that of the alligator in their struggle, so I fired widely several times in quick succes- sion, in the vain hope of frielitening the beast away. But my shots were unheeded, for they were soon abso- lutely entangled in an unequal wrestling match, as with a quick movement, the alligator threw itself upon the wretched man. "The boat!" I said, leut my men shook their heads. She was lying useless on an oozy bed of mud, and no amofint of poling would move her into deep water within at least an hour. So I continued firing, and then rushed desperately in the water, with the ides of wading towards the man. But it was useless. Ere I proefeded ten yards the mud and slush were up to my middle, and I could barely move my feet; so I returned to the shore. , It was too late to do anything, for slowly, but surely, the alligator was gaining ground; its neck and body were craning over the man's shoulder, while he tried to dig it off with his useless weapon. There ,as a momentary struggle, a sort of spreading wriggle, as though the alligator was putting still more weight into its body; a faint cry, a splash, and the water threw around a 'few circular rings as they sank beneath its surface. In vain I watched the water, with fajut hope of seeing the man rise once more to renew the unequal contest. Not a sign ner vestige again appeared, and below the dark surface of the silent stream the brute lay Sprawling above its unhappy victim until he was drowned.—Sierra Leone; or the White Man's Grave, by G. A. Lethbridge Banbury. WARRINGTON 'DIOCESAN INSTI-

The anniversary of the Clergy Institutions of the dioceses of Chester and Liverpool and the arch- deaconries of Manchester and Blackburn, was cele- brated yesterday, at Warrington. The proceedings commenced by the holding of a business meeting in one of the rooms of the Institution. The choir was occupied by the Very Rev. the Dean of Chester, in the absence of Lord Winmarleigh, the President, and there were also present—the Yen. Archdeacon of Macclesfield, the Yen. Archdeacon of Manchester, the Revs. Canon Birley, Canon Hopwood, Canon Robin, Canon Ward, Canon Livingstone, Canon Pen- rhyn, Canon Tonge, Canon Stowell, Canon Greenall, Canon Heywood, F. W. Willis (Rector of Warring- ton), T. Rigby, J. J. Langbani, E. D. Garven, H. S. Byrth, J. G. Haworth, A. P. Holme, E. H. Spooner, E. C. E. Carletorr, S. Wilkinson, H. A. Hignett, and IL A. D. div.head: -.S.HEPAL REPORT.
div.p: THE -.S.HEPAL REPORT.

The Retr. Canon Gyeenall (honorary secretary) read the annual report. It stated that they were met that day to celebrate the 191st anniversary of the,Charity. It was for the relief of the widows and orphans of the clergy ! who had officiated in their last sphere of duty in the dioceses of Chester and Liverpool, and the archdeaconries of Manchester and Blackburn. It also provided grants for the free ,education of the daughters of deceased clergymen in its branch institution, the Clergy Daugh- ters' School at Warrington, which was founded in 1844 —44 years ago. Since the last anniversary- four of the pensioners—one widow from Chester diocese, one from Liverpool, and two from Manchester—had died, and the names of two other widows from Manchetter had been withdrawn. Two Chester widows formerly on the list renewed their applications for as.sistd-nce, and there were ten new applicants—two from Liverpool and eight from Manchester. There were now on the list 20 widows and seven orphans from Chester diocese, nine widows and eight orphans from the Liverpool diocese, and 31 widows and 18 orphans from the Manchester diocese. This was a total of CO widows and 33 orphans, making altogether 93 applicants. There had been six free scholars in the Clergy Daughters' school clueing the year, two from each of the three dioceses Their school fees had been paid by the pension fund. The committee felt that the pre- sent satisfactory state of the Clergy Daughters' School fully warrants them in asking for increased support for it, that they might be able to extend its benefits, which are of such value to the clergy. The Powys scholarship had again fallen to a pupil from the Liverpool diocese. -The meeting would be asked to sanction pensions; dona- tions, and payments for free scholars in the Clergy Daughters' School to the amount of £2,145. The income of the Charity forlhe year ending the 31st of December last was as follows :—Special donations, - £6O 4s. Od. ; interest/on invested capital. £7ll 18s. 4d.; offertories, £565 2s. 7t1.; subscriptions, £7BB as. Od. ; unappro- priated fund from the Chester and Liverpool Dioceses Finance Association, £l7O Os. Od., making a total of £2,295 6s. 11d. This, compared with the income of last year, shows a falling off of £95 16s. Bd. on the total amount, but the offdrtories alone were £lO9 13s: 5d., and the subscriptions £lB Os. 6d. less than last year. Fortunately this was counterbalanced by- a small increase in the amount of special donations, and in the grants ! from the unappropriated funds of the Chester and Liver- pool Finance Association. But, in the face of increasing ! claims, it was, a serious diminution. The committee ! hope that it has only to be known to call forth increased effort on the part of the friends of the Institution, especially of the clergy of the different parishes. The Committee felt very strongly that if the Institutions did not receive the support to which they were entitled, it was owing in a great measure to the fact that their claims were not more generally made known, and advo- cated from the pulpits in the three dioceses. Mrs. Barley, of Allerton Hall, widow of the late Mr.. L. R. Barley, had intimated that under the wjll of her husband a legacy of £250 was bequeathed to The pension fund, and a similar sum of £250 to the Clergy Daughters' School, but both legacies were subject to her own life, and that of her son .after her. The Committee felt that they could not pass over in silence the death of their old friend, Mr. Quekett, the late Rector of Warrington. For 22 years he was the hon. secretary of the Parent Institu- tion, and on his resignation of that position he was unanimously elected a life member of the committee. His long ana faithful service to the Charity deserved the most grateful recognition, and ought never to be forgot- ten. The Committee regretted to have to report the death of Mr. Prescott, of Dalton Grange, whose loss they deeply lamented. In addition to the election on the committee of four clergymen and four laymen, who retire by rotation, but are re-eligible, there were five vacancies—two in the Manchester contingent of clergy- men, caused by the resignation of the Rev. Canon Pit- cairn and the Rev. F. B. Wright, and one in the Liver- pool contingent of clergymen, caused by the resignation of the Rev. M. Stevenson. Amongst the laymen Mr. Bidet,, in the Manchester contingent, retired, and the death of Mr. Vrescott caused a vacancy in the Liverpool contingent.—The report was adopted unanimously_
PENSIONS AND GRANTS.

The following pensions and grants were made : Chester-20 widows, £490. 7 orphans. £135, 2 free scholarships in the clergy school, £9O ; total for Chester, £715. Liverpool-9 widows, £293, 8 orphans, £145, 1 free scholarship. £45 ; total for Liverpool, £395. Man- chester-37 widows, £585, 18 orphans, £315, 3 free scholarships, £135; total for Manchester, £1i,035. THE COMMITTEE OF MANAGEMENT. - .

The following members of the Coml./a-ie.; •of Manage- ment, who retire by rotation, were re-elected :—The Revs. Canon Robin, and Canon Heron for Chester; Canon Maclure for Manchester, and Canon Eyre for Liverpool. The following retiring laymen were re- elected :—Mr. Henry Stanton, General Sir R. Wilbra- hard, K C. 8., and Lord Winmarleigh for Manchester, and Dr. Watkins for Liverpool. Canon Pitcairn and the Rev. F. B. Wright resigned from the committee. The meeting appointed in their places Bishop Cramer Roberts (illackhurnl, and the Rev. G. W. Reynolds, The Rector of Warrington was elected in place of the Rev. M. Ste- venson, who retired. Messrs. George Blaithwayt and H. Woodcock were also appointed to vacancies on the committee.
THE NEXT PREACHER': It was stated that tlfe Dean of Chester would be the preacher next year, and that General Sir It. Wilbraham had been selected as President of the Institutions for the year 1889.
FUTURE ANNIVERSARIES.

It was resolved, on the motion of ARCHISEACON of MACCLESFIELD, seconded by the ARCHDEACON of MAN- CHESTER, that in future the anniversary be held on the thitd Thursday in July instead of the first Thursday in August.
NOTICE OF DIOTION.
The Rev. CANON -S-T-0-IVEL-L-gaTe. notice that he would at the next meeting, propose that the clergy making an annual collection for the institution be regarded as mein. bers.
SERMON AT THE PARISH CHITRCH.

Those present then adjourned to the Parish Church, where a service was held, and a collection, realising £26 110 s id, made in aid of the clergy institutions. The nis- i hop of Manchester (the Right Rev. James Moorhouse, DJ).) preached from I. Samuel, iii., 21. Referring to the Clergy Institutions, the Bishop said in a pure-minded and good man there was no anxiety so keen as that ex- perienced at the thought of leaving unprovided his loved ones—his wife and his children. The income of a clergy- man usually was not too large forthesupportof a family, after deducting from it all that he gave to charities. And that being so, it was surely necessary and right, and in accordance with the precepts of the most en- lightened self-interest, that they who bad been given freely of this world's goods should help the clergy, and should minister to them of the good things of God.
THE LUNCHEON. '

Lunch was afterwards served in the Institution. Lord Winmarleigh presided, and there were a nuluber of ladies present. After lunch the president proposed the "health of the Bishop of Manchester," who responded briefly-, and expressed his pleasure at being present. He thought that such meetings as that did much to broaden one's experienceh of his fellows, and was good for them

The inquirylby the Manchester Deputy City Coroner touching the death of Frank Cullen, of Glossop,who died at the Manchester Royal Infirmary from injuries received in the Hyde junction railway accident, was concluded on Wednesday. The jury nturned a verdict of "Acci- dental death."

HEAVY THUNDERSTORMS.-A heavy thunderstorm visited London and the home counties during Wednesday night. A serious landslip was caused on the Great Eastern Rail- way between Ilford and Chadwell Heath, stopping the traffic. The main streets of Romford were under six feet of water on Thursday morning. Great damage was also caused by the overflowing of the river Stort. On Thursday a severe thunderstorm passed over Flintshire, and three men, hay-making, were struck by lightning. From various parts of the country come reports of dis- astrous floods. Extensive damage has been done to pro- perty around Enfield. Several bridges were washed away in the south, and many houses are flooded. Many cattle, horses, and pigs were drowned, haystacks demo- lished, and crops destroyed.

div.head: WARRINGTON UNION ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.
div.p: WARRINGTON UNION ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.

The monthly meeting of this Committee was held at the Workhouse, on Friday morning. Mr. W. Darbyshire presided, and there were also present the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Messrs. Greening, Ratcliffe, W. Long, J. Houghton; J. C. Sutton (clerk), and W. Owen (valuer). ' APPEAL BY A PIIBLICAN.-Mr. Ankins, solicitor, ap- pealed on behalf of Mr. Richard Naylor, against the as- sesment of the Pear Tree Inn, Burtonwood. The present gross estimated rental is £73, and the rateable value is put at £63.—On the motion of Mr. GREENING, seconded by Mr. lieTcurvu, it was decided not to alter the assess- ment, a motion proposed by Mr. Houghton, seconded by the Chairman, that a reduction of £5 be made, having been rejected. _ _

WARRINGTON WATERWORKS COMEANY.—Mr. E. J. Nicholson, solicitor, appealed on behalf of the Warring- ton Waterworks Company against the following assess- ments :—Pipes, mains, &c., within he urban area, gross £3,600, rateable £3,060; pipes, mains., &c., *within the rural area of Warrington, gross £3OO, rateable £255; lodges, reservoirs, &c., Winwick, gross £9OO, rateable £675. Mr. Nicholson said the fact was there had been several increase's of assessment in the course of the last few years, and the last one was very serious, namely, as , regarded the municipal portion of Warrington, from I £1.980 to £3,096 rateable, and from £127 to £255 in the extra municipal—an increase of over £1,300 in [ Warrington alone. In addition to this they were heavily assessed for Winwick, and in the Che- shire townships. He supposed that as there were many technical details to be considered it' would not be possible for them to consider the appeal that day, but that they would refer it to their advisers. He added that the increases in the assessments had been so serious and frequent that they thought it was time to appeal against them.—The CHAIRMAN said he supposed that when the increases had been made from time to time the overseers had made them upon some system.—Mr. TUNSTALL (as- sistant overseer), said they had to some extent, but to a certain extent it was guess work.—Mr. Nicnor.soß thought Mr. Tunstall would admit it was very much , guess work ; he thought their system was to raise the [ assessment until the company objected.—lt was de- cided to refer the matter to Mr. Owen and Mr. Tunstall, who will report to the committee. COCKHE'DGE MILLS.—The VALUER reported with regard to Messrs. Armitape and Rigby's Mills, Warrington, that the assessment had been fixed by the Committee in 1881, after valuation, at rateable £2,704, with an abatement for partial occupation of £704, leaving the assessment gross £2,577 10s, rateable £2,000. Lately the empty space in the spinning mill has been filled up, and the weaving shed has also become more fully occupied, but In this shed there are still 2,176 square yards unoccupied. The overseers had raised the assessment to rateable £2,655, and Messrs. Armitage and Rigby appealed at their meeting in June last, when the matter was re- ferred to him (the valuer). He had gone care- fully into it, and had had several interviews with Mr. Robert Davies, who represented the appellants, and with their clerk, Mr. J. C. Sutton. Mr. Sutton and he had agreed with Messrs. Armitage and Rigby, subject to the_Authority's approval that an additional assess- ment of £3OO rateable should be made for the additional occupation of the buildings, making the assessment, gross £2,950, rateable, £2,3oo.—The report was adopted. FRIENDS' ScHoot., PENKETH.—The appeal against the assessment of this school—£l2o gross, £lO2 rateable— again came before the Committee, but, on Mr. Darby- shire, who represented the appellants, vacating the chair, it was found that there was not a quorum present and that, therefore, the matter could not, be decided upon. It was accordingly referred to Mr. Owen to re- port. This was all the business of public interest.

div.head: AN AWKWARD PREDICAMENT.
div.p: AN AWKWARD PREDICAMENT.

From school to work is a transition of considerable im- portance in the life of every worker. It is one of those events which Are never forgotten in after life however bad or treacherous the memory may be. It occurs at a time when the mind is very impressible, the character easily moulded, and when the memory is plastic and tenacious. Then, to a young mind there is a very striking difference between the surroundings of a school and those of a workshop, a warehouse, or a factory. In the former the sole object is the acquisition of knowledge, in the latter the acquisition of money. My first situation after leaving school was in a Lanca- shire cotton mill, before the enactment of the Ten Hours Bill. And one Saturday afternoon when all the wages had been paid, the machinery all cleaned, and the work- people all gone, the overlooker requested me to sweep the" weathercock " before leaving. This weathercock, as he termed it, was a sort of chimney or outlet for the dust and dirt wafted by means of revolving fans from the blowing-room below—an invention, I believe, of Richard Arkwright the second. It was easily reached by means of a ladder, and that part of the roof on which I had to stand being flat, there appeared to be no risk in the work assigned to me. In commencing operations I found that I Gellici not reach the back of the instrument without getting bodily into it. This I resolved to do, but had no sooner entered than to my astonishment and diimay, it swung round to the opposite side, from which no exit could be made. Seeing the dangerous predica- ment I was in, an indescribable feeling crept over me; but instantly recovering self-pbssession, I thought as it had turned so easily and unexpectedly from east to west, it would surely be possible to reverse it. But how? that was the question. To accomplish this desideratum vigorous jerking appeared to be the only means at hand. To do this I found it requisite to grasp firmly the pivot, lie on my stomach, and placZ'my legs outside. But even then, I failed to propel it back to its original position, though several times very near it. One attempt after another, in various attitudes, were made, but all to no purpose. Having exhausted my strength by these repeated efforts, I pulled myself together and began to think anxiously about my prospects of release. So far I had managed to retain self-possession, and was sufficiently cool and collected to call to mind incidents of difficulty and danger recorded in biography, such as Bruce and the spider. I felt cheered by the recollection of the, couplet— ' If one plan fail thee, try another, One effort more may clear the way. Summoning my somewhat recruited energies, I again made a series of desperate efforts to obtain a footing on the roof of the building, and at intervals shouted with all my might, but failed to make any one hear me. The mill, I may add, was situate on the outskiets of the town, and the "weathercock." with its occupant, were then facing the fields beyond, otherwise my signals of distregacould hardly have failed to attract the notice of some one. Some two hours had now elapsed since the accident occurred—hours of intense mental and bodily activity, and this activity having been altogether fruitless, I began to feel myself in a very unpleasant position. Am I doomed to remain here till the engine starts on Monday morning, and lose my life at last perhaps? I asked my- self. Then, the bare possibility—to say nothing of the probability—of spending two nights and a Sunday under such circumstances was horrible to contemplate. 1 fas suspended, as it were, over the side of a building six storeys high, and self-release appeared to be utterly impossible, unless I could plant my feet upon the coping stones, and thence reach the aperture in the roof through which I had ascended. For a short time I entertained the thought of attempting fhis feat, but was deterred by the reflection that I was unaccustomed to "giddy heights," and that one false step would be certain death. Then, I thought, if I am here on Monday I shall be smothered with dust, but that seemed preferable to being dashed to pieces. I had besides some faint hopes of attracting the attention of the night-watch when he made his rounds through the mill. While exerting:myself, bodily heat had been sustailed, but now, being still, I began to feel cold and chilly. Perched at a height of more than six storeys, without jacket and with an empty stomach, no wonder that one's animal beat diminished in the cold month of March.

The shades of evening were now hastening on apace. Some sparrows I had noticed on the building had re- tired to their nest. A church spire in the distance had become more shadowy, and night, the "sable goddess," was gradually rendering my peculiar situation still more distressing. Not a sound was heard, save an occasional whistle from a railway locomotive. With this exception all was silent as the grave. -• • • -
Better dwell In the midst of alarms Than in this terrible place,

I thought. The sensations thus experienced were such as no pen of mine can fully descQe. Never before, nor since, have I been subject to anything like them. When re- flecting on them, as I have often done since, I have been ready to eXclaim with the Psalmist, "We are fearfully and wonderfully mate." Thoughts of home and family took possession of my mind. I was more especially concerned about my mother, for I knew she would be the, greatest sufferer from my prolonged absence. Poor soul! she could not have imagined the situation of her missing boy, although, as I afterwards learned, she was apprehensive of some accident having happened. Inquiry Was made at the mill, and from everyone who was likely to know anything of my whereabouts. The inquirers were in- formed that the last person I was seen speaking to at the mill was the overlooker, and to his house they went. He had gone, some two or three hours before, to a public-house, and when found he was too drunk to speak coherently. Determined, however, not to leave , him until he had elicited some information, my father ir took the overlooker by the shoulders, and shook him 1 until he was sobered enough to exclaim "fan" and "weathercock." These two words put the inquirers on the right track. They went to the mill again, and, accompanied by the night watch, entered the building to inspect the fan and the weathercock. It was then midnight. I had heard the clock in the church tower strike twelve, and having given up all hopes of relief, for that night at least, I had yielded to a drowsy 1 feeling, when I was aroused by the sound of footsteps. , and familiar voices greeted my ear. "Thank God !" I ex- claimed, "deliverance is at hand." "I am here, father," I shouted loudly. "Keep still," he responded, ‘• don't move an inch until we bring you to this side." This was the work of a few minutes only. I could hear some one assuring my mother that her lad was safe and sound. _ _ .

Reader, I will not attempt to describe the scene that followed. Suffice it to say it was one the writer can never forget. It gave him new and ennobling views of human nature, more especially of woman, that "peer- less, price)ess, matchless dower of Nature's treasury." A. T.

div.head: HER BROTHER'S KEEPER.
div.p: HER BROTHER'S KEEPER.
BY MRS. J. K. SPENDER, Author of "Mr. Nobody," "Parted Lives," "Both in the Wrong," "Recollections of a Country Doctor," "Trust Me," &c.

div.head: CHATTER IIL A MOTHER S BEQUEST.
div.p: CHATTER IIL A MOTHER S BEQUEST.

It was with a piteous sense of disappointment and I failure—always hardest to bear in childhood, which expects so much—that Ursula awoke on the follow- ing morning. The downy pillows, soft blankets, and fine white linen sheets, though they excited her wonder, could do nothing to lessen the aching of her heart. For Ursula was practical as well as imaginative, and bid lair to develop. into one of those managing women who like planning and ar- ranging for the benefit of those they love. Now that her fairest scheme had collapsed like a soap- bubble, she was unprovided with any other outlook far the future, either for her suffering mother or her helpless little brother. She could not be sine even in the light of the early morning how much of what had happened on the previous day had been real, or how much was still a dream. Nor did it comfort her much that after being dressed again in the; old clothes so carefully brushed and mended by Mrs. Machurchan's atten- dants that she scarcely recognised them, she and Ray were driven back to Langbourne in a luxurious closed carriage, accompanied by a fine footman in livery, as well as a fur-coated coachman. It was, or • course' to be expected that either the carriage should vanish into thin air, or that it and all its grand appurtenances should turn into pumpkins and mice. And something of this sort actually did happen. Fol if the carriage did not vanish into thin air, it suddenly disappeared round a corner of a lane after the children had been put out to walk, before they came in sight of Langbourne. It was a very dejected little couple which walked in hand in hand whilst Peggy was paring the potatoes for the dinner; they fully expected a scolding, and dreaded above all things a return to school. But to add to the wonders of the previous day, Peggy said not a word of what had happened, going on with her potato-paring' and only 'looking a little curiously at the truants. More than once, indeed, she commenced an inquiry which she as abruptly broke off, and finally relieved her feelings by tramping about and banging doors. Nothing was said about school till the next day when Ursula put on her hat to prepare for her usual trudge. The old nurse stopped her, telling her she was not to go. "Why not?" asked the little girl,, a sudden light in her eyes. "There's them as knows," said the old servant oracularly. "Oh, then," said the child, its the fairy grand. mother?" Peggy looked round sharply. • " There's one thing as l'd advise ye—don't go talking none o' yer nonsense about fairy grand- mothers to your poor mamma—its upset her more than I've Seen her upset this many a day, let alone the puddings and things as come with the message, and which burns her up as she eats 'em, as if them -jellies were made o' Coals of fire. Couldn't I make her things as good, which would not give her they , feelings, poor lamb, after all she's gone through ?' - It was difficult to make head or tail of this apeeeh, but by degrees it dawned upon the child that the fairy grandmother must have sent a message to tell her mother not to be frightened on the night when she and her little brother had fled to St. Agatha's. Also that the various dainties suitable for an invalid (which suddenly appeared at the cottage) had possibly emanated from the same mysterious source. Though why these things should burn her mother was one of the mysteries which remained difficult of explanation—the more so that Ursula had stealthily tasted the jellies and found them agreealsleto her own palate—such childish peccadilloes never having been represented to her as wicked. There are some mysteries which, even in after life, must remain difficult of solution, and a practical little body like Ursula Campion will probably do wisely in asking no questions about them. Strange things continued to happen during that summer. Not only did jellies and cream continue to arrive at intervals, which their mother oddly re- marked seemed " as if they would choke her" when she tried to eat them, but one day the carrier called and delivered a parcel with a new serge frock for Ursula, and a cloth suit for Ray, to say nothing of a flannel dressing-eown for the invalid: trimmed with dainty lace. it like the bounties showered by the benevolent beast on Beauty; but in this case there was no Beauty as Ursula reflected, and the anonymous donor was scarcely likely to be a beast. 'Still there was an, interest in the g:fts whict savoured of' fairyland, and . Ursula could 'not . think' why her gentle mother should turn impa- tiently from the pretty pink dressing-gown—a marvel of millinery in the way .of ribbons and lace —and says complainingly, "Take it away, Peggy, I cannot bear to look at it. As if she did not know that I should value one kiss, dne word of sympathy, one line even in writ- ing, better than all these nameless gifts!" Ursula thought her mother capricious. Mrs. Campion's dejection rather increased than les- sened, though her cough Was somewhat better during the warm days of summer. The little ones were happy enough till th 4 season of autumn set in; then their childish superstitions returned in full force. Ursula had plenty of stories to tellstbout dragons and ogres who crunched the bones of 'their victims. These dismal tales multiplied with the shortening of the days,w hen the grasses ceased ,to flower, and the butterflies to perch on the blossoms; when the swallows were no longer toe be seen darting here and there in search of flies; when there seemed to be a new solemn stillness in the air; when the leaves were all aglow with the colour of death, and the wind whispered mysterious messages in the chil- dren's ears. For it was not only that the sunlight was veiledwith blue vapour rising from the valley, or with drifts of fleecy cloud, but Peggy would not let them venture near their mother's sick room. She hualied them in their laughter as they went up and down the stairs, and shewed utter indifference to the state of their wet stockings. Poor Peggy had never failed before in her duty to the children, but during the last few montlk she had been, as the Germans say, zersTlittert.— torn in pieces by the bewildering cares of life. All the time she could spare from her household duties had to be spent in the sick room, where her I mistress lay hour after hour, looking with her clear- cut features like a sculptured figure on a monument. Her deep eyes a little in shadow, with large black centres to the dark blue irises, and arched eye brows al- most as black, had a weary expressiou in them, as if they were tired of life. The thick masses of her dark brown hair were thrown back on the .pillow, and framed her well-modelled but proud and somewhat sad forehead. It was the set of her well-shaped head on the small slanting shoulders, and the delicate chiselling of the features which had led 'people to call her in her girlhood, the goddess. Badly dressed as she was—for she had refused to put on the pretty dace-trimmed wrapper—yet her garments, made by herself, still draped her, in spite of her emaciation, like an anti Tie statue. "You might get money if you chose as a model," her husband had said to her in one of those des- perate moods in which he could scarcely be held re- sponsible for the indignity to which The subjected her vide. " When you walk it is like Ifermione descend- ing from her pedestal, and your head is as small as that of the Venus de Medici." She vouchsafed no answer, but her delicate and mobile nostrils, which looked as if they had been chiselled in ivory; quivered as she turned her head from him. He had said too many Wings of this sort, and was too thoroughly out of sympathy with her for to. care much about them. would you like us to write to- Mr. Campion ?" Peggy asked, wistfully, one day late in October, when the wind had been .tearing furiously at the trees, and the children could wade ankle-deep through the dead leaves as they lay piled on one another; where they had drifted in the lanes. There were few flowers now, but velvety gray-green- nettles and., tall teazles, which held up their heads as if pre- tending to put a good face on it, and do their best to keep up a pretence of being alive through the winter. The insects had come to the end of their well-rounded

little lives, and cameo-like views of the distance could be seen between gaps in the hedges. "Would you like us to write ?" repeated Peggy, who had received no answer, doing her best to silence the little ones, who had come in with flushed checks and eyes as bright as those of squirrels, dragging branches with the fluffy seed vessels of the clematis, blackberry boughs that were still green, and fir cones which they had picked up, and which would soon be dry and brittle. There had been a time when Mrs. Campion had taken great interest in these things; but she looked away from them now, and she even looked away from her own, little ones, whose boisterous spirits were too much for her. There was a curious expression in
her face, almost bordering on a smile, m sly/ answered the old woman's inquiry, "No certainly; do not write to him. It must be warm and comfortable where he is in France," and she shivered.

Time was when she would have answered Peggy very differently; when—oblivious of the old woman's presence in the intensity of the anguish of her breaking heart—she had given utterance to the cry, "0 my God he is sorry he has married me 1" No human interposition had been of any use then, when a step couldstill flutter her pulses, and a voice had power to stir her heart. Peggy's own heart had often ached with a great grief for her young mistress. There had been times when she had even feared permanent alienation,of the intellect, when she had been called to Agnes Campion in some of those painful hours of prostration after passionate scenes of arguing, remonstrating, and sobbing. Even on such occasions the faithful attendant had dared to ask no questions. But the sight of the young lady, who had once been so admired, lying powerless on the sofa, with her beautiful eyes wide, open, and a look in them as if she were haunted by a perpetual vision of evil,.would have been enough to touch colder feelings than Pegu's. At suth seasons of abandonment, when the man who had sworn to honour and cherish her bad torp himself roughly from her detaining arms, she would look as if those eyes only were endowed with life and the vitality in the other parts of her body dying out. Peggy knew this was the beginning of fatal ill- ness. But she asked no questions then and she asked no questions now, when Agnes Campion gave her strange directions with regard to the message which should be given to her husband. "He is eating ices now with a party of favoured friends at the Maison Doree, and to-night he will pace the, streets of that glorified Paris, which he always loved so much, when the stars are shining. How I used to lie for the hour together and listen for his coming, and only hear the measured step of the sergeant de ville—What a fool I was I No, Peggy, we will not summon him just yet from his amuse- ments ; all in good time." The old woman assented wonderingly. She was used to these sorts of mood, when a strange, new light would kindle in her mistress's face; and she often wondered if those eyes, which she had known since Agnes Campion was a child, could be endowed with a, sort of second sight. For Peggy was a bit of a heathen, as Mrs. Ma clurchan had declared. The old servant had re- volted from the religious teaching of the elder lady's household.

For the mistress of St. Agatha's manor house Made the mistake which so many make of mixing up gloom and religion as inseparable, and I doubt if the early Christians would aave recognised ,her rigid formulae about trifles—her second Decalogue of "-Thou shalt nots"—as having iduch more to do with Christianity than poor Peg's heathenism. ' "Till the children to keep downstairs; I am not strong enough for them to-day; and, Peggy, I should not like them to have any recollection of me which would haunt their young imaginations by-and-by," said Mrs. Campion, as she authoritatively dismissed herold attendant.

"0 dear, what shall. we do next? She's woi9o than she's ever been," cried Peggy, wringing her hands, when the doctor arrived a few minutes afterwards. "My good woman, do not despair. You must do your best as you have done all the time," said Dr. Havard, with a face which was composed, and even cheerful a.susual, as he threw the reins to his groom and dismounted from his gig. He was brought into such familiar intercourse with the tragedies of life, that, in common with most members of his bene- volent profession, he never lost his presence of mind. ( He was not in the least taken aback when, with- out waiting for a mandate from him, his patient said to him quietly, whilst she looked at him with those shining eyes, 1 " Dectoi, the time has come. I would not let you ,send for the parson when you asked me, and, now it lis too late—l have only you." He rdid not 'deftly the statement, though he warned her not to over exert herself. Could he have succeeded in deceiving her he knew it would have made no difference? It was doubtful even if such a deception would have ensured her a couple of hoursmore of a troubled existence.

" Doctor Havard, I have never thought much aboufreligion. It is all such a mystery, and the people I --have loved here have treated me so badly they have lessened my faith in—in—" " In the love of a Heavenly. Father—that is your mistake," he said, bend'ug his head. " Verha_ps so ; it io all such a mystery. My husband laughed at such things ; but you were the first scientific man to tell Me that it did not seem to you ridiculous to believe that men and women have spirits within them which we do not see." He bowed his head once more and answered, " There you make a mistake again. It is because you have not mixed with our world, or you would know that there are very few scientific men who deny the existence of such spirit, and a great many who, like myself, believe that it exists and will survive' the body." There Was an interval of silence, during which she lay thinking. Then she added passionately. "I begin to think that if there is such a heavenly Father I ought to feel like Wolsey, that if I had served Hun half as faithfully—as—as I have served my—husband (she brought out the word with a jerk, it was so rarely she uttered it), He would not have deserted me."

"Be sure He does not desert you," said the doctor, gravely raising his eyes. "I have no one else to canfess to, and so I confess ti you. Perhaps ik there are—as I remember you once startled me by saying you thought . possible spiritual intelligences moving vast 'Rortions of the natural world which seemed to be inanimate— such messengers from God may take my confes- sions to Him. -

He was bound again to caution her, so pas- sionately did she give utterance to this cry of a hungry soul deserted by those who should have solaced it in the hour of trial. It was curious how ' well she had remembered the conversation, though Ids remarks had been couched in language which he ,scarcely eiipected her to understand. "You are right to warn me," she said, letting her head fall back again on the sofa. "It is selfish to . speak of myself, for I must reserve my strength. My kind friend, whenever you come to die, it may be a comfort to you to remember how a dying woman thanked you. When, all men forsook me and blamed me, you only remained kind to me. I think it was your kindness which made me first believe in the possibility of that heavenly love. And it is that kindness which makes me presume on you still. I cannot believe that.my mother, whatever she may have said about it, will, in the end, quite forget my helpress little childre,n. They must return to the care of a man who is as fascinating as he is un- principled, and, oh, doctor, you know if there is that, law which I used to read about in the newspapers and so many books, if the children—the innocent children —are to bleed for the sins of the fathers, it seemed to me so dreadful I never knew it before I was married ; but if—if it is true, then little Ray may inherit that frightful —" He interrupted her and hushed her excitement. He himself had thought much and often of that law of vicarious suffering, and of inherited predisposi- tions. His heart had cried out for mercy on the suffering little ones,. though he saw the law to be inevitable. " Nye do not see the end yet; we cannot judge till we see the whole. .You will know sooner than I. We must be content to wait with mysteries," he said, trying his best to soothe her, as she added with a gasping sigh, "It was when I first knew about this that I un- derstood how guilty I had been. Doctor, if you know any other. self-willed girls who will not take advice, tell them when they are fascinated by men utterly without principle that it is not Only their own lives they may ruin, but entail ecurse of suf- fering on children yet unborn." "hush, hush," he said, seeing how terribly she must have suffered, before she could bring herself twice to reiterate the same phrase about women who were "fascinated," and men "utterly without prin- ciple." He did not attempt to argue the matter with her he had to brace himself for what followed. He was prepared for it in a measure, and yet it was a heavy burden to lay on a man hampered with a large practice, who himself had been anxious to avoid the cares of domestic life.

It was hard to deny yourself the luxury of havinc• children of your own, and yet to undertake to look after another man's children, and that man an irre- sponsible sort of vagrant like Leonard Campion 1 The dying woman never knew the effort it cost Dr. Havard not to deny her when she entreated him to do his best to look not after the physical,but after the mental and moral needs of the young souls she left behind her.

"1 do not ask you to give them money—money is nothing to the care and attention you have given to me—their undeserving mother. But, oh, give me a faithful promise you will do your best to protect them from following in the footsteps of their tattier. What can I give you in return? I have nothing to Live you. I am portionless. disinherited. Perhaps in.

fleas-en as on eartn. But U some of yrour ideas Pren to be true, and if—if lam privileged to ask ger, angels to watch ovei you, think, in every treatnu` air, in every ray of light, that those ministrants al near who are yet privileged to look upon the faceo God." She was eloquent, as she hadbeen when he knewher first—a highly-educated girl,whose cultivated intelli- gence had been as remarkable as her beauty of form and face. It had been hard then to refuse her anr thing, and it was harder still now, when, vehe. mently, with her dying breath she was imploring blessings on his head. If he assented it was because he was human, and no man with any vestige of heart could have refused. "Kiss me," she whispered, like a child, when st last he got up to leave her. "I shall never see yes again with my earthly eyes !" And as he stooped and gently touched her marble forehead with his lips, he sealed a sacred contract with as pure a kiss as that which Michael Angel° might have pressed on the lips_of Vittoria Golonus',_ a last rite which the great painter-poet after-a-arcs lamented not having paid in one of the most touch' lug of his sonnets. (To be continued.)

div.p: FOREIGN NII;WS.

THE EUROPEAN SITUATION :—GERMANY AND FRANCE. ,BrroraN, MONDAY.—A Copenhagen newspaper having stated that the French despatch boat La Mouette was to 143 ave the harbour of Copenhagen before the arrival of the German Emperor in order to avoid the necessity of galuting the Imperial flag, the French Minister at Copen- hagen has publicly explained that the vessel in question Vas compelled to leave Copenhagen on pressing service. COPENHAGEN, MONDAY.—The King proceeded to sea early this morning, in the royal yacht Evannebrog, Ilscorted by number of ironclads and torpedo boats,

and met th(- German squadron at the southern entrance to the Sound. Hi.; Majesty and the Ctown Prince at once went aboard the Hohenzollern, and 'welcomed the I:niperor William to Denmark. The Emperor then re- turned with the King to the Dannebrog, which arrived here shortly before noon.

- COPENHAGEN, TUESDAY. The German squadron Weighed anchor at three o'clock this morning, and pro- oeeded to sea, escorting the Imperial yacht Hohenzollern, With the Emperor William on board. The King of Den- Mark has conferred the Order of the Elephant on Prince Henry, and the Grand Cross of the Danebrog Order,' set brilliants, on Count Herbert Bismarck. The German ttnperor distrihuted many dec,oratlons, including the Black 'Eagle, to Prince Waldemar. THE WHITE CAPTIVES IN THE SOITDAR OATRO, SUNDAY NlGHT.—Advices from Wady Haifa state that letters received from Omdurman throw quite a new light upon the situation of the white captives 'there. The Mandists are said to treat the European inisoners well, providing the latter do not attempt to escape or hold a clandeStine'correspondence with any- one. Abdulla Khalifa, the present Mandi, wishes to obtain aS many Europeans as possible to instruct his Sonaanese. and it is stated that within lour weeks five Europeans have been captured in the environs of Wady, Haifa. The kandi is declared to be amassing wealth by means of ransoms and the sums,recived for exemption of mili- tary services, and be is declared to have expressed his Willingness to release 'Lupton Pasha on payment of £3,000, and to liberate the other Europeans at prices varying according to their usefulness to him. FIGHTING 'IN AFGHANIS'rAN. CALCUTTA, SUNDAY Nrour.—Reports from the North- West cOnfirm the rumours of the massacre of Afghan Soldiers by the Shinwarris. The southern Ghilzais are again showing signs of restlessness, and the Ameer has sent reinforcements to Muickur. The Szamazai have re- __ _ _ . .

cently been severely beaten by trinra Khan, losing six of the most influential man and 2,000 cattle. Serious fight- ing has also taken place between the MeSlem and Kaffirs in the Dir district. 'A Kaffir chief en route to Cabul, to Visit the Ameer, has been assassinated. THE EMPEROR FREDIMICK. BERLIN, SUNDAY NIGHT.—The following semi-official denial is published in the Cologne Gaortte:—" The Berlin Papers are notnsharned to reproduce from a sensational London paper the story that Queen Victoria took with her to England the Emperor Frederick's diaries, and re- fused to deliver them to the Emperor William, in spite of the latter's express request. The story is too silly to • need explicit contradiction but it is sad to see that German journals should deem it right to spread such stories about the Emperor and Empress Frederick with- out taking the trouble to obtain authentic information on the subject:" THE CHRISTIANITY CELEBRATION IN RUSSIA. In connection -with the celebration of the nine hun- dreth anniversay of the „conversion of Russia to Christianity, it was decided that the festivities should last three days—the 27th, 29th, and 29th ult. On Friday the City ef Kier was brilliantly illuminated, and likewise the shore,of the Dnieper. The President of the Slavonic Society, Count Ignatieff, had induced the principal railway 'companies to issue gratis first-class return tickqs to all the foreign guests. The Austrian Blithe- Mans, orSittle Russians, who were expected to celebrate the day in their own country, and to send several depu- tations to Kieff, drew back at the last moment. They have made the satisfactory discovery that their ancestors were converted a century before the Great Russians. It is telieved in Russia that the Austrian Government rendered them invaluable assistance in making the discovery. A magnificent church was con- secrated on Friday at Khorson, near Sebastopol, on the Spot where Vladimir the Great was baptised. A great Meeting was held in connection with the religious fes- tival. when many priests attended from distant coun- tries. Numerous congratulatory addresses were read, including one from the Archbishop of Canterbury, TERRIBLE VOLCANIC ERUPTION. SITANMAI, FELD ty Nionr.—Details have been received of an eruption in the Bandaisan volcanic region, fifty leagues from Yokohama. Nearly 1,000 persons have perished, including 100 visitors to the thermal springs, and several villages have been destroyed. A fresh crater has been formed,- and is still casting up rocks and ashes. ILLNESS OF THE POPE. _

The'Pope contant-t-ei;eriousry—u-nwell", and it is stated that for the last week he has been losing strength. His Holiness has been suffering, from liver complaint, for whicivhe has been ordered to take mineral waters before Ms breakfast. Notwithstanding his indisposition, Le. XIII receives visitors and attends„ to ecclesiastical business. AN -EXTRAORDINARY ROMANCE AND TRAGEDY. An extraordinary drains has just occurred on the Lake Of Bienne, in Switzerland. A journeyman watchmaker, living at t-aint-Imier, had fallen vio!ently in love with a Young lady of the neighbourhood, who returned his Passion. She was of remarkable beauty. As soon as her family heard of the affair every attempt was made to Put a stop to the meetings of the couple. A day or two ago they contrived to elude the vigilance of the girl's relatives' and travelled together to Bienne. Where they passed the night. The next morning they hired a boat, and when they had got about two hundred Yards from the shore the mart was seen to attach the anchor rope to his companion's body, after which, pro- ducing a knife, he attempted to open the 'veins in her arm. Meanwhile. the spectators of this decidedly un• Peasant scene had sprung into the boats which were lying near, and were pulling with the utmost energy towards that in which the watchmaker and the girl Were

seated. Perceiving that they would not long be left to carry out their work of self-destruction unmolested, the man threw down the knife, and, seizing a revolver, fired twice at his companion, but without wounding her. Fie then turned the weapon against his own breast, and. seizing the girl round the waist, he sprang with her into the lake. Their would-be preservers arrived too late on the spot, and it was some time ere the bodies could be recovered. The girl and her paramour—who was a married man with four children—were tightly locked in each other's arms.

div.head: EXCITING _SCENE AT DOUGLAS.
div.p: EXCITING _SCENE AT DOUGLAS.

• \ As the last boat fey Liverpool—the Mona's Isle—left the Victoria Pier at nine o'clock on Saturday morning, , a visitor rushed frantically about, as though disappointed - at losing his passage, and exclaiming, "Who'll bring a boat to fetch me," dashed over the pier into the water. It sass low tide at the time, and the fall was about 30ft. from the pier, into about 15f t. depth of water. A great croyrd was present, and the excitement was intense St the .cry of a " man drowning," on bearing which the lines, life buoys, and other similar appliances were immediately put into request, and will- ing volunteers were at hand, foremost of whom was David Kewloy, better known as " Dawsey," who plunged off the pier without divesting himself of any clothing, and laid hold Oft the man, who by this time was unconscious (being in s fit). A lad threw a line to "Dawsey," but in doing to tumbled in himself. Then a boatman named Robert Nichols iumued in to the rescue of the lad, followed by J3l7tri Lewin. Five persons were then in the water struggling for life. It VMS raining hard at the time, with a heavy rolling surf dashing against the 'wall of the pier, and in its rebound washing the unfortunate persons seaward. " Dawsey," though a strong swimmer, and having been instrumental on several occasions in saving lives, was on this occasion nearly losing his own life. Fre helcren to the man with one ham), and though hampered by a Kee 1712 btly wound round the 'other hand, prevfmting him using it, he struggled on tenaciously despite the (lathing sea immersing him, in the hope of accomplishing his purpose. The steam ferry boats wore all lying at tine Battery Pier, and on bearing the cries for assistance the Jumbo cast off, and Was soon on the scene. but not a -moment too soon, for 4 Dawsev," with somewhat of a dea.th grasp of the man, was sinking with him when Me ,crew of the Jumbo banled both of them on board, as well as the other three. The man who caused the scene was still in a fit when rescued, nnd in that condition was sent to the hospital, :Where he receivti medical attendance and was dis- charged during the day. This is the 25rd life "Dawsey" %as been instrumental in saving. and yet, it is said, his !services have received no acknowledgment from either .the, Humane Society or any other source. Had not the 'Jumbo been onporttmely ready the whole five would un- doubtedly have been drowned, as from the rough state of the weather no boats were about.

RAPIDS.—The Umbria, which has arrived at Queenstown from New York, re- Ports that on the 14th inst. a gang of men, during a drunken freak, hoarded a driving, boat on the Mallawan River, and decided to run the raids. When in the middle of the rapids, the steersman took his paddle out Alf the water for an instant, and the current, which was terrific, swumg the-boat roand, and the 14 occupants were dashed to death on the rocks. div.p: IMMRIAL PARLIAMENT, ,

HOI.TSE DF LORDS.—MmmAr. The Lord Chancellor took his seat shortly after 4 p.M. Lord STANUtit of ALDERVEY inquired what steps had been taken by the Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal with reference to the conduct of Mr. Kirkwood, SesslonsJadge at Patna, who was alleged to have acted in an arbitrary i manner n a case in which a !Endo() girl was a COM- plainant.—Lord Caoss stated that Mr. Kirkwood had been severely censured, and was to be removed from the judicial service, though he had given notice to appeal. Lord MACNAGHTEN moved the second reading of the Fishery Acts Amendment (Ireland) Bill, which, under certain conditions, gives the Lord-Lieutenant in Council power to issue an order st'..kppin,g trawling.—Earl CADMAN said the Government regarded the bill as per- fectly inoffensive, and would give it their support-- The bill was read a second time. _ .
The Indian Council Art, 1876, Amendment fill having been read a third time and passed, their lordships ad- journed.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MoNnir.

The Speaker took the chair at 35 p.m. The House agreed to the Lords' amendments on the Manchester Ship Canal Bill. The Brighton Marine Palace and Pier Bill a the Preston Corporaffnn Bill (Lora) with an amendment opposed by the promoters, -were ordered for the third reading. Amid loud cheers from the Irish members. Mr. Dillwvn presented an enormous and extremely bulky petitien. from 63.000 adtilts of South Wales, praying for there- lease of Mr. John Dillon from gaol. The petition was 150 heavy that Mr. Dillwyn had to 'be assisted by Mr. Stuart Renciall in carrying it to the table of the House, where a short summary of its contents was read by the Clerk, amid renewed iheering from the lelsh benches. Mr. Brunner presented a similar petition. but not of such great volume, from the inhabitants of Wigan.

QUESTIONS. A question was addressed by Mr. JORDAN to the Chief Secretary, as to whether Colonel Turner, at tato evic- tions on the Tandeleur estate, ordered the soldiers to fire if the occupants of the beleaguered cottages did not comply with his demands.—Mr. BALFOVR admitted that Colonel Turner gave such instructions, Nit added that the rides of the soldiers were not loaded. They were merely pointed at the occupants of the dwellings in order to intimidate them.

SE-A'rou inanired whether the Chief Secretary was preparedto test thelinding of the coroner's jury in the Mandeville case, to which Mr. BAT.VOUR, amid derisive cheers, said he was quite prepared to do anything which might help the people of this country to come to a true conclusion in regarclto this subject. Mr. JORDAN pressed the Chief Secretary to grant an inquiry; and Mr. 'BALFOUR made an answer, which seemed to suatzeSt that he preferred to believe in the testimony of his own officials, rather than anything that could 'be said by the hon. member mentioned. Mr. aotuorow who was received with loud derisive cries from the Irish members, was imformed by Mr. Sigma that the Government could not advise the Queen to appoint a thanksgiving day for the deliverance of this country from the Spanish Armada. Mr. ANDRRSON inquired of the Chief Secretary whether in view of the verdict given by the jury on the Mande- ville inquest, the Government would suspend the official responsibld for his treatment.—Mr. BALFOUR replied that in his opinion the verdict of the jury was entirely unwarrantable by the facts laid before thern.—This announcement was received with loud laughter from tha Opposition benches.

The House then went into Committee on the Members ,of Parliament (Charges and Allegations) Bill. Mr. SEXTON moved the first amendment, that five judges sbotild form that Commission, instead of three. In addressing the House, the bon. gentleman pointed out the enormous work which the Commission would be called upon to no, if they were directed to inquire into the doings of the Land League in the various counties in which it had been established during the nine years of its existence.

The HOME SVCRETARY said he could-not accept the amendment. It was sufficiently serious that three judges should be withdrawn from their ordinary duties, but it was a still more seriou4 proposalthat five judges Should be required to leave the Befich.

Mr. PARNELL said this bill provided a substitute for a jury, but a jury in England consisted of 12, and in Scot- land of 15, men, and y,et the Government proposed to leave a matter of the most important'kirid, with far- reselling issues, to three judges, and therefore to make the 'decision practically depend upon two men. The SOLICITOR-GENERAL for SCOTLAND Could not see how the reasoning of the hon. gentleman held good in (Wring. for lay commissioners and then sneaking of "un- known barristers" as he did. Were the lay commis- Sioners to stay at home while the judges went abroad to take evidence?

'On a division the amendment was rejected by 233 against' 195. I Mr: W. H. Swum proposed that the commission should •consist of Site James Hannon, Mr. Justice Day, and Mr. Justice Smith. The names were put separately. To "Mr. Justice 'Flaneeifs appointment there was no demitr, but the name of Mr. Justice Day cave rise to a long,' animated, and somewhat painful debate.

Mr.' LABOLICHERE started the opposition 't7 quoting .some opinions reflecting upon Irishmen generkiiy which the' learned Judge in question was reported .to ImvP ex- pressed in connection with a case at Liverpciel in 188( —Mr. Asquvrit thought the Government should have ,consulted the Opposition 'soory! selecting the Jud,es, and Mr. T: P. O'CoNNoa st.t.Tested the withdrawal of Mr. Justice Day's name, a process which Mr. FINLAY -asserted would carry with it an imputatien.--Mr. W. H. SMITH asserted that he had never heard .a whisper against Mr. 'Justice Day's impartiality.—lt,.Temained for Mr. Jottx MORLEY to add a sensational •element to the discussion, which he did by quoting a lettevreceived, he said; from a high authority, wherein the learned Judge. ref erred to was described as a man of rlth Century views and." a Tory of the old high-flyer, non-juror type." Clamour was raised for the name of Mr. Motley's cor- respondent, and this was giyen to the House,-as it had been previously to Mr. W. IT Smith. It tumed;out that ' the writer qf the letter was Mr. Adams, vrho.rat with Mr. fiustice Day on the Belfast Riots Commission.—Mr. BALFOUR contended that the sole aim of the Government had been to secure Judges of absolute impartiality. The discussion was described by Mr. Gr.‘nTroxn as being-' odious and painful," and he added that' if the judges had been drawn by lot the GovernMent would have done' better with the composition of the Gominis- sion. He said: There are at least a dozen judges to none of WhOGI would objection ,have been taken or (Tit iciStn directed. 'This is not a question of Mr. Justice Day being convicted of any offence it is a question of a man being anpointed to an office of extraordinary delicacy and difficulty in the discharge of the duties of Which he is to be deprived of the aid and safeguards under which he has hitherto acted. The appointment must be•rubove objection or reasonable or rational suspicion, and -when' you say-the terms we require are too severe' my answer is that 'nearly every judge onthe bench will be regarded as absolutely, fulfilling these iconditions under these cir- enmatanoes. I lament that her Majesty's Government appear to have treated this as a sort of perfunctory duty without thcromsh and minut6 inquiry. He should, he said., give a distinct, decided, but paintul vote against the -appointment. Mr. Amaseseis moved the omission of the word "tithe- gations" in the second clause.--The ROWE SECRETARY defended the ,szse of the word, and Sir W. Ilincoom. spoke of it asthe letting in of every kind of tornado,of calumny.—Mr. WHITBREAD said the bill as it todd' would not enable hon. members to meet any charges. against them.,--Sir J. Goasr reViied that if the word' " allegationa" were not inserted the Commission migist refuse evidence of the authorship of the letters attr;-; buted to MT. Tomei!, on the ground that it was not a charge.—The Douse divided, when the amendment, was defeated by"2Bs to 200. Mr. IL T. limn -moved to add after allegations "of complicity with murder or violence."--The lioNs SECRETARY objeeted to toning down the inquiry. The Government wanted to refer the Whale matter alleged, , add there could 4lae nothing unfair in that.--Mr. CHAMBERLAIN declared that the amendment was not wide enough, and would met carry out the object of the mover of it.

div.head: "JUDAS. CHAMBERLAIN."
div.p: "JUDAS. CHAMBERLAIN."

- Mr. PARNELL, rising.shortly before 12 O'clock, said: I had not the opportunity of thanking the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Chamberlain) for the kind reference he made to me, and the lansoilicited character ii 3 was good enough to afford me on the last occasion of this debate. (Laughter and "hear, hear.") He spoke of days long ago when he entertained a better opinion of me than he is able to entertain now. 1 care very little as to the opinion of the right non. gentleman. (LaufAter and cheers.) I have never put forward other men to do dangerottS things which I shrunk from doing myself —(cheers),—and I l'ave never betrayed the secrets of my comrades in Council. (Loud cheers.) My Principal recollection of the right hon. gentleman before he became a Minister was that be was always most anxious to put me and my friends forward, to do work which he was afraid to do himself—(cheers),—and after he became a Minister my principal recollection of him was that he was always most anxious to betray to us the secrets and counsels of his eolleagues in the Cabinet —(cheers),—and to endeavour, while sitting beside those colleagues and while in consultation with them, to un- dermine their counsels and their plans in our interests. (Cheers.) If this inquiry be extended into these mat- ters—as I see no reason why it should not,—l shall be abundantly able to make good my words—(cheers),— both by documentary evidence—not forged—in the handwriting

At this moment-12 o'clock—Mr. Courtney rose and left the chair. There was a scene of intense exeitement. The Irish members cheered vociferously, and the eheers were mingled with derisive cries aildressed to Mr. Chamberlain, The expressions, "Infamous Chamber- lain," "Judas Chamberlain," rang through the Chamber.
