--- The right hon. gentleman responded by taking off his hat and bowing to 'the Irish members. When the Speaker tritered the House, Mr. JOSEPH CRAMBERIAIN said he regretted to have to cal/ the attention of the Speaker to a personal incident. The moment the debate was adjourned Mr. T. P. O'Connor made use of an expression of an offensive character used to himself in the House. He had called him 'Judas Chamberlain." That expression was subsequently repeated by Mr. Biggar. He often passed over such expressions, but on the present occasion the incident was so marked that it appeared to be his duty to call attention to it. Mr. PARNELL asked whether, as Mr. Chamberlain did not hear the expression alleged himself it was in order for him to call attention to it? The SPEAKER said that if the exp;ession was used, and IT the person against whom it was used brought it forward, it was his duty 'to take notice of it. Did the hens, member use the expression? Mr. T. P. O'Commn said he did. Mr. J. REDMOND explained that Mr. Biggar only re- peated the expression when Mr. Chamberlain asked what It was, as Mr. Chamberlain did not appear to have heard it himself. ' Lord HARTINGTON corroborated the statement of Mr. Redmond. Mr. T. P. O'Ccerson: I don't think! should be justified in asking the House to prolong this discussion. I think it was an expression I ought not to have used, and if you call on me to withdraw it I will do so. The SPEAKER: I hope under the circumstances the Rouse will permit this proceeding to go no further, the hon. member having expressed his regret. Mr. T. P. rreosNort: You rightly interpret my lan- guage, Mr. Speaker. The matter then dropped. The Consolidated Fund (No. 3) Bill was read a second time. After a 'long discussion on a Culross (-Perth) educa- tional endowment scheme, known as Geddes Trust, the Rouse rejected a motion made by Dr. Wallace to refer the scheme back to the Educational Endowment Com- missioners by 95 votes to 56, and adjourned at 1 40 a.m.
HOUSE OF LORDS. -TUESDAY.
The'hord Chancellor took his seat at 4 15.
—.— --- STANDING Orimins.—Earl CADOGAN proposed to Ralf the House to consider the report of the Select Committee on the Standing Orders on Thursday week.
THE LIBEL LAW AMENDMENT BILL.

Upon the report being brought up, Lard lIERSCHELL moved the emission of the words "a goad fide" before "public meeting," in Clause 4.—The amendment was negatived. 'Further on, in the same clause, Lord Tizascrtata pro- posed the substitution of the words" of public concern" for "published in the interest of the public."—Lord BRAMWELL said his noble friend's amendment appeared to him to be a limitation upon the present •privileges of newspapers.—The Earl of MtLLTOWN thought it would be wise to retain Ite words " for 'the public benefit." --- The proposal was agreed to.--Lord MONKSWELL proposed a law 'clause 'to the effect that when any person makes aapeech ton meeting at Which to his knowledge a reporter is present, and a report containing the libellous words, purporting to be a report of such speech is published in any newspaper, then on proof of its accuracy the person should be made responsible.—After some discussion, taken part in by Lord Herschell. the Marquis of Salisbury, the Earl of Milltown, and the Marquis of Waterford, Lord MONKS- WELL consented to withdraw the clause with a view of its presentation in an amended form on the third reading. At the end of Clause 5, Lord MONKSWELL moved the addition of words providing that "in a consolidated action under this section, the jury shall assess the whole of the damage (if any) in one sum; but a separate ver- dict shall be taken against each defendant • and if a jury shall have found a 'verdict against the defendants thus, they shall proceed to apportion the amount of damages."—Lord EnaltwELL was of opinion that such a provision would lead Pa ,cohfusion.—:The proposal was , eventually agreed to.

that he had urged Mr. Parnell and his friends to do things from which he shrank himself, he did not think, even if it were true, it was a serious accusation. He was willing to leave himself in the hands of friends -or foes to say whether a charge of cowardice could reason- ably lie against him. The other charge, that whewa Cabinet Minister he had in communication with Mr. Parnell betrayed the secrets of his colleagues must refer to the period between 1880 and 1885, and he did not re- member having at that time either direct or indirect commntheations with Mr. Parnell. Mr. Parnell hav- ing, once or twice assisted his recollection, Mr. Cham- berlain remembered that there were two periods when he was in communication with Mr. Parnell directly and indirectly. One was in respect of his Kilmainham im- prisonment, the other when Mr. Parnell called to see him on the Sunday after othe assassination of Lord Frederick Cavendish in Phcenix Park. But the whole of these communications he had made known to Mr. Gladstone, Lord Hartington, and other colleagues specially interested in the matter. He had also heard from Mr. Parnell in the matter of the scheme of Na- ' tional Councils for Ireland. But on that, as on other occasions, he had made knoWn,to his colleagues all that had taken place. His statement of the facts was to some,extent corroborated by Mr. Gladstone, to whom and Mr. Forster the nature of the intercourse with Mr. Parnell had been communicated,. Mr. Reid's amendment vas eventually rejected, as was one proposed by Mt. Anderson asking that the charges and allegations should be set out in a schedule attached to the Bill. On a subsequent amendment, Sir W. IlAncounr sug- gested that the Government in introducing the Bill were acting in collusion with the proprietor of the "Times," a suggestion which the Solicitor-General for Scotland said he met with the most unqualified and un- cenimonious contradiction.' Sir W. HARCOURT said he would withdraw the state- ment when it was denied by ' the First Lord of the Treasury, and his refusal to do so for some time after re- peated and emphatic denials from Mr. Smith gave rise to a scene of great excitement. Mr. STAVELEY HILL entreated the Government to accept the amendment—which was one to give the Commissioners power to investigate such of the charges and allegations as they might think fit—and said the person who would be on his trial was the Attorney- General for the speech he made in the recent action. The attack of Sir W. Harcourt on Mr. Smith was fol- lowed up by succeeding Radicaland Nationalist speakers, although the alleged ground for it was repeatedly denied. The amendment was rejected by a majority of 43. The next amendment proposed was one by Mr. SEX- TON providing that the names of the persons against whom the charges and allegations were made should be inserted in the Bill. Mr. T. HEALY remarked that if his name were sche- duled he would stop at home, but if not he would go abroad for a long holiday. After a lengthy discussion' Mr. W. 'H. Smrra, at twenty-five minutes to one o'clock, moved the closure. The CnAinmAN pit the question "that the ques- tion be now put," and this was agreed to without a divi- sion. The Committee then divided on the amendment : —For the amendment, 204 ; against, 259 ; majority, 55.

Sir JOHN Simow then oposed an amendment to con- fine the inquiry of the Special Commission to the action of members of Parliament. He moved to omit the words "and other persons." All that the country wanted to know he maintained was whether or not the hon. member for Cork wrote the letters which had ap- peared in the "Times." Mr. Siirrra, at a quarter to two o'clock, moved that the closure should be applied. The CHAIRMAN, amid cheers from the Nationalist ben- ches, refused to put the motion. Mr. PARNELL moved to report progress. The House had now been sitting eleven hours, and this was a very important amendment that needed further discus- sion. The Committee divided—For reporting progress 165; against, 219. Mr. Suicrox moved that the Chairman do now leave the chair, contending that the large minority that yoted in the last division was entitled to consideration. The thieram&ii,cleclined to put the motion, because he thought that if a division was taken on the amendment that night the object of the Opposition could be discus- sed on subsequent amendments. Mr. T. HEALY continued the discussion, and upbraided the Government for not replying to the• argument of the Irish members. It was impossible for the frig' members to rest under this cloud of obloquy, and if Mr. Walter refused to give evidence as to how he got the letters the judges might then say they must now inquire about other persons. .whereupon a train of prisoners might be pro- duced to swear the character of the Irish members away. Mr. Gosotimq said there were some speeches that ought not to be answered. (Cheers.) How could his right hon. friend wi.h any dignity repeat the statement that Mr. Healy ventured to treat in the way he had done. His right hon. friend had stated in the clearest terms that no communication whatever was entered in- to. (Cries of " No, no. He never said that.") No corn-1 munication with‘Mr. Walter had in the slightest degree borne upon the introduction of those words "other per- sons." (" Oh, oh.") The Irish members scoffed, as much as to say that was false. (Irish cheers.) The CHAIRMAN : If I could identify any member recognizing that with approval I would at once name him. Mr. GOSCH.EazAttted that 'no communication with the editor or proprietor of the " Times " bore in the slieht- er test degree on those words. They were in the original reference settled.by the Cabinet, ;and it was settled on the first day that the right hon. gentleman introduced it. The words were in the notice given on Friday. It was the Cabinet that settled those words without any communi- cation with the proprietor of the "Times." They were in the original =proposal, and therefore the last two speeches of Mr. Healy fell to the ground without a sha- dow of foundation or justification. (Cheers.) Mr. PARNELL eAked who attended that Cabinet meet- ing. Why, out of his place and out of his order, it was the counsel for the" Times" newspaper. (Irish cheers.) He complained with much vigour that they could not get a single straightforward statement on that subject from any minister; but when the end of this long story was reached on the side of the Irish members would be the victory and Mahe Gove.unnent's side the shame and disgrace. (Chem.) • The Committee then divided :—For the amendment, 166; against, 222. Progress was then reported. The House adjozirried at 3-45 am. HOUSE OF COMMONS, WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at a quarter past twelve o'clock. .
SUNDAY Craysma.—Mr. SEAGER HUNT presented a peti- tion signed by over 217,000 inhabitants of London against the Sunday closing .tif public-houses.

THE PARNELL COMMISSION. The sitting of the House of Commons was wholly taken up with the further discussion in Committee on the Par- nell Commission Bill.—The first amendment was moved by Mr. R. T. REID, and was intended to limit the inquiry to charges and allegations bearing upon the members of Parliament and other persons accused.—To Mr. SEXTON. who regarded the amendment as unnecessary, there fol- lowed the HOME SECRETARY, who denied that the primary object of the bill was either to condemn mem- bers of Parliament or to enable them to clear themselves. The object of the measure was that a cloud of accusation and suspicion might be dispersed or crystallised into a certainty. Thus early in the resumed discussion the Chairman's intervention -was called for owing to inter- ruptions by Irish members, who charged the Home Secretary with making unjustifiable insinuations.— When this incident, which happily was of short dura- tion, had:been disposed of, Mr. MArrunws's admissions as to the scope of the Commission were seriously taken up on the Opposition side of the House as furnishing at last an indication of the cottrse which the inquiry was to follow ; and, adopting this view of the case, first Sir %William Harcourt and then Sir Lyon Playfair and Mr. J. Redmond accused the Government of having completely gone back upon their original position so as to make the charges against members a matter subservient to an investigation of the :doings of political associations. --After something very like a wrangle between Sir W. Harcourt and Mr. A. J. Balfour over the con- duct ,of the Attorney - General in dragging Mr. Gladstone's name into the O'Donnell trial, Mr. J. REDMOND gave an account of the treatment he had met with from the "Times" hi the matter of his atti- tude after the Phcenix Park murders. This story was subsequently referred to by Mr. J. MORLEY as, if true, loading the journal mentioned and its conductors with the "deepest infamy."—Mr. GLADSTONE spoke of the lea- der of the House having made a covenant of the most solemn character which had been entirely, and absolutely changed. Speaking of the notorious letter,involved in the case, he-said he might—after the disposition shown to cast it into the shade—without extravagance call it a forged document. The original issue as put forward in the statement of the First Lord of the Treasury ha 0 been surreptitiously and entirely shifted, and the original charges, if they appeared at all, did so now only as por- tions of a great mass of evidence involving the whole constitution of Ireland and the whole history of agrarian crime and the Land League. In addition to a reference by the Attorney General to Mr. Gladstone's conclusion as to the letter being-entirely unjustified, the HOME SEC- RETARY and Mr. A. J. BAusoun both strenuously denied that there had been any change of front on the part of the C t, the latter gentleman also complaining of what he termed "the amazing deliverance" by the leader of the Opposition ,of a judicial opinion on a matter with which the Commisrion would have to deal.-2-Mr. T. HEALY, after reverting to the insinuations thrown out previously in the deb& as to the collusion of the Gov- ernment with the " Times " in the preparation of the bill, twitted the former with having more desire to make a political business of the Commission than to get at the truth. A long and recriminatory discussion followed, ending in the rejection of the amendment by a majority of 47. The House then resumed, after which the CHAN- CELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, in the absence of Mr. W. H. Smith, gave notice of a motion to suspend the twelve o'clock rule on Thursday, and to put an end to the de- bate upon it at one o'clock. The House adjourned at six o'clock.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIitIRSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat shortly after four o'clock. MISCELLAI-7.oUS.—Lord KNuTsFonn,replying to a ques- tion, gave the same information with regard to affairs ia Zululand as was conveyed to the House of Commons— namely, that hostile chiefsz were surrendering and that the state of the country had improved. The sitting was chiefly occupied with a discussion on the Commons' amendments to the Railway and Canal Traffic Bill, a mea- sure which Lord BRA.BOURNE referred to as being nothing short of confiscation.—An ainendment by Lord HERZ- cram. giving the power to superior courts in certain cir- cumstances to allow appeal to the House of Lords was adopted, and after some discussion the remainder of the Commons' amendments were agreed to.—Their Lord- ships adjourned soon after six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Tnunsney. . . _ . .

-- -- The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past three o'clock. QUESTIONS.—The proceedings in the House were again of a lively nature, so far as they were concerned with the resumed discussion of the Special Commission Bill and questions arising out of it.—Questions by Mr. APLaren about the dangers of level crossings and the convenience of working-men being consulted in the re- gulation of the hours of polling for School Board elec- tions were dealt with, after which, Mr. STANHOPE, repre- senting the War Department, had the opportunity affor- ded of contradicting the rumour that the magazine rifle had been condemned.—Among the remaining ques- tions was one by Mr. Mundella, in replying to which the PRESIDENT of the BOARD of TRADE stated that efforts were being made to secure the adoption in the colonies and foreign countries of legislation on merchandise marks. Afterwards some time was spent in. discussing a motion by Mr. LABOUCICERE declaring that the " Times " by comments contained in a leading arti* on :the previous ' day's debate had been guilty of a breach of 'privilege.— The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER met this by moving "That the House proceed to the business of the day," an amendment seconded by Mr. GLADSTONE, who, hav- ing stated that precedent favoured the adoption of this course, prevailed upon the hon. member for Northamp- ton to withdraw his motion. In these circumstances the amendment was, of course, abandoned, but the matter was not allowed to be dismissed without Mr. J. RED- Hon) reverting to the injustice which, he said, the " Times " had done to him in treating of his attitude after the Phcenix Park murders. This brought up Mr. JOHN MORLEY, one of the memberslectured in the article complained of because he had ,said that Mr. Redmond's story, if true, covered the conductors of the " Times " with the ‘0 deepest infamy." The essence of Mr. Mor- i ley's contribution to the lively discussion was repre- sented by his sweeping remark being repeated uncondi- tionally. THE PARNELL CODIMISSION.—Before the House could proceed with the Parnell Commission Bill in Committee, the Ministerial resolutions framed for the purpose of forcing the measure through at one o'clock had to be got out of the way. These resolutions which were, in the absence of the First Lord of the Treasury, moved by the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, were stoutly resisted by the Opposition, and especially by the Irish members; while from the Government side of thd House Mr. STAVELEY HILL joined in the protest against the course proposed. In consequence of the vehement opposition and the moving of one or two amendments. the Govern- ment were induced ,to offer what was declared tse be an "astounding compromise," placing upon the Chairman the responsibility of selecting out of the amendments remaining at one o'clock sach as he might deem important enough to be put separately. This pro- posal the opposing ranks showed no disposition to ac- cept, and the original resolution was ultimately carried by a majority of 54.—1 t was nearly eight o'clock before the House reached the resumed consideration of the bill, and took up an amendment by Mr. Jusrin Mean= which was intended to place upon the Commission the duty of first investigating the circumstances in which the charges were originally published in the " Times."— The proposal to make this altbration was negatived, as was also an amendment proposed by Mr. LABOUCHERE to make the letters the first point of inquiry.—Amendments were moved and discussed till one o'clock, when the clauses were put, and progress was reported at twenty minutes past one. The House adjourned at ten minutes to two.
THE WALTHAMSirOW MYSTERY. ARREST OF' BARBER.

The chemist's assistant. Barh-r, accused of murdering Mrs. French, was arrested on hat urday, in High-street, 13rentford. P.C. Buchanan was on duty, when he met a man coming out of a coffee shop. Noticinc, that his ap- pearance answered the description circulated, he took him to the station, where he was detained. Barber ad- mitted his identity. and added that Mrs. French took the chloroform while lig was in the shop. He (Barber) endeavoured to restore her, but failing, became neriMus, changed his clothes, and left the house. When arrested Barber said, "I knew what you want I am the man, Barber." He denied that there was any improper in- timacy between him and Mrs. French. He was removed to Walthamstow during the afternoon.

The Recorders, Magistrates. and Olefin; of the Peace Rill, upon the motion Of Earl Brownlow, was read a second time. .
The Distress far Rent +(Dublin) Bill .passed through Committee. THE LOCAL 'GOVERNMENT BILL.

Lord BALFOUR, in moving the second reading of this bill, said in the present.want of system in local govern- ment administration in 'England it was generally felt that a new management was needed. Our present sys- tem had been well fiescribed as a chaos of rates, a chaos of areas, and a chaesea.f authorities. There were 27,900 different authorities taxing the English householders in respect of 18 different kinds of rates, and the state of affairs was very well illustrated by the instance of a farmhouse in Wales, which was said to stand in twelve' ,different areas. His lordship pitied the Poor tenant in this instance, for his life must have been made burdensome by the constant calls of the tax collectors representing the various authorities. The present bill, he did not suppose, was oerfeet.—Lord DFNMAN moved that the bill be read al second time this day six months.—The Earl of Burma- LEY supported the second reading of the hill, The MARQUIS of SALISBURY said the only criticism on the bill to which he felt it necessary to reply was that of the Earl of Carnarvon. The noble Earl, who confined himself to very modest parts of the bill, talked of their ealloping down bill with the reins down about the horses' feet, and no drag on, but he (Lord Salisbury) eould not undwstand where the noble Earl got his poetic simile from. (Laughter.) With regard to all these dangers, he did not know from xyhence they were con- jured. For himself, he did not believe in them, and so gentle was the slope that they were driving down that it was hardly Possible to say whether they were going down'hill or not. Earl Beauchamp, Earl Fartescue, and Earl Fowls hav- ing addressed the House, Lord Penman's amendment was negatived, and thebill was read a second time. ZULULAND.—In reply to the ,Earl of Kingston, Lord KNUTSFORD said it would be unwise, even if it were pos- sible, to give any promise as to what should be done with regard to inter-tribal disputes in Zululand, and he hoped shortly to be able to lay papers on the table show- ing that Usibepu was not to blame for the outbreak in Zululand. He undertoek to make compensation to Denizulu's people, which showed it was not Usibepu's action which led to the outbreak of hostilities. The step which the Government were taking vlicre for the protection of loyal natives. '

Mr. GLADSTONE invited the Thief Secretary to lay on the table the official report ef the proceedings atAhe Mandeville inquest; and Mr. ',BALFOUR promised to do so, if a shorthand note had beerw taken, as he believed was the case. THE PARNELL-T/MES COMMISSION.
MR. CHAMBERLAIN EXPLAINS.

Mr. PARNELL gave notice that he -should divide the Timm on the motion to continue the dehateon the Corn- misaion Bill after midnight, as a protest against the at- tempt of the Government to contitaue a discussion upon an important measure, after the House had already been st work nine hours, when it wa,a impossible for the public to know What was going on. ' At 410, the FIRST LORD of the TREASURE' .mscle the formal maim that the discussion on the Parnell Com- mission Bill should proceed beyond midnight.—A divi- sion was 'immediately taken, and Mr. Gladstone, upon leading the way into the " No" lobby, was loudly cheerd by the Irish members. The right honourable gentleman was followed- out of the House by the occupants of the frontGpposition Bench, and the 7,vhole of the largo body of Irish members present. The result of the division was—
For the motion Against Government majority —72

Mr. PARNELL resumed the debate on Mr.Reld'samend• ment for confining the scope of the bill, and entered into his charges against Mr. Chamberlain of divulging Cabi- net secrets, stating that he would prove these charges 'More the Commission. Ile also bitterly attacked the Government for making the reference to the Commission so wide and vague, denying him and his friends fair play simply because they were Irishmen. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN promptly followed. He began by remarking that he had not the remotest idea what special circumstances Mr. Parnell alluded to in his statement of his former relations with him. Re would not shrink from any inquiry before the Commission if it should ap- pear that the circumstances alleged by Mr. Parnell were germane to the subject, a limitation ironically cheered from the Irish benches. With respect to the first charge,

div.head: ACCUSED 1N COURT.
div.p: THE ACCUSED 1N COURT.

At Stratford (Essex) Petty Sessions, on Monday, William Barker, chemist's assistant, of Walthamstow, was charged, on suspicion, with having caused the death of Annie Mary French, by administering to her a noxious drug. While the cletiv was reading the charge, the accused 'sobbed audibly.—Detectlye-Inspector Glasse said he should only offer sufficient evidence to-day to justify a remand.—Frederick Moyle, the shop-boy, then re- peated the evidence he rave at the coroner's inquiry as to the visits of Mrs. French to the shop. Ile added that he never saw the prisoner take any liberties with Mrs. French. The deceased was at a show last Saturday week in the morning. and in the afternoon the prisoner sent witness for his dinner, and at the same time gave him a note for the deceased, which prisoner instructed him to give to Mrs. French. but not if Mr. 'French was in the kitchen. Witness found Mr. French in the kitchen, and he did not therefore deliver the note. Prisoner sent him again with the note, when he found Mrs. French alone. She read it, and replied "Yes." Witness conveyed this answer to the prisoner, who said, "That's all right?' He then sent witness for a shillings- worth of brandy. Deceased entered the shop about a quarter past three, and when witness returned the front door was closed. The prisoner seemed very dull. Witness had been fetching him brandy all the week. Witness delivered the brandy at the side gate, and was then sent home. He returned in the evening, and, gaining, no response to knocks, scaled the back wall. Hb found the deceased in the parlour on a couch, her feet touching the floor. The brandy bottle was now empty, and a soda water bottle and bowl of water stood on the table. A pair of prisoner's trousers and his hat were also on a table.—Prisoner was asked if he opposed a remand until Saturday next, and he said "I don't know that I have."—He was then removed. STATEMENT BY BARBER. A written statement found on the prisoner gives addi- tional explanations as to why he absconded from the chemist's shop. He says :—Mrs French had complained to me of suffering from the toothache for some weeks, and I had on several occasions rubbed in chloroform or camphorated chloroform. I told her that if she came to me I would give her a draught, and would rub some chloroferm on her gums, and apply some strong caustic, such as carbolic or nitric acid, to destroy the nerve. On this occasion she came to me to carry this out. I fetched in the bottle for the \ pur- pose, one containing a solution of muriate of mor- pima, of which I intended to give her a dose to allay the irritation. Just as I was about to prepare the draught some customers came into the shop, and Mrs. French said to me, in a rather frettish way, "Go and attend to your customers." I left her in the room with the preparations, and on my return I found she had taken thse whole of the strong solution of morphia. On my discovering this, 1 thought it was possible that die had thrown the contents of the small bottle into the fireplace, and upon looking round I could not find anything in the fireplace. I looked at her closely, and found she was reeling. and I rushed into the kitchen and got a little brandy, which I knew to be a stimulant, and some sal volatile, which was in the shop. I gave her a strong dose of the sal volatile and brandy, and undid her dress round the neck, and , fetched cold water to bathe her forehead. Immediately after doing this she fell from my arms, and said she was going to die. I took hold of her, and found her chartee, and thought she could not recover. My first thought was to send for a doctor, but at that time of the day I thought it was probable that ,he was out. I thought it better to stay with her. I gave her some sal volatile again, and afterwards rushed downstairs and changed my clothes. So far as outrage or operation was con- cerned, there was nothing of the sort entered my mind, as it was not necessary. Ilett'arding the letter, it had nothing to do with it. It only referred to some cigarettes whidli she had made for me, and had done so on former occasions.

IRELAND.

D. Redwood, Roman Catholic Archbishop of Welling- ton, New Zealand, has arrived in Dublin, and purposes staying till the close of the week. On Saturday evening two shots were fired at Thomas Murphy, at Farmer's Bridge, near Tralee, by a man wear- ing a red handkerchief over his face. Neither shot took effect. The cause of this outrage- seems to be that Murohy's employer took a road contract contrary to the wishes of his neighbours. - - •

Three young men left the quay at Waterford in a small sailing boat on Sunday. and have not since been heard of. The boat was found drifting out of harbour upside down on Monday, and there is little doubt that it was capsized in a sudden squall, and that the occupants— none being able to swim—were drowned. On Tuesday, at a meeting of the National League, Mr, David Sheehy, M.P., describing the evictions on Colonel Vandeleur's estate, said he never saw more brutal evic- tion scenes than at Kilrush. Mr. Harrington, M.P., said Mr. MandevilVs death would have a powerful effect in directing English public opinion to the treatment of Irish political prisoners. An anonymous donor has sent Colonel Turner, Royal Irish Constabulary, a cheque for £l,OOO, as an expression of sympathy with the force to enable him to assist constables injured in doing their duty, and to benefit those who have displayed conspicous gallantry in the discharge of their duty. Colonel Turner replied by telegram :—" Your just appreciation of the Royal Irish Constabulary is a present doubly valuable, on account of the storm of lying abuse to which they are daily subjected." A serious affray between some troopers of the Derby- shire Hussars and some civilians occurred on Saturday night in Kilrush. The soldiers were returning from some military sports, and, it is alleged, attacked a party of civilians. A conflict ensued, and Captain Welch, R.M., taking command of the few available police, ordered them to draw their revolvers. Large crowds gathered. and extraordinary excitement prevailed. Extra police were speedily sent for. and prevented the spread of the fight. A trooper who was arrested made desperate re- sistance, but was secured. THE O'BRIEN LIBEL ACTION.

The libel -a-otion brought by Mr. William O'Brien, M.P., against the Cork Constitution was continued at the Cork Assizes on Saturday. Mr. W. Ludgate, assistant editor, who wrote the alleged libel, defended the allega- tions contained in the articles. Mr. H. L. Tidy, manag- ing director and editor of the Cork Constitution, stated that he allowed the article to appear, believing it to be true. Mr. Blakeney, agent of the Ponsoi,by estate, deposed that rents had ceased to be paid on the estate. This closed the case for the defendant. Mr. William O'Brien on Monday was awarded £lOO damages. .

div.head: MANDEVILLE INQUEST.-VERDICT.
div.p: THE MANDEVILLE INQUEST.-VERDICT.

The inquiry into the death of Mr. John Mandeville was resumed at Michelstown on Saturday. The Macder- mott, for the next-of-kin, reviewed the evidence at length, and in conclusion lie said the life of John Mande- ville had been unselfish and sell•sacrificing, adorned by many virtues and every endearing quality. After 55 minutes' deliberation the jury unanimously found the following verdict:—" That the deceased died from diffused cellular inflammation, brought about by brutal and unjustifiable treatment in Tullamore Prison." They protested against the system of treating political pri- soners as common criminals, and against the cruel methods by which prison rules were enforced; and con- demned the vile aspersions sought to be cast upon the medical witnesses by Dr. Barr. PUBLIC WORKS.

The fifty-sixth annual re-por-t-o-i-iii.e Commissioner of Public Works in Ireland was issued on Monday. Dur- ing the past year the Commissioners made 1,321 loans for public works, amounting to £829,766 showing a diminution in the numbers of 37, with an increase in the money allocation of £206,66, which is entirely due to increased operations under the Labourers' Acts; 444 loans for an aggregate sum of £36,575 were made to tenants, to purchase their holdings, against 626 loans for £60,955 in the previous year, the falling off being due partly to the unsettled state of the land question, and more searching inquiry into the security by the tenant. The allocations sanctioned under the Labourers' Acts have been on a much larger scale than in any former year. They pro- vide for loans to 497 electoral divisions, amounting to £463,261. giving, with £358,007 previously authorised, a total. of £821,268, which has now been allocated to this purpose. Twenty-four loins were made in 1886-87, to the amount of £89,161, for building 852 labourers' dwell- ings; while last year applications were received for loans amounting to £50,183 for the same purpose, of which 20, to the amount of £34,746, have been sanc- tioned. The arrears on loans advanced for the improve- ment and purchase of lands, have been undergoing a yearly increase, and now amount to £95,533.

div.head: VANDELEUR EVICTIONS. TERRIBLE SCENES.
div.p: THE VANDELEUR EVICTIONS. TERRIBLE SCENES.

Evictions on the Vandeleur estate were resumed on Tuesday in the townland. of Moyasta, abOut five miles from liilrush. Four families were evicted, the resistance in one case being exceedingly violent. This was at the house of Thomas Birmingham, who, with his wife and grown-up daughters defended the dwelling, which was strongly barricaded at both front and rear. From the moment that the Sherrif's party arrived, and during the progress of the siege showers of boiling water mixed with lime and excrement were poured on those below, Mr, Cecil Roche, 11. M., coming in for his full share. Birmingham and his party wielded from within the house a long pole, with which they swept off the bailiffs and police, who vainly attempted to seize the formidable weapon. The temporary success of the be- sieged elicited loud cheers from a thug of people who had gathered in boats on the bay, tThvards which .Bir- mingham's dwelling faces. After a portion of the house wall had been knocked down with the battering-ram, Detective-Inspector Bill and a party of police armed with truncheons rushed through the breach, the former fall- ing headlong inside. Then ensued a fierce scuffle within, which lasted several minutes, Birmingham being at length brought out much exhausted, and having two deep wounds on, his forehead, whilst his mouth was torn from a baton thrust. After his wounds had been dressed by the military surgeon he was placed under arrest, being subsequently discharged. Three other tenants were afterwards evicted, but the resistance offered was only of a formal nature.

div.head: TERRIBLE MURDERS IN IRELAND.
div.p: TERRIBLE MURDERS IN IRELAND.

John Forham was shot at five o'clock on Sunday even- ing, at Mount Cole, near Listowel, wlst returning from Tralee, where he had hired three Itbourers, who were with him on a car. Two disguised men suddenly jumped over a fence and shot him dead. Forham, who was 60 years old, bad been boycotted for taking a farm from which a tenant had been evicted. Lately the police protection afforded him had been limited to a night patrol. He lived at Tullamore, between Bally- longford and Listowel. In making their escape the mur- derers were screened by a wood. The labourers com- municated as soon as possible with the Listowel police, who hurried to the scene of the outrage. On Saturday morning, between eight and nine o'clock, a murder was committed at Glounamuckla, about tee miles from Newmarket, the unfortunate victim brim: James Rouare, and the scene of the murder in the heart of a most disturbed district bordering upon Kerry. The deceased proceeded to a friend's in Glounamuckla, for the purpose of mowing hay for Daniel M'Auliffe, by whom he had been employed as labourer. Rouare went to work, and M'Auliffe, who was standing near him, saw a man disguised with a white flannel over his eyes, and armed with a double-barrelled cue, jump over the fence and walk in the direction in which they we:.e standing. He gruffly asked their names; M'Auliffe complied, but Rouare said his name was John Fleming. The stranger told him to beg his pardon, which heimme- diately did. At that moment the disguised assassin pre- sented the gun and fired two charges in rapid suc- cession into the man's body. Rouare fell on his back, crying out that he was murdered. The disguised man then pulled out a revolver, saying, "If that won't do you, take that," at the' same time 'discharging the re- volver. During all the time the shocking tragedy was being enacted, M'Auliffe, who stood by, says his senses were paralysed for the time being, and were only recalled by the moaniec, of the dying man. Lie states that he cannot identify the assassin. A priest and doctor were sent for, and the unfortunate man was removed to his house, three miles distant. On the way, M'Auliffe asked him if he knew who the murderer was, and ho replied that he did not, but would leave him to God. Rouare barely survived to have the last Sacrament adminis- tered, and the police at Kiskeane were immediately com- municated with. The only motive alleged for the mur- der was that deceased worked for a farmer named Two- mey, who is somewhat unpopular in the district, and has had two policeinen protecting him for some time past. The origin of Twomey's unpopularity is difficult to ascertain, but it appears that Twomey evicted a man for non-payment of rent, but reinstated him. About a month ago a notice was found posted on Rouare's door threatening him with the same death as Quinn, a bog ranger who also worked for Twomey, and who was re- cently murdered in the district. Notwithstanding the notice Rouare worked for- Twomey, as he had received similar notices warning him not to work for several people. Deceased, who was 35 years of age, was mar- ried and had one child. A young man named Cornelius Beeffe has been arrested in connection with the affair.

Mr. Geo. Besviek, a London solicitor, was on Monday seized with illness as he was addressing a judge in cham- bers. He was removed to a private room, where he died. The death is attributed to heart disease. LIBELLING COLLIERY OFFICIALS.—At the Liverpool Assizes, on Monday, H. G. Stock, W. Clark, and John Robinson, underground managers for the Garswood Coal and Iron Company, Wigan, were awarded £l5O damages in a libel action brought against Saml. Woods, miners' agent for the Ashton and other districts. The libel was contained in a speech delivered to a miners' conference at Little Hulton, in which the defendant accused the plaintiffs of having taken certain action against men from spite or from political motives,

No fewer than 23 of the metropontan pulpitz mai& on Sunday, either morning or evening, occupied by American or Colonial Bishops. it the Central Criminal Court, on Monday, the emer.al Mrs. Gordon Bernie and the two other defendants was, ordered to be adjourned to next sessions. Gigner was admitted to bail. On Monday afternoon, while two men named Michael Reynolds and Joseph Lyons were removing some plauks from a pile of wood at the stables of Messrs. Warde and Co., Conper-street, Glasgow, the whole pile fell upon. them, killing Lyons and severely injuring Reynolds. A meeting of the Council of the Yorkshire Miners' Association was held on Monday at Barnsley, to rliqc-usts the proposal for an advance of 10 per cent which is likely to be demanded in October. Nothing definite will be done, however, until opinion from other districts has been obtained.

On Sunday night the mangled body of William Allsops of Ridge Close Farm, Dove Holes, was found lying at the bottom of Black Hole Quarry. He had walked over the qtlarry face whilst on his way home after dusk. The quarry is 30 feet deep. The deceased was 27 years old and unmarried.

KILLED BY AN ELEPHANT.—The last mail from the Congo brings news of the death ot Mr. Deane, the Eng- lishman who, as chief of the Stanley Falls Station, de- fended it against an overwhelming force of Arabs, gad succeeded in effecting a retreat. He was killed during an elephant hunt near Lukolola, by an elephant; whose tusk pierced his neck. ELOPEMENT OF A LADY Till A COACIIMAM.—The daughter, aged 18, of a merchant of Stockport eloped with her father's groom, a married man with four chil- dren. The pair embarked at Liverpool on board the Bothnia, having taken passages for America. The run- aways were brought ashore at Queenstown on Saturday, and Miss Robinson was taken home by her father, who had arrived from Stockport in order to intercept the pair. Atannnzo RAILWAY Aeon:mgr.—An accident of an alarming nature occurred on the Great Eastern Railway, near Thorpe Junction, about 11 o'clock on Sunday. The engine of a train from Thorpe to Clackton-on-Sea left the metals, and all the carriages were more or less damaged. The engine driver, stoker, and several passengers were injured, and there were some miraculous escapes. The line was blocked for thereat of the day, and a breakdown gang was employed all day clearing away the remains of the wreck. WAftHOCSE FIRE.-1 large goods warehouse in Alder- manbury, London, was destroyed by fire early on Sun. day morning. The building, which was occupied by several firms of woollen manufacturers, was first: dis- covered on fire by a policeman, and notwithstanding the prompt arrival and commendable operations by the fire- men, under Captain Shaw' the premises, comprising BilC floors, gutted out. The adjacent buildings were also slightly damaged. S1100(.1190 MURDER AT WOLVERHAMPTON.—A lug murder was committed at Wolverhampton late on Monday night. A number of Italian ice cream vendors were returning from dilston fair, when a dis- pute arose with some other men. One of the Italians. Antonio Fritz, is alleged to have drawn a knife and stabbed Alfred Bateman. a nut and bolt forger, to the heart, causing immediate death. Fritz ran away, but was caught. The knife was not found. ATTEMPT TO DROWN A SWRETHEART. —At Chester Assizes, on Monday, a young man, named John Cocker, was convicted of attempting to murder a girl named Sarah Jane Smith, aged 16 years. The prisoner had been keeping company with the girl, and on the morning of the 16th April he deliberately pushed her into a canal near Bollington, and, with some taunting words, left her to drown. Fortunately the girl was rescued. After she had been got out of the water the prisoner ran back to the place and expressed great surprise at what had , happened. He was sentenced to penal servitude for ' eight years. THE MANCHESTER MURDERER. —Jackson, whose exe- cution in Strangeways Gaol is fixed for Tuesday next, is very quiet, and receives seemingly with every attention the ministrations of the prison chaplain. He is in good bodily health. A large number of signatures have been, appended to the petition in favour of the convict's reprieve, and 150 petition forms have been sent out to the chief towns of Lancashire and Yorkshire. Eighty- five have been sent to the prisoner's father at Thrstal, who is making earnest endeavours to secure the names Of those to whom Jackson was well known. Applica- tions are daily received for petition forms, and a strenu- ous effort is being made to save the convict's life.

"MR. MANTON," OF THE TEMP.—The Duchess Dowager of Montrose has been married to Mr. Marcus Henry Milner. The Duchess is the youngest daughter of the second Lord Decies, and the widow of the fourth Duke of Montrose. Her Grace's second husband was Mr. W. S. Stirling-Crawfurd. The Duchess is well known in racing circles as "Mr. Manton." Mr. Marcus Henry Milner is the youngest son of the late Mr. Henry Milner, of the Old Bank, Leeds, and brother of Lady Gerard and Lady Durham—Society, writes a London correspon- dent, is greatly exercised by the unexpected marriage - of the Dowager Duchess of Montrose. fier Grace, so well known in racing circles as "Mr. Manton," was born in 1818. She married in 1836 the late Duke of Montrosa,. and secondly Mr. Stirling* Crawford, who died in 1883. Her third husband, Mr. Marcus Milner, brother of Lady Durham and Lady Gerard, was born in 1864.

THE CHARGE OF MURDERING A DAUGHTER AT BRAD- FORD.-At the West Riding Assizes. at Leeds, on Mon- day, before Mr. Justice Smith, Wm. Dawson Bolpate, aged 41, labourer, was indicted for the wilful murder of his daughter, Lily Holgate, at Bradford, on March 26th. The girl was eleven years of age, and it was alleged that she died from the effects of taking a large quantity of carbolic acid. She was weak and delicate, and an out- patient at the Bradford Infirmary. The theory of the prosecution was that the prisoner a.lministered the carbolic acid to the child in order that at her death he might receive the sum of £2O. for which amount she was insured. The prisoner paid 2d. a week on the policy, and at the time of the child's death the payments were nine weeks in arrear. The jury returned a verdict of "Not guilty," and the prisoner was discharged. the Judge remarking that he thought the verdict a proper one. _ . _

A GATHERING OF THE CLANS CF RAGS.—A strange funeral has been witnessed at Montmartre, one of the Northern heights of Paris. A girl of nitteteen, daughter of the owners of a large perambulating peep- show which was installed at the fair' in the borough, lately died, and was "waked" in the show. "Mille: de Beaufort was the joy of her father and mother, and was known among all the male and female mountebanks among whom she lived as the" Pearl," by reason of her stainless conduct and her sympathy for unfortunate creatures whom an accident, bad health, or bad times had plunged into destitution. When the peep-shorlirociaered. the " Pearl " always levied a Sipall tax 8-a- Per parents' profits for the gene of Poverty - sp...l*-11 'lnfant -Phenomena," Giants out of work, Pigmies who were "down on their luck." When, she Suddenly succumbed to consumption, the sorrow among the itinerant players and mountebanks was universal and heartfelt. They brought flowers to place on her body as it reposed inside the peep-show awaiting inter- ment, and her funeral was one of the strangest spectaeles that has been witnessed for some time in Montmartre. The hearse was Overed with numerous and handsome wreaths, and behind the chief mourners walked ail the celebrated lion-tamers of Paris; colossal women; skele- ton men; athletic negroes; giants; dwarfs; clowns divested of their war-paint; circus professionals, and all the general personnel of the Fair. THE DOM:LAS BOATING FATALITY.—An inquest, was opened at Douglas, on Monday, in connection with the boating fatality by which Henry Kay, astistant master at Jackson-street Board School, Manchester, and two other Manchester viskors lost their lives. Edmund J. Christian, of Flulrne, one of the survivors, stated that when near Battery Pier, a heavy sea struck the boat, which was on the point of sinking, when Kelly, in jumping off, capsized it. Witness was rescued by the lighthouse keeper, and his companion Moon was dragged ashore by the keepers Milne and Ingram, and In- gram's two daughters. Milne afterwards ran much risk in rescuing ' Griffiths, who was on the point of drowning. The deceased Fletcher was crushed between the boat and the rocks. Henry Moon, a teacher at St. Wilfrid's School, Hulme, gave corroborative evi- dence. Assistant Harbour-master Kelly recommended the adoption of a by-law making it compulsory on per- sons proceeding beyond the line of Battery Pier to take a boatman with them. A steam launch in the bay would be very valuable. Milne having , given evidence, the Coroner summed up, and the jury returned a verdict of accidental drowning. They paid a tribute to the gallant try of the rescuers, and recommended that the Harbour Commissieners should take stops for the better regula- tion of boating in Douglas Bay. ' -

A MURDERER AT EIGHT YEARS OLD.—The latest Parisian sensation is one of unspeakable atrocity: A woman named Siauzade was about a year ago left in a state of destitution with two boys, five and seven years old, in consequence of the death of her hus- band. A friend of the husband's, a blacksmith, named Covencl, took home the widow and the two orphans,.and the mau and woman lived together as ruanand wife. At five o'clock on Saturday morning the blacksmith went tel work, leaving the woman and children in bed. About an hour later she was awakened by shrieks from the yo &ingest, and found him weltering in his blood, his stomach being, literally ripped up and the bowels protruding. The eldez boy was standing by the bed with an open razor in his hand, and on his mother entering the room he imme- diately cut his throat, and fell dying almost instantly. The elder boy soon afterwards died, and the younger child was removed to the hospital, where he lies in a hopeless condition. He was, however, able to speak, and said that Alphonse, the brother, had done it. It tran- spired that Alphonse has for some time past hated his brother with a thoroughly fiendish hatred. Twice be- fore he had tried to kill him—on one occasion by driving a nail wth a hammer into his head. Covenel had two razors, but Alphonse had determined on murdering the child of whom he was so jealous wtla his own. Be had stolen a razor from a shop, and part of the previous evening was devoted to sharpening it. He went to bed that night with the razor by his shi€ atd the firm intes. tion of killing his brother before their mother was up and about. It is probable that his own suicide was also premeditated.

Tories and a Liberal Unionist. It is thought that Mr. JUSTICE DAY will have the decency to with- draw his name, seeing how unacceptable he proves not only to the Parnellites, but to the Liberal party as a whole; but if he is like Lord SALISBURY,/ in looking upon the Irish as Hottentots, he may think it his duty to "let them have it" when he gets the chance. The same disregar,d of fair-play has been shown in the matter of making the in- quiry vague and general, instead of clear and specific. • What the public want to'know is whether Mr. PARNELL has written' the letters which the " Times " has published as emanating from him, and which, if proved, will put the leader of the Irish party on a level with the red-handed assassin. It is a question, too, as to how gar the Irish members have been guilty of "complicity with murder or violence," but when Mr. R. T. REID sought to take this as the basis of the investigation, the Government would have none of it; they rejected the amend- ment by a majority of 52. Mr. ANDERSON desired to provide for the Irish members knowing what they would be called upon to meet by the insertion of a schedule in the bill which should contain the charges and allegations; but this reasonable pro- posal was set aside by a reduced majority of 45. It was then proposed to give the judges some discre- tion by leaving it to them to inquire into such charges and allegations as the' might think fit. But it seems that even the infallible three are not to be trusted; they are to be tied down to inves- tigate all the rubbish in the pamphlet known as "Parnellism and Crime" whether the task occu- pies them one year or ten. The folly 4 taking up such a position was exposed by Sir WILLIAM aut- omata., who quoted from the pamphlet to show that Mr. GLADStONE might be dragged into the inquiry, seeing that he is referred to as having liberated O'DoNovAN Bosse, after he had been sentenced to penal servitude for life. Mr. GLAD- STONE admitted that the allegation quoted was quite as substantial as a number of others that had been made. It was surely not unreasonable he contended, to permit the judges to set aside charges which, in their judgment, were unfit for examination.. But the Government think other- wise; if they cannot prove anything against' Mr. PARNELL and his party colleagues, they believe they can at least harass and annoy them, and put them to enormous expense. That is the height of their ambition; their aim is not justice, but re- venge.

TILE Parlialentary duel between Mr. PARNELL and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN has naturally excited a good deal of attention ; it has, in fact, been the sensa- tion of the week. It is a matter of course to expect the Irish members to feel exceedingly disappointed and annoyed at the attitude of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, for they know that he, more than any other Tember of the Liberal Cabinet, pro.r fessed to be hand and glove with tliem in fighting against Coercion. Mr. PARNELL does not, as a rule, study form in his speeches, but he revealed epigrammatic finish in his attack when he said on Monday night : ,

My principal recollection of the right hon. gen- tleman before he became a Minister , was that he was always most anxious to put me and my friends forward to do work which he was afraid to do him- self—(cheers)—and after he became a Minister in principal recollection of him was that he was al- ways most anxious to betray to us the secrets and counsels of his colleagues in the Cabinet—(cheers) —and to endeavour, while sitting 'beside those col- leagues and while in consultation with them, to un- dermine their counsels and their plans in our in- terests. i (Cheers.)

Mr. CHAMBERLAIN responded to the attack on Tuesday, and made,light of the suggestion that he had at any time displayed cowardice. He did not find it so easy, however, to reply to the charge that he had betrayed "the secrets and counsels of his colleagues in the, Cabinet." It is,true that as to communications that had taken pluck be- tween himself and Mr. PARNELL, so late as 1885, with reference to an extensive plan of local self- government for Ireland, he was in a position to show that he had made known the subitance of those communications to MT.GLADSTONZ, as Prime Minister. Mr. Guroxorre was, however, unable, off-hand, to corroborate Mr. CHAMBERLAIN as to the indirect communications which, it seems, the member for West Birmingham held with Mr. PAR- NELL as to his release from Kilmainham prison. It is instructive to learn that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN negotiated the Kilmainham Treaty; and, as that was, in the eyes of the Tories, an "indelible dis- grace," it will be interesting to . observe whether they will continue to take the right honourable gentleman to their bosoms. But the issue is not whethev Mr. CHAMBERLAIN reported certain com- munications to Mr. GLADSTONE, which he was in • • duty bound to report; but whether he at times reported what had taken place in Cabinet which he was in duty bound not to report. Mr. PAP-NELL says the communications went beyond what the memlier for Wes:.- Birmingham acknowledges. • His words are :

They were communications with _reference to ' what the right bon. gentleman has called my release from Kilmainham, but which I call the Arrears Bill. They were communications with reference to the ' renewal or non-renewal of coercion in Ireland— (cheers)—after the Plicenix Park murders. They i were cqmmunications again, later on in 1885, with I reference to the non-renewal of the expiring Crimes Act of that period, whfich the then Government pro- posed to renew in part, and which the right hon, gentleman represented himself to us as opposing the renewal of within the Cabinet. (Cheers.) So far from his communications being merely confined to the subject of local government for Ireland, the statement of the right hon. gentleman has ,no foundation whatever. He has enlarged upon this I question of local government in Ireland and the I copmunications whick he said I had authorised to Ibe made to him on the subject. Well, Sir, if all the statements of the right lion, gentleman on this matter were perfectly true—if I had authorised ' communications to he made to him on the subject of local government in Ireland—if he • holds, as he alleges, proofs in letters in my handwriting that I constructed this scheme of local government for Ireland, it would not touch the question at issue at all, which has reference to the violation and dis- regard of the right hon. gentleman of his oath as a member of the Cabinet to preserve its secrets. (Loud cheers.)

It is not for us to say that Mr. CRAMBERLAIN Will not be able to clear himself of this imputation of breach of faith, for we have not yet reached the stage at which documentary evidence can be made public. It is sufficient to observe that making charges is a game at which two can play; and that the CHAKBERLAIN who negotiated the Kilmairtham treaty, and who took a vesolute stand against Coercion in 1885, seems an altogether different being to the CHAMBERaIN who in 1888 falls foul of th 3 Parnellites, and backs up Coercion in its WickFdest and most brutal form.

PeOple who have-been prophesying a "boom" in trade as a result of the long spell of depression, seem likely to be disappointed. There is an im- provement undoubtedly; that is to say, things are not as bad as they Were; but we are a long way from the hood times of 1874 and 1875. Perhaps it is better, on the whole, that trade should not im- prove by leaps and bounds. Its efteets are apt to demoralise—to make men extravagant, if not idle,

and then when the reaction comes they are un- prepared for it, and go from bad to worse. It is the easiest thing in the world in good times tip in- crease personal expenditure; for all the gods are smiling and beckoning; but when the tide turns— when the fates frown—Curtailment is of all things the most difficult. Taking everything into account, the present ought to be regarded as a fairly good time. If large profits are not being made, there is still some return for capital, and there is now-a- days so much capital in the market t4at, year by year, it becomes more difficult to ensure its profi- table employment. Mr. GLADSTONB incidentally remarked some time ago that, during the worst period of the recent depresssion, an addition of one hundred millions per year was being made to the national Wealth of Great Britain. It is a matter of course to say that the inevitable tenaency of every addition to the wealth of the nation is to increase the pressure of competition in capital, just as every addition to population tends to increase the struggle for.vcistence. There are some pessimists, keeping their eyes -fixed on these facts, who have come to the conclusion that we are entering rapids which must lead to a social Niagara. A too rapid increase of population is undoubtedly a great evil, and it may be that, with the ordinary increase, we shall reach a crisis in our large cities which will tax the • skill and energies of • our statesmen and philanthropists. But this does not ‘hold good of an increase in the wealth of the nation. Granted that it leads to the competition of capital ; and that the ten- dency is to bring the price of money down. It by no means follows in that case that capitalists, as a whole, are in a worse plight than of old, or that they are rushing headlong to destruction. The employer who makes three per cent, only on his capital of £19,000, is as Well off as to income as he was with six per cent. when he had £5,000. If he has doubled his capital, he can afford to have a less ' per centage ; it is something gained that he has increased his capital at all, and he is in no imme- diate danger of shooting Niagara. There are some writers who contend that the struggle amongst capitalists will go on until they eat each other up after the fashion of the Kilkenny cats. But the struggle is always in progress; as one loses another wins; the weak go to the wall' ; the strongest survive, and will always. survive. Such steady tines as we are now having are therefore for the best; they tend to eqVise the chances of living, and of putting something by for the rainy day. There has been a slight upward movement in wages amongst ;workers in coal, cotton, and iron, and this means that other branches of industry will necessarily more or less feel the good effect. It means, too, that capitalisits have either the hope or the certainty of improving their position and it is due to them to acknowledge that they have been "hard hit" during the past ten years. There is no elation; but, there is no depression. Trade may be said to be in a nornial and there- fore a healthy condition.

The Primrose Leaguers -Of Stretton and Stock- ton ,Heath, were treated to- tea and tattle, at Appleton Hall, on Tuesday afternoon. There was a good deal of apology fot the tattle, which was suPplied by Mr. W. S. Brancker. He warned his hearers that they must not allow the question of "the union" to slip too much in the background ; it had lost them sev9ral bye-elections. But alas it will slip ; there is no stopping it. The cry of "the union in danger" has slipped into limbo; and there is no getting it back.

Mr. Brancker was unconsciously hard on the Government for allowing themselves to be knocked into a cocked hat on the licensing question. It was what he calls "a paltry side issue"; but how paltry must the Government be to surrender so much for so little! Mr. Brancker said he was thoroughly in accord with the old saying—" Don't rob the poor man of his beer." When he has looked around a little more, and grown wiser, he will know that there is a no )7 saying which runs —" Don't rob the poor man by means of the beees

There was a rather unusual case heard at the Runcorn County Court on Tuesday. A retired Runcorn publican was sued for £9 held in stakes in connection with a bowling match. The plaintiff, a Liverpool man, finding that the game was not going to his liking, declared off because he was not permitted to stop and mow the; green. What an idea! If it had been too "fine," he might have wanted to. suspend the game for a week—till the grass grew. The jury, like sensible men treated him as a "lost " player, and gave a verdict for the defendant.

At the quarterly meeting, on Saturday, of the Newton Division Conservative Association, con- siderable credit was taken for the Parliamentary work accomplished by Mr. Legh, the member for Newton. It was said that he-had looked after the Warrington district during the absence, through an accident, of Sir Gilbert Greenall. It would be interesting if some one would explain what differ- ence it would havd made if both members hacl been absent. It would, in Sam Weller phrase, require spectacles of double million magnifyihg power to distinguish the seßrices which either of them has rendered.

The presentations to the Rev. J. A. Drummond, and more particularly the speeches that were made on Tuesday evening, show that his four years' work has won him the highest esteem of all clas- ses. But why, when he is so useful, so influential, and so revered, should he have to go? It is a re- flection on the State Church that such a thing should be. As the new Vicar requires two curates why should not Mr. Drummond be ap- pointed as one? What would be thought of a new editor who got rid of an old member of the staff who had done good work, and kept things going in the "interregnum."

Speaking on Wednesday of the insufficient ac- commodation for the press at the Liverpool Assi- zes, Mr. Justice Stephen said :—" The reporters, are practically the , ears and! eyes by which the public take part in what passes in these courts, and I earnestly hope that those who have authority in that behalf—the Corporation of Liverpool, or whoever it may be—will take proper measures to afford proper accommodation for the reporters, and if that gallery is not sufficient I should hope that some other part of the court which is suffi- cient may be set aside so that proper accommoda- tion may be given." jManagers of meetings would do well to take a hint from Mr. Justice Stephen; they sometimes neglect to make provision for the press.

ADUL'TERATELI WHISKEY AT WIDNES. A beerhouse- keeper named Henry Humphreys, of Anne-st. East, sum- moned to Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, and was fined 5s and costs for selling adulterated whisky. The sample analysed contained`2B per cent, of water instead of the standard allowance of 25 per cent. THE WIDNES FOOTBALL CLUB.—At the Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, before Mews. G. Pilkington and E. K. Muspratt, an application wal made by Mr. Knowles, on behalf of Mr. John.Andenson, Railway Hotel, Widnes, for permission to extend his premises for the convenience of the Widnes Football Club, who had fixed their head- quarters at his house. The application was granted. THE ALEXANDRA THEATRE, WIDNES.—AII application was made to the Widnes magistrates on Thursday, by Mr. Swift, on behalf of the proprietors of this theatre, for ,4 renewal of the original license. The original license was granted for few months, on condition that the pro- prietors should have a fireproof curtain supplied. The theatre had been closed for this purpose, but the contrac- tor was unable to supply the steel plates, which were to partly compose the curtain, on account of a strike at the works. All the other materials had been Supplied, and would be in readiness as soon as the plates were received. A license was granted for twelve months on condition that the curtain be constructed and perfec- t d $i three weeks from date. . NECILECT OF FAMILY AT WIDNES.—At the Widnes Petty: Sessions, on Thursday, before Messrs. G. Pilkington and E. K, Muspratt, James Sennot, a Widnes labourer, was charged with having deserted his three children. Three of the children became chargeable to the Guardians, who had s lent £4- 5s 5d on them. Mr. Treasy, however, in formed the Bench that the prisoner told him on Tuesday that he would not live with his wife, and as soon as he got out of gaol fie would leave her agaire—Prisoner was sent to gaol for three weeks. He was also sent to gaol for a week for having caused, a breach of the peace in Derby-road, FarnwOrth, on the 15th May, in default of finding a recognisance of £lO and one surety of £5 for his good behaviour for three months. NOT HIS BROTHER'S ICEEPER.—WHI. Knight, a labourer, of Chester, was brought up at Runcern Petty Sessions, on Monday' chargecl with having, on the 18th June, ' stolen a vest and a Silk handkerchief belonging to John Hornsby, a navvy, who resides in Pool-lane. The pri- soner was apprehended by the Chester police, and at a former hearing several witqesses swore to the identity of the prisoner, who, however', asserted that it must be his brother, who was "wanted." Superintendent lolling. worth had since ascertained that the prisoner and his brother were very much alike, and that the one who had committed the robbery had lost three fingers from one of his hands. The prisoner was not so' deformed, and he asked that he might be dischazded. The prisoner was accordingly discharged. IMPUDENT THEFT AT Rtrecorer.—At BURCOM Petty Sessions, on Monday, Thomas Jones, a labourer on the Ship Canal works, was charged with stealing a blue silk handkerchief and a ladies' jacket from the shop of Mr. William Craddock, pawnbroker, of Church-st. On Satur- day night, the 21st July. the prisoner went into Mr. Craddock's shop, and after examining some articles, left without making a purchase. Thehandkerchief was then missed. Half an hour afterwards Mr. Craddock's son saw the prisoner take a jacket from a bundiethat was hanging at the door, and heard him declare to some per- son in the street that he would go in and pawn it. The prisoner was wearing the stolen silk handkerchief at the time, and he was detained and given into custody. He was now sentenced to 21 days' hard labour.

VIOLENT ASSAULT ON A POLICEMAN AT WIDNES. John Wright, of 5. Gerrard-st.. was brought before Messrs. Gossage and Brock, at Widnes Pollee Court; on M•nday, charged with having'beendrunk and disorderly and further with having assaulted P.C. Worsfold whilst in the execution of his duties. On Friday night about eleven o'clock P.C. Worsfold apprehended the prisoner on a charge of being drunk and 'disorderly in conse- quence of the complaints of two females. The prisoner resisted the constable most violently, and butted him in the stomach with his head several times; and while they were struggling together he also bit the constable's fin- ger, inflicting a wound from which blood flowed freely. With the aid of Constables Gregory and Field the pri- sober wa's conveyed to the police station and locked up. The magistrates ordered the prisoner to pay a total sum of El 6s 8d or go to gaol for 21 days. THE Murat lica'r DID Iv.—A young man named Thos. Brett, whose home is at 88, Midwood-st.' was placed in the dock at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, to answer a charge of stealing a shawl from the person of Mary Black, a widow, who resides at 20, Elizabeth-st, It was alleged that on Saturdayrnight, while Mrs. Black was walking along Victoria-road in c.oinpany with a man nal-ned Gavin, the prisoner asked the man for a match. He was,informed that his wants could not be supplied, and he thereupon struck Gizvin twice with his fist and knocked him to the ground. He then used most obscene language to the woman, and seizing her by the throat, and pulled her shawl from her shoulders and placed it under his coat. The services of P.C. Evans were after- wards obtained, and the prisoner was compelled to re- turn the shawl to its owner.—Mr. Knowles uppeared on I the prisoner's behalf, and contended that he had no in- I tention of stealing the shawl, but having had some drink he meddled with affairs that did not concern him.—The Bench imposed a fine of 20s, or in default of payment, a fortnight's imprisonment. A HALTON PUBLICAN IMPRISONED IN HIS OWN HOI7SE. George Lambert, Thomas Stephen Jones, and Alfred Holmes, young men, were summoned to Runcorn Police Court to answer a charge of being quarrelsome and dis- orderly in the Village Inn, Halton, and refusing to quit when requested by Charles Whitfield. Holmes did not appear, and a warrant was granted for his apprehension. —The prosecutor stated that on Saturday, the 21st July, the defendants entered his house in a stn. of intoxica- tion, and he refused to serve them with tfie liquor they desired. The merlin, consequence made a great distw- bance and followed the landlord up and down the house. He went into the pantry and the defendants closed the door upon him, one shouting to his friends to go into the cellar and help themselves. He could not get out for some time, and when he did so the defendant • had de- camped, taking with them a board containing a list of the "old scores" owing to him. Several days after- wards the board, which had been broken, was found in a garden in the village.—Lambert and Jones, both of whom denied the charge, were each fined 10s, and costs 9s 6d, or in default, Dcdays' hard labour. BILLIARD MATCH AT WIDNES LIBERAL CLI7B.—A lsard match between six members of the Liberal Club and six members of the Social Club was played on the billiard table at the former club. Much interest was manifested in the match, the room being inconveniently crowded with visitors. Some good play was witnessed, but the Social Club showed themselves much more pro- ficient with the cue than their opponents. During the evening Mr. .1. Morrison, the president of the club, made his appearance, and gtve the visitors a hearty welcome. He expressed the hope that inch gatherings would be the means of drawing all good men and true closer to- gether. At the conclusion of the games a sociable hour was spent, and a pleasant evening concluded about 3.1.1 o'clock. Score : LIBERAL. RTIAL WATCH DEALERS AT WIIKES.—On Thursday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, before Messrs. G. Pilkington and H. Wade Deacon, a young man named Thomas W. Pres- cott, an employe of the Prescot Watch Company, who lives in Widnes, was charged with having caused a dis- turbance in the tent of an auctioneer named Greenwood, erected on Widnes Market Ground. Mr. Knowles ap- peared for the complainant, and Mr. J. 0. Swift for the defendant. It appears that the defendant went into the auctioneer's tent, and stated that a Waltham watch which‘the complainant was selling, and which he said was worth 50s, was not worth above 18s. After creating a disturbance the defendant left the tent. In cross- examination the complainant admitted that he told the public that the Waltham watches were knocking the Prescot watches out of the market, which was denied by the defendanb:—For the defence Mr. Swift denied that a breach oftle peace was committed by the defen- dant. The complainant was a cheap Jack,who professed to come to the town for the'benefit of the working-men, and if he said the Waltham watches were running the Prescot watches off the road, and that the watches which he was selling for 35s were better than those sold by the watchmakers in the town for 50s, he must expect to be contradicted.—The case was dismissed.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fort- nightly meeting of this authority was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday afternoon. Colonel Ashton pre- sided, and there were also present the Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. Aaron, Stokes, Brandreth, Weir, T. Lewis, W. H. Linaker (assistant clerk), J. Farrington (nuisance in- spector.)—The seal of the Board was affixed to a copy of bye-laws for the regulation of common lodging-houses. —The question as to obstruction of drainage in Robin- hood-lane, Helsby, was raised, and Mr. Bmndreth re- ported that he and others of a sub-committee had visited the place and found that, as-vet at all events, there was no nuisance injurious to health, and therefore it was more ba matter for the Highway Board than that autho- rity. The subject then dropped.—The Inspector repor- tea that a sewer at the bottom end of Halton village had been damaged by a traction engine. The damage was not great and he had given directions for the necessary repairs.—ln answer to an inquiry the inspector said the question as to who was to pay for the damage would be brought forward when the bill Was sent in.—The Chairman thought the authority would have to pay.— The Inspector said he understood that a good deal of damage was being done in different parts of the district by traction engines as some.of the weights carried were very heavy.—The matter then dropped.—Plans were ap- proved for hew house to be erected in Chapel-lane, Fr ,iod- sham for Mr. Thomas Howard, of Runcorn; of class- room to be added to the infant school, Overton; and of a wooden erection to be built by Mrs French on Frod- sham Marsh. The plans of seven cottages, proposed to be erected by Mr. Davies, at Frocisham, were considered but were referred back an account of sufficient road space not having been allowed. The inspector reported that he had inspected new shippons at Park Farm, Sut- ton. and found that all requirements had been complied with.—This was all the business.

THE REV. Devin OWEN JONES, of Birkenhead, second minister of the Mount Zion (Liverpool) Welsh Wesleyan Methodist Circuit, which includes Lacey-st. Chapel, Widnes, has accepted a cordial invitation to the Man- chester Welsh circuit. The Rev. Hugh Hughes, of Llan- dudno a powerful revivalist and temperance advo- cate, has been appointed as successor to Mr. Jones. PRESENTATION TO A CURATE AT WIDNES —At a meeting held in the National School, Widnes, on Thursday even- ing, Mr. H. A. Wharton, acting on behalf of the par- ishioners of Widnes, presented the Rev. J. R. Jones, 8.A., with a purse containing £l6 10s, in recognition of the services he had rendered duAng the two years he had acted as curate in Widnes. The reverend gentleman has accepted a curacy under the Rev. J. Wright Wil- liams, Vicar of Rainford. The meeting was presided over by the Rev., G. H. St. Patrick Garrett, B.D.

RUNCORN' GAS COMPANY.—The half veaz,ly meeting of the shareholders of this company was -held at the gas works yesterday. Major Hazlehurst occupied the chair, and there were present—Messrs. Thomas Handley, J.P., F. Rigby, J.P., J. Hindley, R. Forester, W. Whittaker, I and Dr. McDougall. The statement of accounts for the half-year was submitted and approved, and a dividend at the rate of 10 per cent, per annum was declared. Messrs. R. Forester and W. Whittaker were elected direc- tors, and it was resolved to inctesse the aggregate sala- ries of the seven directors from £lOO to £2OO a year. , Dr. McDougall, the only shareholder present, dissented from this course. Mr. Thomas Handley was re-electedl an auditor, and Mr. John Pritchard was elected to a I similar position in the place of Mr. J. 0. Jackson, re- signed. The salaries for these officials were increased, from £lO to £l5 each. __ .

AN ELOPEMENT FROM WlDNES.—Yesterday morning the Widnes magistrates were engaged inquiring into a domes- tic drama that took place on the previous day. Mary Lizdis and Frank Ucas, both of Polish Nationahty, were charged with stealing clothing and a variety of other. articles, the property of the husband of the female pri- soner. It appears that some time ago Mrs. Lizdis eloped from her home, but afterwards on promise of amend- ment she was again received into favour. A few weeks ago Ucas, who at present makes his home in Glasgow, came on a visit to Widnes, and became very friendly with Mrs. Lizdis. Matters reached a climax on Thursday, when Lizdis found that his wife had again deserted him, and had taken with her a box containing, a large quan- tity of materials. Information was at once conveyed to the police station, and P.C. Holbrook traced them to Liverpool, where Ucas and his paramour were about to embark for Glasgow. Both were taken into custody, but the woman gave a desperate resistance to Holbrook, and was with great difficulty secured and brought to Widnes. The prisoners were remandefl until Monday next.
