FUNERAL OF A FOREMAN AT WIDNES.—The remains ot Mr. Charles Jones, of Ch urch-st., Widnes, were interred at the burial ground attached to the, Parish Church, Widnes, on Sunday afternoon, in the presence of a very large assembly of persons, who had gathered to pay a last tribute to the memory of, the deceased Mr. Jones, who had attained the age of 59 years, bad been in ill-health for several years, died on Thursday, and left a widow and five chil-, dren to mourn his loss. For thirty years he had been in the employ of Messrs. Gossage and Son, soap manufacturers, during 17 years of the latter part of that time as a foreman, and he was respected not only amongst his fellow workmen, but also amongst the members of the Wesleyan body, with which he was identified. In the funeral procession were numerous fellow-workmen, co-religionists, and friends, wiz° preceded the ceffin, and following were a number of near relatives. Altogether there were about 170 Persons in the procession. , The coffin was carried to -Hartland Wesleyan Chapel, where the Rev. R. Buedon read the funeral service, and the favourite hymn of the deceased, "I'll praise my. Maker," was sung. Afterwards the mourners pro- ceeded to the Parish Church, where the Rev. R. Burdon conducted the burial service at the grave- side, and made a brief and sympathetic reference t,o the departed brother. LIBERAL FEDERATION.—The General Committee of the National Liberal Federation met in London on Wednesday, Sir Walter Foster presiding. It was resolved, on the motion of Mr. J. Ellis, M.P., se- conded by Mr. Charles Townsend (Bristol), and supported by Mr. J. Brunner, M.P., that a circular be issued to the federated associations reviewing the administration in Ireland. The course of the Opposition on the Charges and Allegations Bill was approved. • RATIONAL ASSO'CIATION OF JOURNALISTS: MEET- ING AT WAnnmarox —A. deputation, consisting of Mr. Mason (Messrs. Lee and Nightingale, Liver- pool) and Mr. Ramsden e' Chester Courant"), from the Liverpool district of the National Association of Journalists, visited Warrington on Saturday. and met the local pressmen at the Old Coffee House Hotel, Horsemarket-st. Mr. G. W. Murdock occu- pied the chair, and the deputation having explained the objeots of the association, it was decided that application be made to the Liverpool district to be admitted as a sub-district. Mr. S. Harrison was ap-

pointed hon. sec., pro. tem., and the names of eleven local press representatives were given in for mem- heroin') DROWNING FATALITY AT RUNCORN.—A sad boat accident occurred at Runcorn yesterday morning. Two brothers named Thomas and James Goode, whose fathez is a boatman residing in Back High- St., were on board the narrow boats A and B belon- ging to Mr. W. Hayes, and about half-past nine commenced to amuse themselves with a game of "tick." In their boisterous spirits they attempted to pass each other on the plank that ran along the centre of the boats, and both fell into the water of the Old Dock at Bottom Locks. James Goode was quickly rescued, but twenty minutes elapsed before Thomas Goode was brought to the surface, and be was then quite dead. The deceased was only eleven years of age. A NEw SEWAGE PROCESS: A RUNCORN INVEN- TOR.—For some months experiments have been proceeding at the Manchester Corporation Sewage Works in Water-st., with a view of converting the sewage into manure, by a new process. Mr. Chas. H. Harvey, of Manchester, and Mr. A. G. Haddock, F.I.C. Government lecturer on chemistry, are the inventors and patentees of a precipitant, which, when pnt into sway, completely deodorizes and purifies it, and Mr. IVhiley. superintendent of the Health Department, has afforded those gentlemen every facility to carry on their experiments. Suc- cessful results are obtained by a simple process, one affect being to collect and use the ammonia to advantage. Yesterday week, Alderman Francomb, Councillor Wright, and Mr. Longdin (borough sur- veyor) of Warrington, visited the yard in Water-st., and expressed their satisfaction at the results ob- tained. Persons interested in the subject, on com- municating with Mr. Harvey, will be allowed to witness the process. Mr. Haddock, who is a native of Runconi, held an important appointment at the works of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company until a recent date.

BELLE VIM GARDENS, MANCHESTER.—Messrs. Tennison, of Belle Vue, have prepared a splendid spectacle. This year the kland of Malta-is the stage. Numerous living men are the actors, and a memorable siege is the ambitious representation— the siege of Malta. How far success is, attained the tens of thousands who witness the grand dis- play testify nightly with their applause. By day the picture is quite a study, as it is a work' of art. The spectator might imagine that•3falta island was really before him. It is difficult to think that you are only looking on a picture, such is the realistic character of the work. The air is fragrant with the perfume of flowers. The conservatories are stocked with rare and beauteous exotics—flowers and fruit. The zoological collection, for which Belle Vue has long been famous, was never so com- plete as now, the collection having been largely increased for this season. The aviaries are replete with birds of variegated and beauteous plumage. who have as much freedom as is consistent with their safety. There is boating on an eight or nine acre lake, the deepest part of which is only four feet, so that if you happen to be "shipwrecked" it only means a "ducking." WIDNES CHEMICAL MANUFACTURERS AND THEIR RAW MATERIALS.—A largely attended meeting of the manufacturers of Widnes was held yesterday week, in Messrs. Gaskells Deacon, and Co's dining-room, to discuss a proposal which had been made by some amongst them—that they should combine for the purpose of .putting down a deep bore hole, with the object of ascertaining whether they could not discover at any distance up to 2,000 feet a supply of material, such as coal or salt, which would be of value to them in prosecuting their large and important industry. Nearly every firm in the town was represented, and as a first step it was resolved that a sum of money should be subscribed with which to meet the cost of obtain- ing the advice of geologists, mining engineers, or those best qualified to form an opinion upon the prospects of such boring, and a anwril committee consisting of Major Cross, and Messrs. F. H. Gos- sage, George Bolton, and E. W. Parnell, was formed to gather information, and to report to a subsequent meeting. The meeting was presided over by Mr. E. K. Muspratt, and vias unanimous in thinking that the above step should be taken, and hopeful, , from what has been done elsewhere, that hidden , treasures not impossible to reach might be.found to be beneath Widnes.

MUTH or MR. CECIL EGERTON. —IVE regret to announce the death of Cecil, • eldest son of the Hon. Tatton Egerton, M.P. The deceased, who had been staying at Folkestone for some time, died very suddenly on Monday. He was in hislBth

year. CaPisinta.P.—An Order in Council has been is- sued, prohjbiting burials "forthwith and entirely in the old part of the Wesleyan Burial Ground at Cadishead, in the township of Barton." Appeals against this order will be heard at Whitehall on the 13th of August. ANTI-VACCINATORS SIIMISIONRD.—At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, before Colonel McCorquc- dale, Messrs. T. J. Gillespie, R. Houghton, and A. C. McCorquodale, Wm. Grirashaw, of Earlestown, was summoned for neglecting to have his child vac- cinated. Mr. D. Garnett appeared on behalf of the defendant. Alfred Cooper, vaccination officer, stated that the magistrates had made an order for the defendant to have his child vaccinated, but the defendant had not complied therewith. He saw the defendant on the matter, and the defendant said he should not have it done.—The Chairman: What is the reason he did not vaccinate the child P—Mr. Cooper: His reason is that one of his children was taken bad after vaccination, and he objects to have another done.—ln reply to Mr. Garnett, witness said he saw Mr. Grimshaw at the offices of the Lon- don and North-Western Railway Co.'s works.—Mr. Garnett: Who gave you permission ?—The Chair- man: I don't think that has anything to do with, , the case.-2-Mr. Garnett urged that the vaccination' officer had not received written instructions in that case from the Guardians.—The Bench fined the de- fendant ss, including costs.--Joshua Richardson, • of Earlestown, for whom Mr. Garnett also appeared, was summoned for a similar offence.—Mr. Cooper stated that he had seen the defendant who said he would not have the child vaccinated.—Mr. Garnett produced medical certificates showing that the child was unfit for vaccination. and that it was a patient at the Manchester institution.—The- case was dismissed.

The 319Jermotts and 'the Connollys, of St. Helens, have been enjoying themselves; there has been quite a series of faction fights—a regular "spree." It 'has been a case of "Row, brothers, "sail on," my "bhoys," &id "paddle your own canoe."

There is a story going the rounds that an in- llabitant of Finland, who had Ted an ungodly life, has bequeathed all his landed property and posses- sions to the devil. It is to be hoped his Majesty will go and take possession of his estate—and stop there.

The people of St. Helens are not likely to be short of •either glass or water. They manufacture one; and have taken to pumping the other very vigorously. This week the foundation stone was laid of new engine-house and boiler-houses at their Kirkby pumping station. They are taking time by the forelock, and water by "main" force.

The Parnell Commission Bill was carried through the House of Commons between one and two o'clock on Friday morning by means of the closure. Last evening Mr. Smith intimated that he expected to take the third reading on Tuesday. The earliest day on which the adjournment for the holidays can take place is Monday week.

A London correspondent says :—"The 14th of August is now montioned as the probalile date of the adjournment. The Government cling to the hope that they may get up on the 11th, but, as usual, Ministers are too sanguine." We are not so sure about that. "The Twelfth" is a sacred day; the House and the Grouse usually rise together.,

The authors of the Greenways' Bank frauds met their deserts, at the Warwick Assizes, on Tuesday. Kelynge Greenway was sent to gaol, for twelve months, and the other brother, G. T. Greenway, was sentenced to five years' penal servitude. The punishment is great, but their grimes were great; and what misery they have caused amongst those who trusted them not wisely, but too well. I

Whilst a Haydock collier was enjoying himself in a boxing booth at Newton races, some one gave him what was called "a tip on`the jaw," while a friend of the " tipper " relieved the miner of his money. However, the collier was sharp enough to seize his man, and hold him till a constable came on the scene. "The straight tip" was given the thief on Wednesday morning; it was two months in gaol, with hard labour.

The Bands in Bank Park are patronised, but not supported, by the public. One evening the total .contribution on the ground amounted to 4d.; another night it was less still-2d! Would it kill anybedy if the Town Council were to vote something for the bands? It would be as legiti- mate as finding money for antiquarian research at Friars Green; and the outcome would certainly be as interesting.
, "Older and madder." The nuchess of Mont- rose; aged 70 years has just been married to her third husband—Mr. Marcus Milner, aged 24 years. But what a world of faults and ugliness

Lies hidden in five hundred pound's a year. Not that a Duchess is ever either faulty or ugly; but make it "five thousand,- and the youthful Marcus will dote on a lady old enough to be his great grandmother.

It is reported that the convict Jackson, who is lying under sentence of death in Strangeways Gaol spends a great deal of his time in reading the Bible and religious literature which is provided for him. Some time also he appears to spend in medi- tation, and it may be, the chaplaiii thinks, in peni- tence." All this, of course, sounds very well, but the public might with advantage be spared the de-. tails of the way in whkch murderers are supposed to blossom into saints; it is unwholesome—not to say demoralising.

It is stated that a German chemist, Professor I Baumann, has hit upon a sleep-giving substance, which is said to be absolutely efficacious. "It is the product of ethyhneroaptan combined with acetone.' It is said to be absolutely harmless, though the name does seem a fearsome thing. Sancho Panza blessed him that first invented sleep, and there are millions who will bless Baumann if he has really succeeded; for --sleep, it is a gentle thing, , Beloved from pole to pole.

Two Widnes pensioners were brought before Mr. Justice Stephen, on Tuesday. One was sentenced to ten months' imprisonment for robbery; and the other to ten months' imprisonment for a terrible assault on his wife. In each case, the sentence was without hard labour," and this was because

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

• _ SUNDAY EVENING CONCERTS AT RUNCORN.—MiII-brow Military Band gave the second codcert on Sunday even- ing, in Duke's Field. 'Unfortunately the weather was again unfavourable, but there was nevertheless a large assemblage of people, who appeared to thoroughly enjoy the music. The performance consisted of the "Halle- lujah Chorus," which was admirably played. . SELLING ADULTERATED LARD AT WIDNES,—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before Messrs. G. Pilking- ton and H. Wade Deacon, John Quin, grocer, Lacey-st., Widnes, was fined 20s and 21s costs for having sold a pound of adulterated lard to Inspector Keighley. Super- intendent Johnston said he sent the lard to the public analyst, who had reported that the sample contained 22 per cent, of foreign matter, to wit, a mixture of cotton- seed Oil and beef stearine. ACCIDENT TO MR. AARON, OF WESTON.—Mr. Edward Aaron. who was one of the principals in the rural fête at Weston, on Thursday met with an, accident in the course of the evening. He was descending from the field to the farm house by means of the stone steps provided, wheri he was suddenly seized with dizziness, and stumbled and fell to the ground. He alighted on his head, and was picked up in a fainting condition, suffering from an ugly wound on his forehead. Dr. McDoug,all's assistant was quickly on the scene, and stitched and dressed the wound, and the injured gentleman is progressing favour- ably under the care of Dr. Carruthers. ELLESMERE-ST. SUNDAY SeffooL, RUNCORN.—In connec- tion with the Methodist Free Church Sunday School, Runcorn, a special train departed for Sutton Weaver about half-past one on Saturday last, and conveyed about 150 scholars and friends to Sutton Weaver. Owing to the inclemency of the weather the children, were unable to extract much enjoyment from the "twat," but never- theless many games were carried on in a spacious out- building belonging to a farm. About five o'clock tea was provided and served by Messrs. Gandy, Minshull, I Clarke Halford, and Newall ; and Mesdames Clarke, Newalf, Gandy, and others. Messrs. Gandy and Halford had charge of the general arrangements. The return journey was accomplished by about eight o'clock. ST. LUKE'S SUNDAY SCHOOL, EttecemlN.—The children attending this school had their annual treat on Wednes- day. About nine o'clock in the morning about 250 scho- lars and friends embarked in a barge, kindly lent Ify Mr. Samuel Taylor, and had a pleasant sail up the Bridge- water canal to Kekewick, where, having disembarked, they proceeded to a field on Mr. Done's farm. With the exception of one shower the weather was fine, and the young people enjoyed themselves by playing the usual games and rambling into the surrounding country. Their comfort was attended to by the Rev. J. D. Thomas, Mr. J. J. Speakman (superintendent), Mr. Lacy (secretary), and the teachers. Buns and milk were provided in abundance. , The party arrived back at Runcorn about nine o'clock in the evening. BOWLERS AT HUNTS CROSS.—A main of bowls was played on the green attached to the Hunts Cross Hotel on Thursday afternoon. The main was conducted on the Waterloo principle, and there were 26 competitors at I is. each. The first and second prizes were divided be- tween Mr W. Hill, a Ditton, and Mr R. White, of Run- corn, while Mr W. J. Moreland, of Widnes, captured the third, and Mr G. Windsor, of Widnes, the fourth prizes. There were in addition nine other prizes. An old-stand- ing challenge for teas was also decided, Messrs Robert Wright, of Runcorn, and W. Hill, of Ditton, "crossed swords" with Messrs W. J. Moreland and J. Stone, of Widnes, in a four-handed game, and the latter pair won by 21 points to 17. There was a good company present, and the green was in excellent condition.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. BY " Anna.."
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. BY " Anna.."

That the general cry is—" All hail to summer." That the teetotal members of the Runcorn police force appear to be "catching it hot from ithe advo- cates who appear in court to defend offenders against the law. That it is hoped the day is far distant when it will be an axiom that a teetotal constable cannot do his duty to the bibulous portion of the commu- nity. That the Runcorn Bench evidently think a tee- totaller can tell when a man is "tight.' That it is whispered that the Runcorn Co-opera- tive Society, which also includes Widnes, will for this half-year only declare a dividend of 2s 6d in the X, the lowest dividend for very many years. That, if true, the poor committee-men will have a dreadful time of it at the annual meeting on Tues- day, and I can.even now almost hear the shrieks of execration that will rise :from the throats of the women shareholders, to whom " divi." is a duty. That thanks are due to Mr. Hankinson for again bringing the state of Waterloo Bridge before the notice of the Commissioners, although there is very little satisfaction to be got from those in authority. Surely arrangements could be made for carrying on the business of a committee during the absence of the chairman on his holidays. That the loan obtained for the purpose of improv- ing the Bridge will be all repaid with interest if the Commissioners do not quickly bestir them- selves.

That Mr. Smith intends to have Public Baths one , of the planks in the platform at the forthcoming election for Commissioners ; and that those who do not declare in favour of what is no doubt a popular requirement, will encounter strong op- position. _ _ _
That a public meeting to enable th 4 retiring members to give an account of their stewardship and declare their policy for the future, might be productive of good. ,
BURGLARY AT WIDNES.

At the Liverpool Assizes on Monday, before Mr. Justice Stephen. Anthony O'Brien (19) pleaded not guilty, and Mark O'Brien (24) pleaded guilty, to having on or about the 18th ult., at Widnes, bur- glarionsly broken and entered the dwelling-house of William Jones, aud stolen a watch and chain, .E 1 in gold, .£1 in silver and copper, and other property belonging to William cones and William Eustace Passey. Jones was the lessee of the Ship Inn, at which the other prosecutor, Passer, was a lodger. The prisoners, who are labourers, lived in the neigh- bourhood of the Ship Inn, and had been drinking there on the evening previous to the robbery. On examination of the premises after the robbery was discovered, a cap and vest belonging to the prisoner Anthony were found in the inn. The watch, chain.

, and money belonged to Passey, and the other pro- perty to Jones. Mark was called as a witness for his brother's defence, lie said that, meeting his brother Anthony at the door, he borrowed his cap, but the vest belonged to himself (Mark), and he committed the robbery himself, the other knowing nothing about it. He had, however, done it under the inspiratiort of too much drink. In cross-exam- ination he admitted having been twice previously convicted. The jury found Anthony guilty also, and the judge sent him to hard labour for four cal- endar months. The elder brother, in consideration of his previous convictions, was sent to hard labour for nine calendar months.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
'The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday. ,fr. T. S. Timmis presioled, and there were •present Major Wareing, Messis. H. Wade Deacon, J. B. Imison, and G. H. Danby (clerk). . . .

The District Education Committee reported that dur- ing Jun d (three 'weeks) there were 186 applications for payment of fees, and they were recommended to be paid in 167 cases. There were 160 persons summoned before the committee for contravention e the Education Act, and 54 persons were brought before the magistrates, and were convicted.—The minutes were apprcrved on the motion of Mr. Deacon. Mu. BOND'S SUCCESSOR.—On the recommendation of the School Management Committee, Mr. C. E. Barlow was appointed a member of the Board in place of the Rev. George Bond.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

The Finance Committee reported that accounts amounting to £1,217 15s 8d had been examined and were recommended for payment. The receipts for the month amounted to £llB4 9s 7d. It was recommended that the seal of the Board be affixed to the mortgage to secure the amount of the sixth loan from the Public Works Loan Board to the School Board for £4,000; and to the re- ceipt and order of the Loan Board's certificate from the same. Major Wareing moved the adoption of the minutes.—The Chairman alluded to the fact that the loan would be repaid in 30 years in half-yearly instal- ments of principal and interest at the rate of 3i per cent per annum. The Board had endeavoured to•have the period of re-payment extended to 50 years, and also to have the interest reduced, but their efforts had been of no avail. The minutes were passed.
A letter was read from the Bdtication Department, sanctioning the bye-laws of the Board with regard to the standard of exemption from attendance at school.

RELIGIOUS EDUCATION. The Education Department has also written asking for information as to the system of religious education adopted in Widnes Board Schools, and also what hymns were sung, if any. It was stated that this information was wanted in consequence of a resolution passed by the House of Lords.—There was no other business.

div.head: MYSTERIOUS AFFLICTION,
div.p: A MYSTERIOUS AFFLICTION,

In the autumn of 1885, Mr. Thomas S. Atkinson, of 95, Harcourt-st., Dublin, was seized with a mys- terious ailment, which made life a burden. Shoot- ing pains in the chest, singing in the head, and rushes of blood from one side of the head to the other, were some ot the symptoms of his complaint. He says: "The doctor prescribed for and advised me; I took his prescription and followed his advice, but got no better. The spasmodic attacks at night were very severe: and thinking it very likely that I would die in one of them I went into the Meath hospital the first week in March, but;their treatment failed utterly to relieve me, and in April I was dismissed from hospital as incurable. All this time I was suffering from what I now know was kidney clispase,but which in the hospital was not thought worth inquiring into. At this time I was in a very bad state, haying lost three stone, my legs felt cold, my feet swelled, great bladders formed under the eyes, and night and day I had to pass water every half-hour and was consumed with an extraordinary thirst. It was at this time I saw an advertisement of Warner's Sayz Cure.' and on reading it carefully I came to the conclusion that ' it described exactly the way I was affected. In Novem- ber I commenced the Sire Cure,' and I felt better after the first bottle, and after the second began to pull upl flesh at the rate of two pounds each week, and now, after taking some thirty odd bottles of the SAFE Cure,' lam quite well. I can sleep all night as soundly as I could fifty years ago. I have entirely lost the spasmodic attacks. lam now as healthy looking and active as any man of my age in the kingdom; and contrary to the advice of every medical man I consulted I have not taken one drop of stimulant since I commenced taking War- ner's SAPS Cure 'last Novkmber."

SERIOUS ASSAULT AT MAREET-GATE.—Thomas Chap- man, a labourer, residing in Starkey-st, was brought up in custody. charged with having assaulted P.S. Cheeney, at Market-gate, on the previous night. It appeared that prisoner was one of a number of corner-men who persisted in loitering about Market-gate. When the officer ordered him to move from one corner, he went and stood at another, and at last, after being Moved several times, he struck the officer a violent blow be- tween the eyes. Councillor Francomb : And there is a long listtagainst him since; (to the prisoner) : You have missed your vocation; you should have been a jailor, you are so fond of prison.—The Chief-,constable: He only came out yesterday. Duckett, Church- st.; John Carter, horse dealer, Frodsham Bridge; Ethel New Marsh, Halton; and Elizabeth Pover. ASSAM.% ON A BOlL—Sarah Shaw, a married woman, of Clifton, was summoned for assaulting Gabriel Bar- rett, 4 years of age, son of the lock tenter at Sutton.— The defendant did not deny having thrashed Use boy, but called a witness to prove that she had received great provocation through his rude conduct to her young daughter.—The summons was dismissed.

DRUME AND DISORDERLY.—John Dunbobin, of Sutton, and John Fleming, of Halton, were each fined 5s and costs for being drunk; Richard Reece was fined lOs and costs for being drunk and disorderly.—Ellen Brown went to gaol for 14 days in default of paying a fine of 103 and costs for using obscene language in Mason-st. on the 21st ult.—Catherine McCann, who made her 22nd appearance, was brought up to answer two charges of drunkenness. The constables said the woman was quite nude when apprehended, and behaved in a most beastly fashion.—She was sentenced to a month's hard labour.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. J. Brundrit.

DRUNKENNESS.—FeIix McCann was charged with being drunk on the 21st July, and in the Court-room, on Mon- day. As this was the prisoner's 28th appearance, he was sentenced to a month's hard labour—Edward Dubbins, a hawker, of Chester, was lined 10s and costs for having, on the 30th July, been drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart.

THE REGENT'S Piax MIIRDER.—At the Old Bailey, on Thursday, the trial of eight lads for the murder of Joseph Rumbolt, in Regent's Park, was resumed. Mr. Justice Hawkins ruled that there was no evidence against Graefe, Doolan, Gorier, Elvis, Renshaw, and Cole, and the jury consequently entered verdicts of not guilty against these prisoners. They will be sentenced for minor offences.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 4, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 4, 1888.
13CHOOL. FEES.

The School Fees Committee reported that fees had been allowed in 108 cases, 94 of which were old and 14 new cases.—On the motion of Mr. JOLLEY, seconded by Mr. GREENING, the minutes were passed. ,t,as

TILE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL. In answer to a question, the CrAnit referred to certain alterations in the Local Governmeht Bill which affected the Guardians. He said that the allowances which were to be made to Unions under the bill would now be in proportion to the sums hithetto paid by the Government to each Union as grants, thAt was to say Unions which had received £2,000 would receive in proportion to that £2,000, and Xnions which had only received £2OO would receive in proportion to-the £2OO. He could not say what effect that would have upon that Union, but he thought they had received a very good proportion of grants, as they had given much attention to those things which had brought grants. He did not think, however, that it would be of such advantage to the Union as the other arrangement would have been. The Local Govern= ment Bill was now not what it had been—it was the mere skeleton of What it formerly was, and it really I remained purely and simply a County Government Bill with certain financial arrangements attached to it. With regard to the boundary question he added that the Commission had not yet reported.—This was all the business.

div.head: SHIP CANAL WORKS,
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL WORKS,
AND HOW THEY WILL AFFECT WARRINGTON AND THE DISTRICT.
NO. 28.-OADISHEAD AND IRLAM.

Having followed the course of the canal to East- ham on the west, and to Irlam on the east, we may now fairly claim that we have more or less ade- quately fulfilled the intention, which we expressed in the first article of this series, of forecasting, as far as possible the changes to be made on the local sec- tions of the canal. It is true that beyond Irlam many great and important works are to be carried out—among others large and commodious docks in the neighbourhood of Manchester, new roads and opening bridges at Salford and Barton, locks at Barton, and numerous other considerable undertak- ings. But these, as we have said, do not come within the scope of these articles. .In concluding the series we may, howestr, briefly refer to some of the more important of the conditions and require- ments by which the rights of the local authorities in the neighbourhood of Cadishead and Irlam have been protected. For the protection of "the surveyors of highways of Cadishead," it is enacted that in the event of any works or operations of the Canal Company interfer- ing with or prejudicially affecting any sewers or in- tercourses belonging to or under the control of the surveyors or repairable by them, the company shall at their own expense restore and make good the sewers, watercourses, and roads to ihe reasonable satisfaction of the surveyors. One quay, or landing place, on the north side of the canal, at which the surveyors of highways of Cadishead shall be at lib- erty to embark and land free from wharfage rates, goods of all descriptions required for the sanitary purposes of the hamlet, and macadam in breakers, or broken-up cinders, slag, gravel, sand flags, kerbs, or other road material for the use only of the sur- veyors. In , connection with this it is provided that the surveyors shall not make any claim for compensation for the loss of any existing wharfage rights by reason of the execution of any of the canal works. It is further laid down that in the construction of the deviation line of the 1 Warrington and .Stockport Railway the company are not to close any portion of Moss-iane until they have constructed the new road referred to in last week's article. The "surveyors of ' highways for Irlam" are similarly protected. The quay or landing place mentioned above is to be at their ser- vice as well as at that of their neighbours at Cadis- head, and for a like purpose and under like condi- tions. In the portion of the act allotted to the "surveyors of highways '' of Lower Irlam it is also provided that in the deviating of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway the bridge for carrying the new pardon of the railway over Liverpool-road is to have a clear span of not less than thirty-six feet, measured on the square, and a headway of not less than. eighteen feet; and approaches of the same width as the bridge, and of gradients not steeper than one in thirty, these approaches to be eonstruc- ted to the reasonable satisfaction of' the surveyors. In case the making of the canal and its incidental works interfere with the sewers, watercourses, and roads of the' surveyors of highways of Higher Ir- lam " the Canal Company is here likewise under legal obligation to make good the injuries. For Higher Irlam a quay or landing place will be made some three or four miles further inland than that for the use of Cadishead and Lower Irlam. At it they will have the same privilege of landing, free from wharfage rates, materials required for the sani- tary and highway purposes of the district, and in consideration of this, will, like the others, forego any claim far compensation for the loss of any exis- ting wharfage rates. Somewhat to the west of this quay at Higher Irlam the Canal Company will, in addition, provide and maintaha a ferry across the canal suitable for the conveyance of vehicles, horses, and cattle, and they further undertake to at all times provide the necessary labour to work the ferry by night and by day, whenever required for the use of the public. The exact site of this ferry will be such as the sur- veyors of highways of Higher Irlam and the Flix- ton, Urmston, and South Barton Highway Board shall reasonably approve of, and the working of the ferry will be in accordance with bye-laws to be made and enforced in accordance with the provisions of the Ship Canal Act. Proper and convenient ap- proaches to the ferry are to be made and maintained by the company on both sides of the canal, of not less than thirty feet in width, measured on the square, and with gradients of not less than one in thirty. These approaches are to be so made that they will communicate with existing roads in as direct a manner as shall be reasonably practicable. At some point between the quays for the use of Lower Irlam and Higher Irlam respectively, an- othaLlanding place is to be prepared by the Canal Corn any for the benefit of the Flixton, Urmston, and South Barton Highway Board, and this Board is also protected with regard to interference with its sewers and roads. The clauses inserted in the Canal Act on behalf of the Flixton Highway Board contain provision for a ferry for vehicles, &c., at the same place as that already mentioned, so that the one ferry will doubtless meet the requirements of both Flixton and Higher Irlana, but in addition to this, the Flixton Highway Board, in conjunction with the surveyors for the hamlets of Foxsbill, Boysnope, and Salteye, has secured the provision that a ferry across the canal, suitabla for the con- veyance of foot passengers, shall be made by the Canal Company, within a short distance of the I ferry for vehicles. This passenger ferry, like that for vehicles, will be maintained by the Company, who will work it, whenever required, by night and by day, for the use of the public, free of all tolls and charges. For the protection of the Barton, Eccles, &c., Local Board, it is laid down that the Canal Company are not to alter, the levels of any of the roads of the district without the consent of the Local Board, and in the event of any sewers, &c., being interfered with, the Company ,is to make good the damage. With regard to the Rural Sanitary Authority; of Bar- ton-upon-Irwell, it is laid down -that if the Canal Company interfere with or prejudicially affect, any- thing in connection with the sew,age farm at nix- ton they are to pay to the Authority such pecuni- ary compensation as will enable them to provide land, machinery, &c., equally efficient for the pur- pose of dealing with, and disposing of sewage, and also such as will meet any additional cost of work- ing and maintaining the "substituted matters and things"; and further that the Company shall indem- nify the Rural Sanitary Authority against all claims, damages, &a.. which shall be imposed upon or incurred by them by reason of the execution of any of the works in connection with the canal.

div.head: MOORE AND ACTON GRANGE.
div.p: MOORE AND ACTON GRANGE.

On these sections, as. along the whole 'of the works, progress has been much impeded by the heavy rain of the last few weeks. Besides stopping work while it las- ted, the rain has collected along the bottom of the cut- ting so that much labour even on fine days has had to be expended in clearing out the water. A small pump has been erected near the end of Moss-lane, Moore, during the past week, and is rapidly clearing off the water in that part of the cutting. A little further down, in the , direction of Runcorn, a large and powerful pump, with ' a twenty inch cylinder, is in course of completion, and is fully expected to start work in about a fortnight's time, when the inflow of water will no doubt be counteracted, at least in that por- tion of the cutting. The navvies of the American type continue their work on fine days, and attempt to make up for time lost during the showers, not always, . however, uninterrupted by accidents. The other day a labourer was engaged in hauling a waggon under the bucket of the navvy at work near Moss Lane, when the wheelsman, not seeing that the man was in danger, , pulled the chain connected with the bottom of the bucket, and the whole load of earth' fell upon the unfor- tunate man, knocking him insensible, and bruising him severely. He declined, however, to be' put in hospital, and was therefore carried to his lodgings. He is now, thanks to his constitution, able to again work. Blasting operations are in tull force, only small quan- tities of rock being, however, loosehed at once. At Acton Grange, the, offices, &G., are almost numerous enough to make a small village, and the place altogether presents an idea ot the nucleus of an Austra- lian or American backwoods town. The large embank- ment for the deviation of the railway here is being rapidly proceeded with, and is now a long wall of earth that completely hides the horizon on that side. The number of visitors to the works has thinned considerably during the last few days, probably owing to the loose character of the soil, and the consequent large quantity of mud in thelv vicinity. WARBURTON. The buildings at Warburton are numerous and com- pact, and some considerably larger than on any other section. The smiths' shop contains six fires, and the church when completed will be a handsome structure. The interioris already complete and has sittings for up wards of 600 persons. There is an American organ played by a young lady in the neighbourhood, and a choir has been formed consisting of the employees, their sons and daughters. The Rev. Mr. Jenkins officiates, and thew are services on Sundays and Wednesdays.

There is also a Sunday school, at which the superinten- dent is the Rev. Mr. Jenkins.. The reverend gentlemanl visits his flock during the week, and delivers tracts, and also copies of the Testament free to those who like to avail themselves of the privilege. There are also the tea, coffee, and cocoa rooms, where 200 people can sit down at one time. There is also in connection with the room a bakery where baking 'is done at very low char- ges for the employees. The Liverpool British Work- man's Public House Company-, Limited, have charge of the building. , BARTON. The work on the section from Warbuton to Barton so far has not got beyond stripping the soil and niaking preparations for the erection and working of steam nav- vies. Offices, storerooms, and huts are being put up, and it is expected that in two or three weeks' time they will be inhabited and machinery got to work. The prin- cipal works here are the railway deviations' Nos. 4 and 5.; , the former will require a new embankment two, miles two furlongs nine chains, and the latter two miles three furlongs five chains. At present the rail- ways run almost about on a level with the present land where the canal crosses and they will be required to have a clear headway above the canal level of 75 feet. An alteration has recently been made in the staff. Mr. Mills, formerly with Messrs. Lucas and Aird, has taken tho place of Mr. Luke, who has gone to the works at Neston Point. The length of this section has now been definitely settled, and it extends from Warburton Bridge to Sticken's Cut.

div.head: MANCHESTER:
div.p: MANCHESTER:

Section eight, from Manchester to BartOn, apparently suffers more than the others through the recent heavy rains. Work is now going on on the whole length of i the section, and now the Ship Canal Bill No. 2 s prac- tically passed, a much greater number of men are expec- ted to be set to work on the site of the Manchester and Salford Docks than has hitleerto been the case. STORAGE OF EXPLOSIVES. At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Mr. Al- fred Thomas and Mr. C. Reynolds, Mr. W. E. Lea, of the firm of Messrs. Lea and Son' ironmongers, High-st., ap- plied for permission to erect a store for gunpowder and explosives near Bates Bridge, Halton. In answer to questions from the Bench, Mr. Lea stated that the firm had a store at Weston capable of holding 4,0001bs of ex- plosives, but this was not now sufficient, as thera was about 30011 as a day used at the Manchester Ship Canal Works. The proposed store was about 500 yards away from the works of Messrs. Wigg Brothers, and Steele, who were not aware of their intention to erect this store, nor was it necessary that they should as the building was beyond the stipulated distance.—Mr. Thomas said if the Bench sanctioned the erection of this store they would be almost bound to grant the license and that they did not feel inclined to do.—Mr. Lea said the store would be nearest to the Ship Canal Works, for whose con- venience it was desired to erect it.—The Bench decided to adjourn the application until Monday next, so that two Runcorn magistrates could consider the question. THE FIRST VFSSEL.

The first vessel, steam or otherwise, that has been built for service on the Manchester Ship Canal has been constructed for the use of the Company's Chief Engineer, Mr. E. Leader Williams, when making surveys of the works. It will, of course, until the water is in the Ship Canal, have to be used on the Old River Navigation and the Bridgewater Canal. The building of such a vessel has been rendered necessary owing to the long distance some parts of the canal works are from the nearest rail- way stations, and Mr. Williams's time is too valuable to be lost in unnecessary slow travelling, or in needlessl travelling backwards and forwards between his office and the works when making his surveys. To obviate this, the vesSel is fitted up with an office, containing lockers and drawers for plans, drawings, &e., and this room can be turned into a bedroom when necessary, so the Company will have their engineer virtually living and sleeping bn the works. In addition to its being most useful to the engineer, the Executive Committee will also find it convenient when making examinations of the progress of the works on the canal. The vessel is called the "Progress," and is what is technically termed a steam launch; its length overall is 70 feet, with 12 feet beam. The propelli9g power is supplied by one of Cochran's patent upright boilers, working at 1001bs. pressure. It is fitted with two pairs of engines (twin' screws), which combined, are 20 h.p. The diameters of the cylinders are 41,inch and 8i inch, with a 6 inch stroke, and its speed under favourable conditions is seven knots an hour. The engines, boiler, and galley are placed amidships, and there is stowage room for 21 tons of coal. The fore saloon, which is 17 feet by 10 feet, will be used as an office, andis fitted up withtables, lockers, and drawers. By a peculiar arrangement in the construction of the seats they can be utilised for beds when required. The aft saloon, which is 21 feet by 10 feet, is used as a dining room, and fourteen Persons can dine at once. It is fitted with tea and coffee silver ser- vices, and all the spoons, knives and forks, soup ladle, and cruet stand are of silver. The seats in this room also are so constructed as to admit of their being turned into beds when necessary. Each saloon is fitted with a hand- some chandelier. Further aft is a fresh-water tank, which will hold upwards of 400 gallons. The lavatory and w.c. are all placed aft. There is a small forecastle, used as a store room, wherein are the general stock of stores, lamps, oils, paints, ropes, chains, &c. The vessel carries a lifeboat, 13 feet by 4 feet 6 inches, and two life- buoys, also fog-horns, flags, and flag-staffs, and two an- chors. She also carries a gangway for facility of em- barkation. Her general design and build has been so arranged as to give her a very light draught, and she only draws 2 feet forward, and 2 feet 1 inch aft. Her crew consists of the following :—James Ward, Warring- ton, captain; Benjamin Rowbotham, Isle of Wight, engineer; Benjamin Lee, Winchester, steward ; John Monk, Warrington, boy. At present the "Progress" has no particular place to lay by, but we understand a dock will be eventually made for her at Pomona, Manchester. The "Progress" has been built, and her engines and boiler supplied by Messrs. Cochran and Co., Bidston Wharf, Birkenhead.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. The Rev. G. F. Roberts presided, and there were also present Messrs. Greening, Isherwood, W. Houghton, Jolley, J. Houghton, Eckerslev, Ratcliffe, Darby- shire, Clarke, Humphreys; J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), C. H. Ward (workhouse master), and Mines (superintendent of Padgate Schools). . THE RE-VACCINATION QUESTION. Among the cheques placed before the Board was one I for £9 16s 6d for Dr. Peacocke for having re-vaccinated 134 of the children at Padgate Schools.—Mr. DARBYSKIRE moved that the cheques be paid with the exception of this one, which be left over for a fortnight, as he wanted to get some farther information. The children, he said, were re-vaccinated on the recommendation of Dr. Peacocke, but the Board did not direct Dr. Peacocke to re-vaccinate though they certainly approved of his recommendation.—Alr.. GREENING proposed, and Mr. JOLLEY seconded, that all the cheques be passed.—Mr. CLARKE said he would second Mr. Darbyshire's proposal. He held it was illegal for the Board to pay such a bill. He thought he had authority for saying that the persons who had been re-vaccinated never applied to be re- Vaccinated, and by Act of Parliament that Board had no authority to pay for re-vaccination except in the case of applicants. According to Act of Parliament they might pay for applicants as low as 12 years of age, and, where there was immediate danger, 10 years of age, but they must be applicants. Another reason why he seconded that proposal was that it seemed to him a waste of money to pay for re-vaccination, and then to be told that there was no protection. The doctor had told them the previous day that the children were not ab- solutely protected, but that if smallpox made its appe,arance , among them, they would not have it quite as bad. He (Mr. Clarke) said that even that was only an assertion which it was impossible for the doctor or anyone else to prove.—The CAMBRIAN said it was not competentlor that Board to .go into the question as to the benefits or otherwise of vaccination. The matter came before them in this way; on the recommendation of their medical officer the Board made an order that certain children should be re-vacci- nated. That order had been carried out by the medical officer on the instruction of the Board, and now he had sent in his account for services rendered. Mr. Darby- shire was quite right in asking the Board—if the Board thought proper to concede the point—to allow a little more time to take the bill into consideration if he thought it was not of a satisfactory kind.—Mr. JOLLEY asked the clerk if the charge for re-vaccination was a legal on. He was quite satisfied that they gave the doctor instruc- tions, and as to Mr. Clarke's statement that the children were not applicants he presumed that the Board had authority to empower the doctor to re-vaccinate the children.—The CHAIRHAN said that as to the question of application, for re-vaccination that was a matter in which the initiation had been taken and must be taken by the Guardians who were in loco parentis to the chil- dren.—Mr. ISHERWOOD said he would support Mr. Dar- byshire's proposal, because when the subject first care before the Board it was asked .if re-vaccination woUld involve any extra charge, and the question was then laughed at, and it was said that it was not a monetary transaction at all.—The CLERK said he had a clear re- membrance of what took place at the meeting referred to by Mr. Isherwood. The question was put to him what Dr. Peacock would have for re-vaccination, and he replied is 6d a case, which was according to his agreement with the Board. He remembered that Mr. _Greening said that with him it was not a monetary transaction at all. But whatever influences might have operated upon the minds of Guardians at the time, there was now a clear claim to the payment of the money which they could not resist either morally or legally.— Mr. JOLLEY maintained that it,had not been a monetary transaction with Dr. Peacocke, but a performance of duty.—The proposals were then put to the 'meeting, five voting for Mr. Darbyshire's, and six for Mr. Greening's, which was accordingly agreed to.
GIFT OF PLOWERS. In the Workhouse Master's journal the thanks of the matron for gifts of flowers from St. Paul's and St. Paul's Mission were recorded. The number of inmates in the house was 322.

div.head: BRUTALITY TO 'A WIFE AT WIDNES.
div.p: BRUTALITY TO 'A WIFE AT WIDNES.

At the Liverpool Assizes, on Tuesday, James Dug- gan, 36, labourer, was indicted for having at Wid- nes, on the 26th May, unlawfully and maliciously wounded his wife, Julia Duggan, with intent to do her grievous bodily harm.—Mr. Cooper prosecuted, and Mr. Cottenham defended.—Counsel for the pro- secution stated that the prisonm and his wife had lived at 14, High-st., Widnes, for about six years. On the night of the date named they were drinking together at various public houses returning home at ten o'clock. There they quarrelled about one of the children, and, following his wife into the scullery, he struck her, caus- ing her to lose a quantity of blood. Subsequently in the bedroom the neighbours heard the quarrel continuing, and a noise as if someone was being butted against the wall. The prisoner beat and kicked his wife until she became unconscious, and she was found in that condi- ' don lying on the floor next inorning. The neighbours found that she had been pretty nearly kicked to death, and, in fact, her injuries came near proving fatal, for peritonitis set in, and for some time she lay at death's door, and her depositions had to be taken.—The prosecu- trix was called, but she gave her evidence very reluc- tantly. She said she was in drink by the time they ar- rived home on the night in question, and did not recol- lect what took place. She remembered falling in the kitchen, and she must have been struck. She was sure the prisoner did not use a knife in the bedroom. She attributed her illness to the fact that she lay on the floor all night naked, and close to an open fireplace. She told the judge that her husband was a pensioner, and would lose his pensibn if convicted. She begged his lordship to let her husband go home, as she and her family were starving, and said he had suffered enough already.—The medical evidence showed that the prosecutrix was in a horrible state when found by the neighbours next day. For five days her life was in danger. There was a clean cut wound, apparently inflicted by a knife, behind the head, and another wound near. The forehead was blackened with bruises, and other parts of the body bore evidence of very violent treatment.—Witnesses deposed to hearing the noises in the pFisoner'ts bedroom the greater part of the night.—The defence was that the injuries were caused by falling.—The jury found the prisoner guilty, and he was sentenced to ten month's imprison- ment, with hard labour. ROBBERY WITH VIOLENCE AT WIDNES.

\ At the Liverpool Assizes, on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Stephen, Peter Glevey (27), labourer, described as an Army pensioner, pleaded not guilty to having, at Widnes, on the 21st May, feloniously, robbed Thomas Lewis, and storm from his person a silver watch, value .£5 ss, and at the same time using personal violence. Mr. Cooper conducted the prosecution, and Mr.,Segar. siefended the prisoner. —Mr. Cooper stated that on the day in question the pro- secutor was in the Railway Inn, Widnes, along with other men who included Glevey. Prosecutor paid for drinks for them, and left at closing time. After leaving the Railway Inn considerably the worse for drink, he went down towards the river, but on the way was at- tacked by the prisoner, who loved him down and took his watch and chain from him. He ran away, but next day at St. Helens he produced the watch, which he got a friend to pledge for him. He afterwards went to the police station to prefer a charge against someone, and the police, who were on the outlook for him, took him into custody and found upon him the pawnticket relating to the watch. Prisoner's defence was that the prosecutor had given him the watch to pawn.—The Judge, in the course of his address to the jury, expressed regret that the law did not permit them to examine a prisoner on , his oath, and ho. hoped the time would soon come when they would be able to do so.—The jury found the prisoner guilty of robbery without violence, and the judge sent him to gaol without hard labour for ten calendar months. He explained that he passed sentence of im- prisonment without hard labour in order to save the pri. soner's pension of 6d a day, because he always felt sorry that it was the effect of a conviction for felony and a term of imprisonment with hard labour deprived a man of his pension. He had always thought this rather hard, because a peision obtained after service in the Army appeared to him to be given for past good conduct, and he did not see why subsequent bad conduct should de- prive a man of it. He believed that prisoner had given way to temptation, and he did not think it impossible that he might have had some notion of rough joking or some more or less drunken violence rather than deliberate robbery.

div.head: WOUNDING AT WIDNES.
div.p: WOUNDING AT WIDNES.

At the Liverpool Assizes on Thursday, before Mr. Justice Stephen, Timothy Mitchell, ,twenty-four years of age, labourer, pleaded not Aunty to having at Widnes, on the 7th ult, maliciously and felo- niously wounded Patrick Kelly, with intent to do him grievous bodily ham. Mr. Shand prosecuted, and Dr. Commins defended. It appeared that be- tween seven and eight o'clock on the evening named i the prosecutor was n Warrington-road, and heard the prisoner, whom he had not known before, re- turn an uncivil answer to someone who was asking for a certain number in Warrington-road. Prose- cutor, remonstrating with him, said he might at least have returned a civil answer to the question. The prisoner turned upon him and struck at him. They had a .struggle and fell to the ground together. While in that position prosecutor felt the prisoner biting a niece out of his under lip, and he called out' "lie's -biting my face off.' Someone pulled the prisoner off, ad another bystander handed the prosecutor the piece of the lip which the prisoner had spat out. He wed to a doctor, who stitched up the wound, but the piece was not restored. Prosecutor was forbidden to speak for three days, while the wound was healing. Prosecutor at the time was -almost sober, and the prisoner was almost drunk. The jury found 'a ver- dict of unlawful wounding. Dr. Commins, for the defence, represented the affair as the thoughtless act of a drunken man. The judge geminded the prisoner that he had previously suffered fifteen month's imprisonment for wounding. He was afraid that prisoner's drunkenness either made him very brutal, or let loose the ferocity of a dretuken man. The prisoner: I will promise not to take drink again. The Judge : Yes, but in order to give you no temptation for some time I will send you to hard labour for 12 calendar months.

CADBURY'S caution the public 'against adulterated Cocoas, sold as pure Cocoa, to which about 4 per cent. of Alkali and other agents are added, to give appa- rent strength to the liquor, by making it a dark &hour. This addition may be detected by the scent when a tin is freshly opened. No Cocoa can be stronger than Cadbury's, which is guaranteed absolutely pure.—Advt. \

BOATING AND BATHING ACCIDENTS.—Nine volunteers belonging to the Merthyr Vale detachment of the Vol- unteer Battalion of the Welsh Regiment, who are now encamped near Cardiff, went out for a row on Wednes- day evening in a small boat. By some unexplained ac- cident the boat was overturned, and six of the men were drowned. Their names are James, Potter, Colston, Webber, Cimmon-s, and Brown. All resided at Merthyr Vale. During a violent storm on Wednesday, a cutter engaged in the Medway Yacht Club race was capsized, and an occupanb (Mr. Taylor, of Whitstable), drowne d On Wednesday morning the Rev. W. Home, of Dreg- horn, Ayrshire, was swimming in the South Bay, to the south of the Spa, Scarborough, wherrhe was drowned.

Cheerless weather wel- comed the return fixture between the afore-mentioned clubs at Warrington on Saturday, and only a meagre number were present to witness the opening of the match. A slow drizzling rain commenced directly Kentfield, the new acquisition to the Lancashire county ranks, sent down the first over. The wicket was all in favour of the batsmen, and Tinsley played the bowling freely, whilst Crosfield was lucky to remain so long as he did. The last-named had to leave at 25, a smart catch at cover- paint dismissing him. Clarke joined the Warrington professional, and soon caused 50 to appear on the indi- cator. A splendid ball from Kentfield disturbed Tin- sley's bails; and after Clarke and Lawton had taken the total to 80, it wee decided to abkndon the match as a draw. Kentfield bowled three wides. Score :

NOTES BY THE WAY.

The weather has greatly interfered with cricket this week. .Tho rain interfered with the Surrey v. Austra- lian match on Tuesday, and it was in consequence post- poned. On Wednesday it was found that there was no possibility of finishing the match, and the game was therefore abandoned, the draw being greatly in favour of Surrey. When stumps were drawn on Tuesday the score stood--Surrey, 135; Australians, 52 and 33 for two wickets.

If we are favoured with anything approaching decent weather, and I lay particular emphasis on the "if," it Is the intention of J. H. Warren, the St. Helens long dis- tance champion, to see what he can do from Land's End to John O'Groat's upon his three-wheeler. Jemmy is certainly a rod stayer, and I know of no man who so thoroughly enjoys the distance fever, but it will take some moving to lower George Mills's five days and ten hours' record over the end to end course.—" Athletic News." Soon after play had been commenced in the return Igame betweeu Warrington and Rusholme, a slow, driz- zling rain made the cricket anything but pleasant. War- rington won the toss, and elected to bat. J. J. Crosfield and Tinsley were opposed by Kentfeld and Hammtt. The score rose rapidly, but at 28 Crosfield had to retire. Clarke made his appearance, and runs were piled on until a splendid ball from Kentfield lowered Tinsley's off wicket. Lawton came next, and the score was taken to 80, when it was deemed advisable to abandon play for the day, Clarke being 29 (not out), whilst Lawton was 12 (not out). The professional cyclists, F. Wood and Temple, con- tested a series of short distance races round the Ayle- stone track on Saturday. The ' distances were quarter, half-mile, and a mile, the winner of any two to take the stakes—£so. Results—Quarter-mile, Temple 1, Wood 2. Time, 40 1-ssec. Half-mile, Temple 1, Wood 2. Time, 33 2-ssec. Temple thus won. If the elements are fAvourable on Bank Holiday there is no doubt that the sports in connection with the War- rington Football Club will prove successful. The entries are large, and there will, it is anticipated, be sorhe well-contested events to be witnessed. In addition to local athletes, entries have been received from all parts of the country. It is stated that the club are to opa their season on the 15th of September by a match with Tyldesley, the present holders of the West Lancashire Cup. It is stated that the forthcoming season will witness some important changes in the composition of the North End team. N. J. Ross, the well-known full back, has obtained his release and signed for Everton, and his brother is expected to follow. Neither Robertson nor Thomson has been re-engaged. The team will doubtless be Trainer, Holmes, Howarth, Graham, Russell, Saun- ders, Gordon, Edwards, Goodall, Dewhurst,and Drum- mond.

div.head: FALLEN AMONG THIEVES AT _ _ EARLESTOWN.
div.p: FALLEN AMONG THIEVES AT _ _ EARLESTOWN.

At the Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Messrs. James Mars. on.and James Tinsley, Luke Tully, ellias Edward Higgins, a War- rington man, was brought up on remand from New- ton charged with having stolen from the person of Dominick Hevy, collier, 3s Gd, at Newton races, on 12th of July. The prosecutor said he met the pri- soner after the races at Newton, :aid was asked by prisoner to treat him to a.glass of beer. He did so, and afterwards accompanied him to a boxing lsooth ,in the Market Place. While there a man whom he lbad previously seen talking to the prisoner touched ' him on the cheek. .He turned round to see what was wanted, and Higgins immediately put his hand into his pocket and took the money out. Prosecu- tor " collared " him and demanded the money back. Higgins denied having taken it, and prosecutor called for a policeman and gave him in charge. P.C. Parker gave evidence to the effect that he was on duty at the races in plain clothes, and he there received the prisoner into custody. When he got him to the police station he searched him, and found 3s 6d in his pocket. He then formally charged him with having stolen the money from Dominick Ilevy, and prisoner replied "1 didn't\do it." Prisoner now pleaded guilty, but urged that he had been in prison on remand since the 12th ult. I Superintendent Weir stated that that was the pri- soner's own fault, as he gave a false name, refused to make any statement as to where he came from, and also refused to be photographed. Prisoner was sent to gaol for two months with hard labour. On hearing the sentence a wo.nan in the court began to weep loudly, and had to be removed. It transpired that the woman was the sister of the prisoner.

LORD ROSEBERY AT BOLTON.—There was agreat demon- stration of Liberals at Bolton on Saturday. Some thou- sands of the Liberals resident in the borough and in the adjoining county Parliamentary division of Westhough- ton met, and after walking in procession through the streets assembled in a great tent in afield adjoining the residence of Mr. Edward Cross. the Liberal candidate for the Westhoughton division. The Chairman delivered his opening address, and then called on Mr. J. W. Scott to move the first resolution. 11fij. G. Harwood rose to second the resolutiou, and was in the middle of a spirited harangue when suddenly, and without the least warning, the platform was seen to move for a few feet to the left of the chairman and then collapse. The occupants of the front benches clutched nervously at the arms of their chairs, and then tables, vases, palms, chairs, and people were mingled in a confused mass on the floor. Only a few, however, lost their equilibrium. Their rest sprang quickly from their seats and avoided anything like a fall. For a moment or two considerable consternation pre- I vailed, but on its being discovered that no one on the platform was hurt, the feeling of alarm gave place to one of amusement at the occurrence of such an awkward contretemps. The Earl of Rosebery was the chief speaker at the meeting. His speech was almost wholly directed to the Irish question. He pointed to a number of cir- cumstances which, he considered, are making for Home Rule, and expressed a strong conviction that thee' haras- sing and irritating" policy of persecution now being pursued in the sister country is doomed to failure. A resolution approving of Home Rule for Ireland and con- demnatory of the Irish policy of Her Majesty's present advisers was adopted unanimously.

The Oil for veterinary purposes is placed in yellow wrappers and is quite a different thin.. from the Oil in white wrappers. The former contains ingredients particularly adapted for use On animals, and is far superior to all other liniments and embrocations for veterinary purposes. The public are particularly cautioned to use. the Oil in yellow wrappers only for veterinary purpo,ses. The ,price of the Oil is within the reach of all, viz., two shillings and sixpence per bottle, of all dealers in veterinary medicines, or free by parcels post from the proprietors. We should most 'certainly say, from the enormous popularity which the Oil has attained, not only in this country but in every part of the civilised world, that no stable or kennel will be complete without St. Jacobs Oil in yellow wrappers. It is now used extensively and with wonderful success by the leading Job- Masters, Omnibus and Cab Companies of London and, provincial cities, in all cases where an outward application is indicated. The West-End Omnibus Company, of Auckland:New Zealand, of which Mr. S. Child is manager, writes to the Doily Herald of that city :—" We have much pleasure in bearing testimony to the efficacy of St. Jacobs Oil in yellow wrappers for veterinary purposes. Its success has been particularly marked in cases Of lame- ness in our stables. For man and beast, St. Jacobs Oil is .the greatest pain-cure ever discovered. It seems to possess properties peculiarly adapted for use on horses, and is undoubtedly the most useful and popular liniment in the world." The Trotting Editor of the "Spirit of the Times," New York, after an exhaustive interview with leading horsemen, stablemen, sportsmen, drivers, and breeders of horses, states, editorially, that " St. Jacobs Oil in yellow wrappers will do all that is claimed for it in the cure of sprains, stiffness, lameness, and suffering on man and beast."

_ .The popular veterinary surgeon of New York, Dr. William A. Soula, for nine years in charge of the Third Avenue Tramcar stables, certifies to the curative qualities of St. Jacobs Oil, as superior to all other remedies for ailments of horses, such as sprains, galls, and rheumatism ; that in many cases horses which have been condemned as useless, on account of injuries received, have been per- manently cured by treating such, injuries with St. Jacobs Oil in yellow wrappers without the aid of any other treatment. Perhaps there is no preparation in the world which enjoys the same degree of success and popularity as St. Jacobs Oil. Its sale far exceeds that of any other Proprietary Medicine, and exceeds by ten times that of all other liniments and embrocations combined. This wonderful success rests on the solid foundation of merit which St. Jacobs Oil possesses, combined with original, dignified, and systematic advertising, which has always characterised the announcements of the Proprietors. The name "St. Jacobs Oil" has become a household word in every civilised country in the world. The great success and popularity of the Oil has become the subject of comment by almost the entire Press of the country. In, many instances the leading articles of large and influential papers have been devoted to the details of what seemed to be almost magical cures effected by the use of St. Jacobs Oil in local cases, coming under the immediate attention of the publishers. St. Jacobs Oil is endorsed by statesmen, judges, the clergy, the medical profession, and people in every walk of life.

THE BRITISH WORKIN6r' MAN.

Sir,—ln reading the correspondence in your paper. I see there is one letter on the British workingman. I agree with the writer in refusing to give drink or any- thin, in the shape of it. It's getting time it was done with. But in charging the British workingman with be- ing idle, and skulking his time away to make his job last, I don't agree with him. It's like charging the House of Lords and Commons with being contemptible because some of them are so. I can assure your correspondent I have been in my present employ 33 years; have done my duty, and am not afraid of the books being opened when the time comes. I think "J. G" had better re- turn home and call at the police station to see if any of his countrymen have gone that way. If he had been born 80 or 90 years back, some of our Colonies would have been more congenial to him than Warrington, Yours ice., Earlestown, July 23rd, 1888.
ONE OVER SIXTY.

div.head: BOARD OF GUARDIANS AND PADGATE SCHOOLS.
div.p: THE BOARD OF GUARDIANS AND PADGATE SCHOOLS.

Sir,—lt seems, Mr. Editor, that there are more ways than one in which the ratepayers' money is wasted. We are only just cooling down with our indignation on the gas question, when other bubbles burst. ''Some two or three months ago Dr. Peacock recommended the Board of Guardians to have all the children re-vaccinated at

Padgate School. As a result, it was decided by the casting vote of the chairman that this should be done. All the children were compelled to be re-vaccinated, which was unlawful, for you cannot by law compel peo- ple to have their children vaccinated twice. But the Guardians had said it must be dd'ne, and it was given out that it should be done free of cost. Now what is the result ? On Tuesday last the committee of the Board met at Padgate School, and among other items there was one of £9 165 for vaccinating 134 children. After much discussion, it was decided to pay the bill by just one vote, and that was the vote of the chairman. This is how the ratepayers' money is wasted, for I will ask Dr. Peacock if he dare say that these children will not take smallpox if it comes in thoir midst ? Let the ratepayers open their eyes, and they will find many channels of extravagance, both in the Council Chamber and with the Board of Guardians. Remember the elec- tion time, and send men who will look after your in- terests, and not party jobbery. froping this will be an eye-opener, I am, yours respect- fully,
COMPULSION.

CLAY PITS NUISANCE. Sir,—May I solicit the aid of your valuable journal in directing the attention of the Sanitary Authorities of Warrington to a nuisance existing immediately behind houses Nos. 117, 119, 121, and 123, Orford-lane, namely, clay pits, which, owing to the recent rains. are now filled with water to such an extent as to be h. positive danger to the children of the locality, several instances having occurred which might have resulted in loss of life. In these pits, although within a few yards of the houses named, may generally be seen floating the car- casses of drowned animals; no less than eight, some of them unusually large ones, are at the present time in sight, whilst occasionally a drowned animal may be seen on the banks and sometimes on the road-way. Flock and chaff beds are at times emptied into the water,which may or may not have rested the weary limbs of some fever patient. In this filth, lads (strangers to the im- mediate neighbourhood) bathe, disturbing the carcases which are at the bottom, held down by stones, &c., breaking them loose so that they float on the top of the water, causing such a stench that windows and doors must be closed to keep it out of the houses. The pits are a positive nuisance which must be seen and smelled to be appreciated. And now, sir, to whom must we apply for the remedy ? I have spoken per- sonally to individual members of the Sanitary Committee and of the Town Council, who readily promised to look into the matter, but nothing has been done. . . . .

Learning that the land containing the nuisance be- longed to the Warrington Land and Loan Society, who ought to abate the nuisance, I spoke to the amiable chairman of the Board on the ground and pointed out the carcases floating in the water. He was disgusted at the sight, and candidly confessed to the nuisance, ad- mitting that the town authorities could oblige them to remove it if they would stir in the matter. , Trusting that someone will take this matter up wilt a determined spirit to have the nuisance abated, as it is of about four years standing,-1 remain, yours faithfully, HEART SICK.

div.head: NEW BAND STAND FOR THE PARK.
div.p: A NEW BAND STAND FOR THE PARK.

Si'r,—As I believe that you have been instrumental in gaining at least one subscription for a Warrington insti- tution, may I ask you to again use your influence in the causA of charity, and to draw attention to the condition of the band-stand in the park. The people of Warring- ton are now enjoying good music, free of charge, at least two or three nights per week. This, of course, cannot be done withcut a certain amount of gratuitous assist- ance on the part of the musicians; and I myself think that this assistance would be much more readily given, and much more easily solicited by the Band Committee, if the bandsmen could be provided with a more conve- nient, or, at all events, better repaired band-stand. The present one served very well for the very occasional per- formances that we used to have. Now, however, that it comes to be used three and four times a week, it is found sadly inconvenient. Nor is this all. I hear that it is not kept in proper repair, that the floor is broken and worn out, so that a too pre-occupied and zealous performer might easily slip, the consequences being a false note and an interlude of strong language. , I have heard it stated that a new stand would cost £2OO. If so, I should think the erection of such struc- tures must be a very profitable business, but I don't be- lieve that there would be £2OO worth of work and mate- rial in such a stand, for instance, asthere was in the Man- chester Exhibition last year, and I believe one could he erected at a much less cost. But it has been asked— " Where is the money to come from ?" Well, there are several sources from which it might come very agreeably and be most acceptable. In the first place, I believe it is the duty of the Town Council at any rate to keep the stand in proper repair, in which it certainly is not at present, and as regards a new one, a little of the money which is scattered about promiscuously here and there— say Um cost of a few deputations—might advantageously be spent in this way, and would be more agreeable to the majority of the ratepayers. If, however, the Council do not see their way to change the course of the money in the way mentioned, then if the Band Commit- tee and the public (who are the people interested) would make themselves heard in the matter, I venture to say that there would not be wanting in Warrington a bene- volently disposed individual with a fortune, who would make the inhabitants of this town his debtors to the ex- tent of a new stand.—l am, sir, yours, &c., PRO BONO PUBLICO.
