A youth named William Gaskell was on Wednesday, at Liverpool Assizes, sentenced to five years' penal servi- tude for having stabbed a man named George Knight, who combines the occupation of a smith with that of a professor of 'the noble art." The attack, which was quite unprovoked, was so serious in its results that the prosecutor's life was for some time in danger. NEW ISLE OF MAN MAIL SERVICE.—The Old Manx line have made a working arrangement with the Lon- don and North-Western Railway by which a daily ser- vice will run between Holyhead and Douglas in connec- tion with the mail train which leaves for this route— , Warrington (Bank Quay), Ist and 2nd class only, 11-32 , p.m.; Ist, 2nd, and 3rd class, 10-7 p.m.; and on Sun- days, Ist and 2nd class only, 11-32. The sea voyage will only occupy four hours, arriving at Douglas at 7 am., and leaving at 6-30 p.m, SERIOUS RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—The morning train from Perth ran off the rails at Kincraig early on Thurs- day morning. Three female passengers were seriously injured, and many more were shaken. The traffic was restored during the morning. The mishap was caused by the snapping of the coupling of a waggon, causing a Pullman car, first-class carriage, and a third-class car- riage to be thrown over the embankment, and rolled into a field 30ft. below. Miss Lucy Thomas, of Croxdale- road, London, was most severely injured; but Mrs. Cameron (Perth), Mr. Arthur Thick (Leicester), Miss Kelman' of London, and two others were also severely hurt. All except Miss Thomas proceeded on their Journey.
THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (Continued from page 6.) RUNCORN.

Work on this section is in a kind of transition state. Two of the powerful steam navvies are lying idle, wait- ing a commencement of the engineering operations in the river; and a start is not to be made in the river until arrangements are more fully matured. One steam navvy is, however, forging ahead in grand style, and has I lengthened the cutting to within a very few yards of Norman's pottery. At this point, it may be mentioned, that Mr. Greg,son, the agent, has designed a new bucket for the steam navvy, and Messrs. Rushton and Dunbar, the makers, have constructed a bucket according to his ideas. It has been put to a practical test, and has been found to answer all expectatations. In soft material the bucket carried away upwards of two tons at one scoop, and in harder ground it removed about two tons and a half. The ordinary bucket has only a capacity of about a ton and a half, so that the advantages possessed by the 11 one designed by Mr. Gregson are easily apparent. From Norman's pottery to the Old Mill a line of rails has been laid and it is proposed to carry this past the old Quay Docks to Runcorn Bridge, as the following letter addressed to Mr. Marshall. secretary to the Runcorn Im- provement Commissioners, will show :—" Manchester Ship Canal. Contractor's Office, August 2nd, 1888.— Dear sir,—lt is proposed to lay down a line of rails in connection with these works along the foreshore and cer- tain streets from the Old Quay Dock through Runcorn Bridge. This proposed line is shown red on the accom- panying plan. Will you please submit this to the authorities with a view to obtaining their sanction to the same.—Yours truly, C. A. F. GREGSON, agent."—This communication was laid before the Board of Commis- sioners at their meeting on Thursday, and it was referred for the consideration of the Parliamentary and Legal Committee. It was understood that the matter would be dealt with without delay.. This lint) is a necessary adjunct to the work in the river, and we learn the pile- driving will be commenced in the river at the Old Quay in a month's time, THEL WALL.

The scene at Thelwo-11-is—one of the busiest on the whole works. During the fine weather that has set in this week a palpable advance has been made, the work having previously been impeded to a great extent by the heavy downfall of rain. There is not much water in the cuttings and the excavators are now kept busily em- ployed all day. The cutting between Latchford. and Warburton now extends from Morris Brook yard to the river Mersey, at the point where the Bollin joins it. In this distance, about two miles, the river is crossed five times. The horse and steam barrow roads at Thelwall are viewed with interest, and the embankment where they are still working, is assuming very large propor- tions. Yesterday there were four steam navvies hard at work in the immediate vicinity of Thelwall, whilst one was ready to be set in use, and up the cutting in the direction of Lymm, others could be seen at work in the distance. The weather being fine yesterday, there were a number of visitors inspecting the operations. A Ger- man navvy has been added to the steam power on this section, for which it is admirably suited, the material re- quiring to be taken out being soft soil and sand. Near Statham Lodge a large brick shed is being erected, and the building of a number of lits has just been com- pleted. The German navvy mentioned has commenced at Lymm. . BIXTON.

The new German navvy which has been in course of erection on Rixton Ley during the last two months has now been got to work. This section, encompassed by the river, and the excavations to the whole depth of the canal are an open sand—in fact, were it not for the powerful pump at work in the middle of the island it would be quicksand.

div.head: RURAL FETE AT WESTON.
div.p: RURAL FETE AT WESTON.

A rural fete and sale of work was commenced at Weston on Thursday afternoon, in a field on the farm of Mr. Thomas Ford, with the object of raising if-Inds to wipe off a debt of .£l2O that now exists on the Church schools in the village. Fortunately, fine weather favoured the affair, which proved to be a pronounced success. The sale of work was held in a marquee, and the display of fancy and useful articles was most extensive. The "Weston' stall was in charge of Mrs. Ford, who was assisted by Mrs. Lighburn, Mrs. Barker, Mrs. Bell, Mrs. White, Mrs. Poole, and Miss Ford. The" Runcorn" stall was under the control of Mrs. Maitland Wood, who had for assistants Mrs. Joule, Mrs. Lake, Mrs. Chorlton. Miss Joynson, Miss Wood, Miss Smith, and Miss Imison. A tastefully arranged flower stall was attended to by Miss Isherwood and Miss Bankes. Over the entrance to this tent was a scroll bearing the words" Success to the Runcorn and Weston Alkali Trade," while over the entrance to the ladies retiring tent was " Success to the Sh ip Canal." One of the outb‘fildings of the farm had been converted into a most comfortable refresh- ment room, and the good things were dis- pensed by Mrs. Edward Aaron, Mrs. Aaron, junr., Mr. Thomas Kirkham, and Mrs. James Ford. In the grounds was a picturesque house where fruits and sweets were obtainable, and from which Miss Ida Maud Kirkham, attired in charming style as a flower girl, issued with button-holes for sale. The harelequin dolls of the Misses Broadhurst were in great request to tell the fortunes of the visitors. In the way of' outdoor amusements, there were shooting aalleries and swing-boats that had been hired by galleries Thomas Kirkham at his own cost, while he allowed the proceeds to go to the bazaar fund. There were also arrangements for various. kinds of sports, and there was a greasy pole to climb for those who coveted the copper kettle that rested safely on the top. The work of preparing the field and erecting the various tents, &c., had been admir- ably done by Messrs. T. Ford, J. Wesley Kirkham, T. Kirkham, and G. Bell, while much useful labour was done by Mr. and Mrs. Lightbum, Mrs. White, Mrs. T. Kirkham, Mrs. John Poole, &c. The general work of organisation was performed by the Rev. W. Bryant, 8.A.8.5.C. There was a capital attendance at the opening ceremony, which was performed by Mr. W. H. Verdin, J.P., and amongst those present to welcome hinr were the Revs. A. Maitland Wood (Vicar), J. J. Bryant (Vicar of Whitley), W. Bryant, J. H. Wilcockson, J. H. Steeley, and Jos. Holden; E. Aaron, L. Rosenberg, Captain Clarke, and the ladies and gentlemen previously named. The Vicar briefly introduced Mr. Verdin, who said it gave him great pleasure to be present that day to make the acquaintance of some that he did not know, and to renew his acquaintance with many that he had known for years. (Hear, hear.) With respect to the claims the Weston Schools had upon them, in the first place they were used in God's service on the Sabbath Day. That would appeal to the highest feelings of their natures. Then they were used on week-days for the education of the young; and he appealed to both rich and poor to co-operate to make these schools a success. Ile had been informed that at the last Government exami- nation 96 per cent, of the chihiren succeeded in pas- sing. This was a remarkable average, and was a credit both•to master and scholars, and he hoped that the usefulness of the school would be extended by their speedily wiping off the debt. (Applause.) At the conclusion of his speoch Mr. Verdin handed a bank note to the 'limn Mr. Thomas Ford moved, Mr. E. Aaron seconded, and _Captain ',Clarke suppor- ted a vote of thanks to Mr. Verdin for his presence and —Mr. Verdin briefly responded, and Captain clarke called for "three cheers for the future member of Northwich Division," which were given. The fete was bontinued yesterday afternoon and evening.

div.head: FASHIONABLE MARRIAGE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: FASHIONABLE MARRIAGE AT RUNCORN.

In the presence of a large congregation of towns- people, the marriage of Miss Emily Margaret Lea, eldest daughter of Mr. R. Lea, postmaster, to the Rev. John Jervis, curate of St. Peter's. with St. Mary's, Barnton-on-Humber, was celebrated at Runcorn Parish Church. The neighbourhood of the post office was gay with bunting, and on the tower of Holy Trinity Church, with which the bride- groom was formerly associated, a couple of flags fluttered in the breezes. The wedding was at the fashionable hour of half-past one, and the numer- ous wedding guests were conveyed to the church by four coaches, each drawn by a couple of grey horses snpplied by Messrs. Yarwood. As the bride went down the centre aisle, leaning on the arm of her father, Mr. Johnson sent forth a peal of joyous music from the organ. She was attired in a dress of ivory satin, with cascades of lace, and sprays of orange blossoms, her head being crowned with a wreath from which depended a long tulle veil. A diamond brooch, the gift of her father, adorned her throat, and she also wore a gold bracelet, the gift of the bridegroom, while she carried a beautiful bouquet. There were three bridesmaids in attend- ance, Miss Nora Lea, niece of the bride; Miss Nellie Jackes, niece of the bridegroom ; and Miss S. Annie Trickett. Miss Trickett was gowned in French grey silk, silk gauze, with gold embroidery, and wore a hat of grey tulle. She carried a nosy of crimson roses, the gift of the bridegroom. The other bridesmaids (children) wore frocks of cream Nun's veiling, with surah silk sashes, and hats of cream lace, each carrying a basket of crimson roses, the gift of the bridegroom. Mr. 11. W. Lea, of Bir- mingham, officiated as best man. The nuptial cere- mony was conducted by the Rev.A. Maitland Wood, M.A., the vicar, and afterwards, as the wedding party left the church. Mr: Johnson played the wed- ding march on the organ. At the entrance the happy couple were greeted with a shower of rice.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 4, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 4, 1888.

Luneheon, supplied by Mr. Gault. of Liverpool, was provided at the residence of the bride's father, and the guests included Mr. and Mrs. Lea, Mr. and Mrs. E. Lea, Mr. J. and Miss Lea, Mr. Edgar and Miss Nora Lea, Mr. H. W. Lea, Mr. and Mrs. Jarvis, Mrs. and Miss Nellie Jackes, Mrs Hemus, The Misses Trickett, Mr. J. H. Stakeld, Mr. and Mrs. Whittaker, Miss Hunt, London, the Rev. W. and Mrs. Preston, and the Rev. G. Fisher. During the atternoon the newly-married couple departed for the Isle of Wight, where they intend to spend the honeymoon. In the evening, Mr. Lea entertained the post office clerks and officials to dinner at Mr. Gorst's restaur- ant, High-st. About 2.4 persons sat down to an excellent repast, and after the cloth had been ' cleared Mr. Lee took the chair. The health of the bride and bridegroom was drunk with the usual honours. Mr. Gleave proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Lea for thegkindly feeling and generosity that had prompted Elia to let them have a share in the festivities of the occasion. Mr. Christie seconded the motion, which was carried with enthusiasm. Mr.'Lea responded, and said he was pleased if they had enjoyed themselves. A vote of thanks was also accorded to Mrs. Gorat for the excellent manner in which she had catered for her guests. The following is a list of the presents :—Silxer tea ser- vice, Mrs Lea, Runcorn ; bank notes and diamondbrooch, Mr. Lea; two cushions, Miss Lea, Sutton; silver cruet and Ottoman. Mr and Mrs W. E. RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. TIIESDAT.—Before His Honour Judge Ffoulkes. Tire Lost. SHOP Booxs.—Thomas Williamson, grocer, Church-st, sued Walter White, labourer, Queed-st., for £2 8s Id, being the value of groceries supplied.—Mr. Wynne Humphrey appeared for the defendant.—The de- fendant's wife was called, and produced the remains of a shop book which she alleged was the only one in her possession, the plaintiff having mislaid the other shop books whilst they were in his possession, for the purpose of being written up. She be- lieved that she only owed £l.—His Honour, after look- ing through Mr. Williamson's books, remarked that they appeared to be well kept, and gave judgment for the plaintiff for £2 5s sd, to be pald at the rate of 3s per month.

AN ENGINE TearisAarrore.—An action was brought by Messrs. Lea and Son, ironmongers, Church-st, to recover from Charles G. Sadler, of Croydon Grove, Croydon, the sum of £5 is Bd, being the difference in the price of an engine supplied to the defendant after crediting him with the price of the engine replaced.—Mr J. Burton represented the plaintiffs.—Mr W. E. Lea, a partner in the firm, put in a letter written by the defendant a month after the engine was supplied, stating he was well pleased with the machine, which was .perfectly satisfactory.—His Honour said under these circumstances he could not receive a complaint only made when the payment was demanded. He gave judgment for the plaintiffs, payment to be made within 14 days. I JOINER'S CLAIM.—Roger Crompton, joiner, of Clyde- st., Chorlton-on-Medlock, Manchester, sued Edward Page, of the Queen's Hotel, Runcorn, for £1 17s. 2d. for materials provided and work done. The defendant had paid 355. into court, an amouit he contended he had tendered the plaintiff, and also filed a counter claim for 31s. for board and lodgings.—Mr. Wynne Humplfrey was for the defendant.—The plaintiff gave evidence that the work consisted in making a bedroom into two rooms, and he had tendered a bill for £2 es. 2d., which he con- sidered reasonable. He allowed 12s. for hedging at ,the hotel, and sued for £1 17s. 2d. He denied that any money had been tendered him.—Mrs. Page gave evidence that the plaintiff undertook to do the work for 255. to 305., but she decided to give him an extra ss. for repair- ing some windows.—Rose Paul, a servant, and Mrs. Whitfield, a charwoman, corroborated.—His Honour gave judgment for defendant on both claim and counter claim. A BOWLING MATCH DISPUTE.—James Gornall, of 54, Hygiea-st., Liverpoel, brought an action against George Hayes, retired publican, Runcorn, now residing at Helsby, to recover the sum of £9, deposited with the de- fendant as stakeholder in a boxling match. There was a further summons against—Tonn Bebbington, landlord of the Bridge Inn, Ashbridge-st., to recover a deposit of £1 in regard to the same match, and it was decided that the verdict in the first case should settle the second case. A jury was empanelled to hear the case. Mr. Little, bar- rister (instructed by Mr. J. Burton) appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. A. Fletcher, of Northwich, was for Hayes.—Mr. Little stated that the match took place on Bebbington's green, on June 18th, and was between Gornall, the plaintiff, and Wm. Rhodes, of Runcorn, a joiner. The stakes were £lO aside. It was arranged that the green was to be in good order, but Gornall dis- covered that the grass had not been mown, and after playing half-time, as the defendant and several other persons would not allow him to have it mown, he an- nounced that he would not go on with the game, and asked for his money to be returned. The defen- dant refused, and Gornall gave notice that he wnpld sue Hayes for it. In cross-examination by Mr. Fletdher he denied that he was a professional bowler, but admitted that he had not worked at his trade as a collier for seven months. He was in Runcorn for four days before the match and played on the green. For the defence Mr. Fletcher centended that Gornall did not say a word about returning the money until after it had been paid over to Rhodes. It was most unfair for Gornall to want to mow the green when half the game was over. His Honour having summed up, the jury gave a verdict for the defendant, with costs.
PRESCOT BOARD OF _GUARDIANS. "

The fortnightly meeting was held at the Union Work- house, Wniston. on Thursday afternoon. Present—Mr. J. Kenwright (chairman), Rev. Dean Finegan, Messrs. W. Swift, E. Burehall, J. Ellison, Joseph Birehall, R. Twist, J. Buckley, T. Eatock, J. Griffiths, W. Tyrer, C. B. Johnson, J. Fisher, J. Leatherbarrow, T. F. Hill, R. A. Graves, J. W. Wareing, J. Ranson, J. Whalley. T. Musson, Stevens (Her Majesty's Inspector), and S. H. Hartley (clerk). RELIEF.—The Workhouse Master reported there were 479 inmates this week, 488 last week, and 434 in the cor- responding week last year. There had been 54 vagrants relieved, and the same number last year. VACCINATION.—The Clerk reported the receipt of a let- ter from the Local Government Board asking for infor- mation as to the children vaccinated in the district. The forms had been sent to the respective vaccination officers.
ANEW NIIRSV.—The Local Government Board wrote sanctioning the appointment of Miss Martha Jane Pro- bert, as nurse at the hospital, at a salary of £3O per an- num, with rations and other allowances. _

THE VACANCY AT FIUYTON.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board, dated 30th ult., intimat- ing that they bad issued orders for the election of a guardian for the township of Huyton-with-Roby, in the room of Mr. W. G. Ashton, deceased.

INCREASE OF SALARY.—The Local Government Board wrote assenting to the proposal of the Guardians to in- crease the salary of Mr. A. Pennington, relieving officer for Sutton, from £lOO to £l2O per annum. AN ASSISTANT OVERSEER'S BOND.—Mr. John Kitchen, assistant overseer for Parr and Sutton, wrote that he had sent a proposal for the amount of security insisted on by the Guardians, namely, £l,OOO, to the London Guarantee and Accident Co., and expected to hand them the bond early next week. I EMIGRATION OF PAUPER CHILDREN. Mr. Richard Dale, of Liverpool, wrote that the Catholic Children's Protection Society would be sending a party of children out to Canada on the 16th inst, and they would be glad to take a number of children from the Prescot Union if they wished to send them.—The Clerk suggested that the matter should be referred to the Visiting Committee. Tho Catholic body contemplated erecting a large school in the neighbourhood of Liverpool. for 'the accommodation and education of their own children, and he thought it would be better for the Guardians to keep the children in their own country. It would be impossible to have the children ready to send away at the time stated.—The Rev. Dean Finegan said it was a question of doing what was best for the children; and on his suggestion the Clerk promised to write to the Local Government Board on the subject. THE COUNTY PRECEPT.—The Clerk said he had received the county rate precept. The general rate was slightly increased, but taking the wholeof the several items, there wa a'a considerable decrease. EXTENSIVE ALTERATIONS TO THE WORKHOUSE—At a meeting of the Building Committee, on tne 30th July, the Clerk submitted a report from Mr. Gandy, architect, based on the remarks of Mr. Heft- ley, the Government Inspector.—lt was unani- mously resolved that the Boys' Home, as recommended, ,

be constructed, and that the Infectious Diseases Hospital be enla,rged as suggested. It was also moved that a new Board-room and necessary offices-be erected at the corner of the field belonging to the 'Guardians en the Warrington-road. nearest to the chapel, and that the ac- commodation which the present Board-room and offices would afford b 3 devoted for the old and infirm inmates. An amendment that the question of the erection of the new Board-room be postponed for six months received only 2 votes for, and 8 against. The motion was de- clared carried. It was al & decided that subject to the approval of the minutes, that Mr. Gandy be instructed to prepare draft plans.--Mr. Hill moved the confirma- tion of the minutes, and said that the whole subject of Government Inspector Henley's remarks had been re- ferred to the Building Committee , whose recommendations were as stated in the minutes. He urged the necessity for Proceeding with the matter without any unnecessary de- lay owing to the•great want of accommodation. He thought they would agree with him that appearances at present were strongly in favour of an increase rather than a decrease of the number ofinmates.—Mr. Leather- barrow seconded.—Mr. Johnson moved an amendment that the two first recommendations be adopted, and that With reference to the new boardroom be referred back. He said during the last 21years they had spent 410,000 and he was not in favour of still further increasing the rates. He thought the question of a new boardroom might remain over for the present. Mr. Warebag thought the Guardians should have further opportunity of considering the proposals which involved such a revo- tion in the establishment, and such a large expenditure of money.—The Rev. Dean Finegan was in favour of the amendment, which h€ seconded.—Mr. Stevens (Government Inspector) said the scheme ap- peared to have been well considered, and to comply very closely with what Mr. Henley seemed to think was re- quired.—For the amendment there voted the Rev. Dean Finegan, Messrs. Johnson, Twist, Musson, and E. Bir- chall, and there was a large majority against it.—The minutes were then passed in their entirety. This concluded the business.
DEATH AND BURIAL OF MR. ALGERNON C.
TALBOT. OF ASTON HALL.

- On Tuesday the remains of Mr. Algernon C. Talbot, the owner oT the Aston estates, were in- terred in the private burial ground. of the family at Aston. Mr. Talbot, who was only 29 years of age, had been in delicate health for some time past and having spent last winter in Cannes, was at the time of his death, on Friday of last week, residing at Bournemouth. He was the eldest son of the late Captain Charles Chetwynd Talbot, and succeeded to the Aston estates in 1869. The body, which was enclosed in thrtile coffins, was conveyed from Bourne- mouth by rail on Monday, and arrived at Halton Station at nine o'clock in the evening, where it was met by Mr. ICharles Aston Talbot. the youngest brother of the 'deceased ; Mr. Henry Linaker and Mr. C. E. Linaker, the agents of the estates ; the Rev. E. Marsden, vicar of I Aston; Mr. H. G. Linaker, and a number of the tenants and workmen on the estates. From Halton it was taken Ito Aston Church, where the opening sentences of the burial service were read by the vicar, the Rev. E. Mars- den. The interment took place on Tuesday afternoon in the presence of a large gathering of tenants and villagers. Every sign of respect to the deceased was manifested in the neighbourhood, the blinds of all the houses being drawn, and many evidences of the deep regret that was felt were to be noticed during the sad ceremony. The officiating clergYmen were Rev. E. Marsden, vicar of Aston; the Rev. Arthur Talbot, rector of Church Eaton, Staffordshire, uncle of th.‘ deceased ; and the Rev. H. B. Blogg, vicar of Frodsham. The service in the church was taken by the Revs. E. Marsden and H. B. Blogg. On the procession leaving the church for the graveyard, Mr. Tiley, the organist, played the Dead March in "Saul." On arriving at the grave side the coffin was lowered into the brick grave prepared to re- ceive it, which was draped with ferns and white roses. The service at the grave side was read by the Rev. Arthur Talbot. The simple, but expressive inscription on the plate " Alg,y," died 27th July, 1888, aged 29 years," twas chosen by the sorrowing widow. The bearers were tenants on the Aston Estates. A large number of beautiful wreaths and crosses were sent by relatives and friends undermentioned and others :—Mrs Talbot, widow of the deceased; Mr. C. Talbot, brother; Mrs Gramshawe and Mrs Jefferson, sisters; the Dowager Countess of Shrewsbury; the Rev. Arthur Talbot; Mr. Gerald F. Talbot ; Mrs Fenwick (Erbistock Hall) ; Mr. and Mrs F. Greenfield; Mr. W. C. ;Woodhouse (Lon- don) ; Mr. C. Gramshawe ; Rev. E. and Mrs Marsden; Mr. and Mrs Linaker, Mr. and Mrs C. E. Linaker, Mr. Thomas Rigby, Mr. and Mrs W. Wilkinson, Gardener and wife, Aston Hall, Mr. James Lowe, Mrs Buckle, Mr. Rough, Mr. Beam and family, Mrs Spender, and Miss Savage. Among the mourners present at the funeral were Mr C. A. Talbot (brother), Mr Jefferson (brother-in-law), Grimshaw (brother-in-law), Mr. Greenfield, sen. (father- in-law), Mr. Greenfield, (brother-in-law), Mr. R. Green- field (brother-in-law), Mr. A. Chetwvnd (cousin), Mr. H. Linaker (agent- to the estate), Mr. C. E. Linaker, Mr. Thomas Rigby (Sutton Mills), Mr. E. Wallington, &c. The underbearers were Messrs. W. Wilkinson, J. Camp- kin, W. Lowe, J. Bate, X. Astbury, P. Mounfield, J. Bellington, and W. Bean. The deceased, it should be added, was a very considerate landlord, and was deeply respected by all who came in contact with him. He leaves a widow and infant dau&ffiter. The estates, we understand, descend to deceased's younger brother, Mr. Herbert Talbot, who is at present in California.

Improvement Commissioners should pay to the city treasurer—in respect to the first visit paid to a ship by the medical offcer, £5 5s ; for each subsequent visit, £3 3s; for disinfection of a ship by the inspector, LI is;' the cost of disinfectants ; the sum charged for tug hire. If the sick persons. are removed to the hospital at Bromborough, the Commissioners should also pay the expense of removal and the chitrge for nursing, board, and medical attendance, a sum which cannot be deter- mined before hand as it would be greatly influenced by the character of the disease, and the occupation of the hospital, whether solely used for Runcorn cases or in con- junction with those belonging to Liverpool. All ships would be treated as if they were Liverpool ships, and no expense ' would be incurred beyond what was absolutely necessary. It is recommended that the foregoing conditions be ap- proved.—Mr. Lightburn said this was a case of Hobson's choice. The Board was compelled to make arrangements with Liverpool people, and these were the arrangements that could be made.—Mr. Meadowcroft argued that each case would cost £6O, and that the arrangements were annecessary,—Mr. Smith said Mr. Meadowcroft ,for- got that whatever money was spent could be recovered from the captain or the owners of the ship.—Mr. Light- burn quoted from a communication from the Local Government Board to show that' they were required to make these arrangements in justice and equity, the cost for each cholera infected ship would probably be not more than £l6.—The recommendations were adopted, Mr. Meadowcroft desiring' the secretary to record his vote against the motion.
THE ELECTION.

As the next Board meeting would occur on the day of election of Commissioners, it was decided to hold the next meeting on Wednesday, the sth September. The arrangements for the election on the 6th were left in the hands of the chairman.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting Of tile—B—oard was held at the Town Hall, on Thursday. Mr. W. Fisher pre- sided, and there were present—Messrs. Lake, Wis- wall, Lightburn, Timmins, Smith, Mellor, Hankin- son, Grice, Dobson, Speakman, Linaker (law clerk), Marshall (secretary), and Barker (surveyor).

div.head: CONORATUL- ATIONS TO MR: TIMM'INS.
div.p: CONORATUL- ATIONS TO MR: TIMM'INS.

The Chairman -s—aid---tbei,-the Board, would all agree with Mtn when he expressed his pleasure at seeing Mr. Timmins once more amongst them. (Hear, hear.) For the last few months Mr. Timmins had suffered from a most severe sickness, and many people were under the impression that they should not have him any more.—Mr. Timmins said he was grateful to the members for the kindness they had shown towards him. lie hoped he should be spared many years to be amongst them. The Medical Officer (Dr. McDougall) reported that dur- ing the past month the number of deaths registered was 20, of which four were inquest cases. These deaths showed an average death-rate of 13'18 per thousand per annum. Exclusive of the inquest cases the death-rate was 10.2 per I,ooo.—Mr. Dobson : Very satisfactory indeed.

HIGHWAY MATTERS. The Highways and Building Committee recommended: That the footway opposite Mr. Bate's two houses jn Greenway-road be paved, and that a crossing be con- structed at that place. That a footway be formed in Pool-lane. That the plan of Messrs. J. and W. Farrell for the erection of four houses in Waterloo-road be ap- proved.—Mr. Mellor moved, and Mr. Hankinson seconded, the adoption of the minutes, which were adopted.

div.head: ALL ABOUT AN OFFICE BOY.
div.p: ALL ABOUT AN OFFICE BOY.

" The Finance Committee reported that the receipts for the month amounted to £369 10s, and accounts amount- ing to £663 lOs had been passed for payment. Recom- mended, that the committee be empowered to engage a youth to act as messenger at the Town Hall, and that he be paid at the rate of 6s per week.—Mr. Grice moved, and Mr. Wiswall seconded, the adoption of the minutes. Mr. Grice remarked that it was necessary to have a boy in the office to go errands for the secretary and Mr. Barker. It would save the time of these officials and of the workmen who were now employed delivering notes, when they might be more advantageously em- ployed.—Mr. Speakman suggested that the committee consider as to the appointment of a man and his wife as caretaker of the Town Hall, the man in addition to act as messenger. He argued that this would effect a say- ing.—Mr. Li,ghtburn said that suggestion might be adopted at some future time 'but he would be no party to removing Mrs. Jackson, Who, with the aid of another woman, kept the offices and other rooms in a manner that reflected great credit upon her.—Mr. Meadowcroft supported Mr. Speakman's view, and the Chairmari spoke in favour of the proposal.—Mr. Smith said it surely did not need' all this quibbling and discussing to appoint an errand boy, who was quite necessary for the officials.—Some further discussion took place as to the duties and position of the boy, and upon the question as to who should control him.—lt was ultimately deci- ded that he should be under the orders of Mr. Marshall. The transaction of this business occupied half an hour.

HEALTH COMMITTEE. This committee recommended that notices be served on the owners of property in Salkeld-square to drain and pave the square to the satisfaction of the surveyor to the Commissioners. That notices be served on the owners of property in Back Mersey-st. to game a pro- perly constructed channel to be' made,in skich street. That the Inspector of Nuisances beprovidedwith uniform clothing, consisting of one cap, one coat, one vest, and two pairs of trousers, and that the tendqr of Mr. S. Coventity for furnishing the same, for the sum of five guineas, be accepteth—Mr. Lightburn and Mr. Smith seconded the adoption of the minutes. The latter gentleman remarked with regard to Mersey-st., &c., that he should like to urge upon the surveyor the necessity of taking up the setts in Mersey-st.' and making it clean, and thus show the inhabitants in that locality a good ex- ample. The street was in a very dirty condition.—Mr. Grice said it was in a disgraceful condition.—The Chair- man said it was made doubly worse through the night- soil contractor's carts that passed along that street being in a dilapidated condition. The minutes were then passed. RUNCORN SHIPS AND CHOLERA. The Health Committee's minutes also cpntained the following—With regard to the application made to the Liverpool Port Sanitary Authority to carry out the pro- visions of the cholera ' regulations on behalf of the Runcorn Urban Sanitary Authority, the Health Committee of the , Liverpool Corporation have submitted the following conditions for approval : (a) "That the arrangement be determinable by three months' notice on either side." (b) "That the Runcorn

div.head: INPROVEITE_NTS TO ENIOGEWATER CANAL.
div.p: INPROVEITE_NTS TO ENIOGEWATER CANAL.

A letter was read from Mr. W. H. Confer, manager to the Manchester Ship Canal (Bridgewater Undertak- ing) who stated that being desirous of improving the Bridgewater Canal at the Sprinch, Runcorn, a small portion of Caithness-st. would be required for that pur- pose, and as that street had been placed upon the books of the Commissioners, he applied for it to be removed therefrom. The portion of the street referred to was not used by any person other than the company and its tenants.—The letter was referred to the Parliamentary and Legal Committee.

div.head: WATERLOO BRIDGE.
div.p: WATERLOO BRIDGE.

Mr. Hankinson drew the attention of the Board to the dangerous condition of Waterloo Bridge. This was a matter that interested the public deeply, and he hoped the Chairman would do his utmost to get the committee appointed to do do something —The Chairman said there. had been a multiplicity of correspondence with the Ship Canal people on the subject, and something he hoped would soon be done. The chairman of the committee was away on his holidays, or the members would no doubt have been called together to coasider a letter re- cently received.—Mr. Smith thought they could have appointed another chairman and let the thing go on.— Mr. Speakman felt sure that the matter would be amic- ably arranged in a short time.
TRE_NIGHTSOIL CONTRACT.
The Board went into committee to consider a recom- mendation of the Health Committee that steps be taken to terminate the night soil contract in accordance with the terms of the agreement.
RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS„

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Dutton Workhouse. on Tuesday afternoon. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were also present Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. Aaron, T. Lewis, Brandreth, Speakman, Stokes, Mclntyre, Jones, Lightburn, Hall; W. H. Linaker (assistant clerk). Mr. Jones gave notice that,At the meeting on August 28th he would introduce a scheme for the more trades- manlike and better identification of the drapery and clothing samples, and which would simplify the duties of the master, minimise the labour, and save the time of the Guardians when tile question a these contracts is before the Board.—The Workhouse/Master reported that the Vicar of Runcorn had sent a large quantity of flowers for the inmates of the workhouse. The thanks of the Committee had been passed to the donor of the flowers.— Amqng the cases brought before the Board by Mr. Ward, relidvingefficer, at Runcorn, was that of a child aboht sixteen or eighteen months old, which he said had been placed in the yard of his house by two young women and left there. The child was now being provided for. —Mr. Aaron asked if anything had been done in regard to appointing a guardian for Frodsham, in place of Mr. Hadfield who had resigned, and the Chairman replied that they were waiting for the necassary order from the local Government Board.—The rest of the business was routinc

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

The Dean of Chichester was on Friday morning re- ported to be slowly sinking. Cnicurr.—At Hastings the Australians closed first in- nings for 168, the Englishmen being all out for 53. David Imrie, a steel worker, was run over and cut to pieces on Friday, on the North-Eastern Railway near Consett.

A youth aged 17, named Grant, was on Friday sen- tenced at the Old Bailey to live years' penal servitude for forgery, by which he obtained £2OO. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone left London on Friday morn- ing, driving to Berkhampstead, on a short visit to Lady Spencer Churchill, and will afterwards proceed to Hawardefi.
Samuel Bird, of Nailsworth, was firing a gun on Thurs,. day evecing to amuse his children, whea a charge struck a boy, aged three years, son of a neighbour, causing im- mediate death.

Amy Elizabeth Follies, 19, has obtained a verdict for 275‘ at the Birmingham assizes, against Matthew Henry Wilson, a jeweller's traveller, of London, for breach of promise of marriage. -:COMPENgATION FOR A RAILWAY ACCIDENT. At the Liverpool Assizes, on Friday, a stone merchant named Westwood, of Liverpool, sued the London and North- Western Railway Company for damages for personal in- juries. The jury awarded £450 damages. THE MURDER NEAR LISTOWEL.—Patrick Beiley, John M'Ellistrum, and Wm. Meara were arrested near Castle- island on Friday on suspicion of complicity in the murder of Foreham, near Listowel. They drove towards the scene of the murder, near which the two fast-named were absent some time from the car.

FRIGHTFUL EXPLOSION.—TVVO GIRLS KILLED. terrible explosion, resulting in‘ the loss of two lives, occurred at the Fireworks Factory of Mr. Cadwell, Wandsworth, yesterday. afternoon. Mr. Cadwell is a large manufacturer of the paper percussion caps, which are used for toy pistols. Three sheds, situated ,in the field at the side of Garrett-lane, are used for this purpose, and between one and two o'clock two sisters, named Eliza and Elizabeth Thornton, were having their dinner in the centre shed. They were joined by two other girls, Lucy Harwood and Rose Thornton, who ha 4 been home during the dinner hour. About five minutes to two a terrific explosion was heard. People who rushed to the spot were horrified to find that of the centre shed nothing. remained but a few charred embers, while that on its left was in flames. , The third shed was shattered and the contents utterly destroyed. The unfortunate sisters Thornton were found to be dead, the bodies, which were mangled almost beyond recognition, being .found some yards from the hut in which the explosion had occurred. The girls Harwood and Sawyer were also fearfully in- jured, and it was feared that there is little hope of their recovery. The dead bodies were taken at once to the Mortuary,-and the injured girls conveyed to the Wands- worth Infirmary, where every effort is being made to alleviate their sufferings. The origin of the disaster is unknown.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORD'S.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORD'S.
The House met at four o'clock.

MISCELLANBOUS.—The Marquis of SALISBURY, replying to Lord Napier of Magdala, said Her Majesty's Govern- ment could not press on Italy a mediation in respect of Abyssinia which had already failed.—Lord ELPHIN- STONE, replying to Lord Sidmouth, said it would be desirable to have first-class docks at Gibraltar. The Admiralty had considerel the question, but no complete scheme was before them.—On the motion of Lord Dun- raven, the 'reference to the Select Committee on the Sweating System was enitarged to include the whole of the United Kingdom.—The Libel Bill was read a third time.—Several other gills were advanced, and the House adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The Speaker took the chair at shortly after three o'clock.

QUESTIONS.—There was a small attendance of members when the House met, the majority of the questions on the paper being devoid of general interest.—The Horan SECRETARY informed Mr. Pickersgill that there was a bill in draft which would repeal the " whipping " provi- sions of the Act of George IV.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, in reply to Mr. Causton, stated that he was prepared to pdstpone the Van arid Wheel Tax Bill tol the autumn session.—The FIRST Lord of the TREASURY, re- plying to Mr. Dillw3rn, announced that the Tithes Bill would be postponed to the autumn session:—ln reply to further questions, Mr. W. H. SMITH gave a pledge that the House would not be called together for the autumn session during the month of October. SUPPLY.—PUBLIC MEETINGS, &C.—The House went into Committee of Supply.—Mr. JACKSON moved a vote of £7,712,000 on account for the civil service —Mr. C. Giudimi referred to the disturbances that had taken place in the Metropolis With regard to the holding of public meetings. He was of opinion that all unpleasant- ness might have beers avoided had a competent man been at the head of the police force, instead of a psalm- singing sanctimonious swash-buckler.—Mr. •McLAREN condemned the conduct of the Secretary to the Local Government Board in going to Rochester and speaking , in support of Colonel Hughes Hallett. He moved the reduction of his salary, but the CHAIRMAN informed him the proposal was out of order. It had not been, proved that Mr. Long went there in his official capacity.—The HOME SECRETARY insisted that Trafalgar-squareAvas an improper place for public meeting, and defended the ac- tion of Sir C. Warlen. SENTENCE prz A MAGISTRATE.—MT. JOHN MORLEY called attention to the case of Mr. Latchford, who had most unjustly been committed to prison for taking part in a riot.—Mr. A. BALFOUR justified the sentence on Mr. Latchford, who, as a justice of the peace ought not to have acted in the manner he had done.—!Mr. E. HAR- RINGTON and Mr. T. P. O'CoNNon insisted that the charge against Mr. Latchford had been exaggerated.—Mr. SHAW-LEFEVRE condemned the action of the Crimes Act as regards the Woodford prisoners.—A long discussion followed, in the course of which protests were entered by several Irish members against the assistance given by the Government in carrying out evictions, anti against the manner in which law and justice was administered In Ireland.—Mr.JoßN &us thought it a scandal that the committee was asked to vote nearly eight millions of money, after a few hours' discussion, for over 100 de- partments of the public service. f LEFT SITTING.]

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

SUDDEN DEATH.—On Saturday afternoon a sudden death took place in the Main-street, Frodsham, between two and three o'clock. The deceased man (Mr. Richard Roberts) was taking [a short walk when he fell to the ground, ,and before assistance could he ren- dered, he expired. It appears that Mr. Roberts was un- til lately a timekeeper in the employ of Messrs. 'P. Kirk- ham and Company, contractors, Runcorn, and resided in Frodsha,m. The certified cause of death was syn- cope. PAROCHIAL COMMITTEES. At the monthly of the Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship Parochial Committees held in the Town Hall, Frodsham, Mr. A: T/omas in the chair, Messrs. Linaker and Davies submitted plans and specifications for the erectijan of a villa residence in Fluin-lane, Frodsham, also for the extension of the In- fants' School, at Five Crosses, and for the erection of a wooden house on Frodsham Marsh, all of which being in accordance with the building bye laws were approved. Plans also were submitted for seven cottages propoised to be erected by Mr. Thos. Davies on a site situate off Marsh-lane, Frodsham. After some consideration, the plans were referred back for amendment.

POLICE NEWS.—At Eddisbury Petty Sessions on Mon- day the magistrates disposed of the following cases: A Trumpery Case: George Moss, a small farmer, of Helsby who was summoned by a boy named George Broster, whose parents live at Barrow, for unlawfully dismissing him, was ordered to pay the amount of wages claimed, £1 is, and the costs.—The bother arose through com- plainant toaching some cream. The Bench characterised the case as a trumpery one.—Mr. W. H. Churion, of Chester, prosecuted, and Mr. A. Fletcher, of Northwich, defended.— Unmuzzled Dogs: The following fines were inflicted on the persons whose names are subjoined for not having their dogs muzzled whilst at large :—George Jackson, costs (4s 6d) ; John Ellis, John Caldwell, Fred- erick Garner, and Elizabeth Wilson (is and 8s 6d costs.) A similar charge against John Davies was dismissed.— The cases which were all from Frodsham, were proved by P.C. cases, arid P.C. Pearson.—Assault; Joseph Allman, a Ship Canal labourer, was fined lOs and costs for assaulting William Dinielow; at Frodsham, on the 25th June.—lt appeared from complainant's evidence that, accompanied by two other men, he was walking along the road when the defendant met them, and snatching one of the other men ont of his way rushed at defendant, and "pitched into him." They had had words a few days previously. The blessed treaty of union' which Mr. Gladstone had prepared was law in the hearts of the Irish race, and to that union they .would be true till death. BRITISH WORKMAN'S ASSURANCE COMPANY, LIMITED, Established 1866. Incorporated under the Compenies Act, 1862. CHIEF OFFICES, BROAD-ST. CORNER, BIRMINGHAM. EXTRACTS FROM THE DIRECTORS' REPORT 1 for the yeir eading Apiil 30th, 1888. Notwithstanding tlee liberal terms and contlitions of the Company's Policies, and the heavy amount paid in claims, and for extension expenses (resulting in the largest increase of new business the Company has ever made in any one year), the Directors are pleased to state that after meeting all pay- ments and expenses, they have been able to carry forward a balance exceeding £15,000. Mr. James Sketchley, one of your Directors, retired in De- cember last for the purpose of travelling, when Mr. J. C. Fowke, who for upwards of twenty years had' been Solicitor to the Company, was requested by the Board to fill up the vacancy, which we are pleased to say he consented to do, and he has proved to be a very important addition to the director- ate. Mr. Powke is not a shareholder, but holds a Policy in the Company upon his own life for £l,OOO, and therefore may be looked upon as a more direct representative of the Policy holders. The total income of the Company for the year was £178,310 18s Bd, being an increase of £21,928 us 9d. The total amount of payments was £163,018 14s Id, leaving a balance upon the year's accounts of £15,292 4s 7d; making the total funds at the close of the year £96,302 19s Od. The amount paid in Claims during the year was £77,479, including £4,411 6s Surrender Claims. The total sum paid up to the 30th April, 1888, was £469,261 is 10d. The number of Assurants upon the Company's books on the 30th April, 1888, was 374,098, and their annual premium would be £198,420 18s 10d, shOvang a net increase of 39,070 Assurants, and £27,820 us 9d. in Premium Income. HENRY PORT, Managing Director, 1). A. BECKETT, Secretary. DISTRICT OFFICE: MARKET GATE CHAMBERS, WARRINGTON. S. GREEN, SUPERINTENDENT,
